query_text: The respondent imported life-saving equipment under Open General Licence (OGL) and claimed the benefit of Customs Notification No.of 1981, which allowed for exemption from customs duty. The goods were then taken to Kandla and sought to be exported to USSR. Whether the show cause notice issued by the appellant to the respondent beyond the period of one year of the import of the items in question is covered by the provisions of Section 28(1) proviso of the Customs Act, 1962 and, therefore, within time. The Customs Act, 1962
ratio: The court held that the goods could not have been validly exported as they had to be for use in India, and the penalty levied was upheld. The court also observed that the notification granting exemption from customs duty could not have been intended for making profit by selling them abroad.
ruling_text: The court ruled that the show cause notice issued by the appellant to the respondent was within time and covered by the provisions of Section 28(1) proviso of the Customs Act, 1962. The court upheld the penalty levied on the respondent for attempting to export life-saving equipment that had been imported under OGL and claimed the benefit of Customs Notification No.of 1981. The court also observed that the notification granting exemption from customs duty could not have been intended for making profit by selling them abroad.

query_text: The appellant applied for a post advertised by the Madras Public Service Commission, making certain false representations in his application. He was convicted for cheating the commission under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code. Whether the appellant committed the offence of cheating under section 415 of the Indian Penal Code by deceiving the Madras Public Service Commission and inducing it to recommend his appointment to the post of Civil Assistant Surgeon, Class II (Men) in the Madras Medical Service. Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The court held that the appellant had committed the offence of cheating by deceiving the Service Commission and inducing it to recommend his appointment to the post. However, the court also held that there was no likelihood of damage to the reputation of the Service Commission as the appellant had served efficiently and obtained good reports from his superiors during the period of his service.
ruling_text: The conviction of the appellant for the offence of cheating under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code was confirmed. The court found that the appellant had committed the offence of cheating by deceiving the Service Commission and inducing it to recommend his appointment to the post. However, the court also held that there was no likelihood of damage to the reputation of the Service Commission. The conviction of the appellant for the offence of cheating under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code was confirmed.

query_text: The case is about a dacoity committed in village Jafrapur at about 9 P.M. The inmates of the house raised alarm and a large crowd gathered at the gate. The dacoits opened fire and murdered three members of the family. The accused were of the neighborhood and admittedly inimical to the family of the deceased. The issues in the case are whether the accused were involved in the dacoity and murders, and whether they were rightly convicted and sentenced to death. The statute involved in the case is the Indian Penal Code, specifically sections 396, 302/149, 148, 395, and 324/149.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the prosecution did not establish the charges against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore they are entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt and should be acquitted.
ruling_text: The present court ruled in favor of the accused and acquitted them of all charges. The case highlights the importance of thorough investigation and evidence in criminal cases, and the need for the prosecution to establish the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The court's decision to acquit the accused due to lack of evidence underscores the principle that it is better to let a guilty person go free than to convict an innocent one.

query_text: The Punjab Government acquired certain lands under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. The acquired lands were valued by the Land Acquisition Officer at Rs.76,029.15 p. The respondent challenged the valuation and the matter was referred to the District Judge under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act. The District Judge enhanced the compensation payable to Rs.2,97,019.15 p. The Punjab Government and the Punjabi University wanted to file an appeal against that order. The judgment of the District Judge was delivered on October 31, 1970. The Punjabi University applied for copy of the decree and the judgment on November 18, 1970. The copies were made available on November 27, 1970. The last day for filing the appeal was Feb 8, 71. The appeal was actually filed on Feb. 10, 71. Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the application of the appellants in these appeals seeking condonation of the delay of two days in filing the appeal. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 18, Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
ratio: The court held that the delay in filing the appeal was due to the mistaken miscalculation made by Mr. Atma Ram, counsel for the Punjabi University. The court also held that mistake by a lawyer is a good ground for condoning the delay in filing the appeal.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court. The court in this case has ruled that mistake by a lawyer is a good ground for condoning the delay in filing the appeal. The court has also highlighted the importance of taking into account the circumstances of the case while considering whether the appellant has shown sufficient cause. The court has also emphasized on the fact that the party which was essentially interested in filing the appeal was the Punjabi University and it had to pay the compensation for the lands acquired. Therefore, there was nothing surprising if the Government had left the matters in the hands of the Punjabi University.

query_text: The Karnataka State Financial Corporation invited applications for recruitment to two posts of Manager (Finance and Accounts). The advertisement prescribed the requisite educational qualification and stipulated that the age and other qualifications were to be reckoned as of 31.7.1995. The appellant and respondents were applicants in response to the advertisement. The written test was conducted on 1.10.1995 and the viva vice was conducted on 25.11.1995. Whether the appellant was eligible for the post of Manager (Finance and Accounts) and whether the respondent No.4 was ineligible as on the date of employment. The Karnataka Financial Corporations Act, 1959 and the Karnataka Financial Corporations Rules, 1961.
ratio: The court held that the appellant was eligible for the post of Manager (Finance and Accounts) and respondent No.4 was ineligible as on the date of employment. The court also held that the judgment which operated on the date of selection was operative and not the review judgment inAshok Kumar Sharmas case No.II.
ruling_text: The court set aside the impugned judgments of the High Court and held that the appellant shall rank senior to respondent No.4 by treating his appointment to be with effect from the date of selection of respondent No.4. This shall be only for the purpose of fixing the seniority and continuity of service only not for entitlement to any salary or other financial benefits. The court's decision highlights the importance of adhering to the prescribed qualifications and eligibility criteria for employment and the significance of the doctrine of binding precedent in promoting certainty and consistency in judicial decisions. The court's decision also acknowledges the need to balance the interests of substantial justice and fairness to all parties involved.

query_text: The case is about a batch of writ petitions filed by private tour operators (PTOs) who were disqualified for grant of registration for the year 2016 for the Hajj pilgrimage. The petitioners were all eligible to be qualified as PTOs for the year 2015 for Hajj pilgrimage but in the process of draw of lots, they were not successful. The issue raised is whether the petitioners who were eligible to be qualified as PTOs for the year 2015 but were not successful in the draw of lots can be disqualified for grant of registration for the year 2016 for the Hajj pilgrimage. The policy presented on behalf of the Government was approved by the court with slight modifications and was annexed as Appendix-I to the order in Union of India v. Rafique Shaikh Bhikan (2013) SCC 699.
ratio: The court held that the petitioners were entitled to be allocated seats in the ensuing year without Qurrah if they remain qualified as PTOs. The court also held that the allocation of seats to qualified PTOs in each category will be done every year on the basis of the overall quota of seats specified in the Annual India-Saudi Arabia Haj Agreement and the number of qualified PTOs remaining in each category.
ruling_text: The court quashed the impugned letters of rejection and held that the petitioners are entitled to damages in public law for the loss accrued due to non-grant of registration for the Hajj of 2016. The court awarded an amount of Rs. 5 lakh per petitioner as compensation. The court's decision is a victory for the petitioners who were arbitrarily and illegally disqualified for grant of registration for the year 2016 for the Hajj pilgrimage. The court's ruling reaffirms the principles of public law and the need to compensate citizens for the violation of their fundamental rights. The court's decision also serves as a reminder to public authorities to act lawfully and to ensure that their actions do not violate the principles of natural justice.

query_text: The respondent, Sanjay Kumar Singh, a Naga tribal, applied for the post of History Lecturer in the vacancy reserved for Scheduled Tribes in the State of P. He passed the preliminary and main examination held in June July, 1996 and was called for interview. However, his selection was cancelled as the Naga tribe is not recognized as a Scheduled Tribe in the State of P. The respondent filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution with prayer to quash the order of the Public Service Commission and to direct the respondents to offer the appointment to him. Whether respondent can claim the benefit of reservation in public service in the State of P. as member of Scheduled Tribe though Naga is not specified to be Scheduled Tribe in that State. The P. Public Services (Reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other Backward Classes) Act, 1994, does not provide any particular definition of Scheduled Tribe. The term Scheduled Tribe can only be understood in accordance with the provisions of Article 342 read with the notifications issued thereunder as interpreted by this Court.
ratio: The Constitution Bench in Action Committee on Issue of Caste Certificate to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the State of Maharashtra Vs. Union of India (1994) SCC 244, interpreted Articles 341 and 342 and held that given caste or tribe can be Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe in relation to the State or Union Territory for which it is specified. The considerations for specifying particular caste or tribe or class for inclusion in the list of Scheduled Castes Scheduled Tribes or backward classes in given State would depend on the nature and extent of disadvantages and social hardships suffered by that caste, tribe or class in that State which may be totally non est in another State to which persons belonging thereto may migrate.
ruling_text: The High Court was of the view that there was no bar under any of the provisions to extend the benefit of reservation to Scheduled Tribe candidates of other States. However, the Supreme Court held that merely because given caste is specified in State as Scheduled Caste does not necessarily mean that if there be another caste bearing the same nomenclature in another State, the person belonging to the former would be entitled to the rights, privileges and benefits admissible to member of the Scheduled Caste of the latter State for the purposes of this Constitution. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court held that the respondent cannot claim the benefit of reservation in public service in the State of P. as member of Scheduled Tribe though Naga is not specified to be Scheduled Tribe in that State. The judgment reiterates the principle that the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes belonging to particular area of the country must be given protection so long as and to the extent they are entitled to, in order to become equals with others but those who go to other areas should ensure that they make way for the disadvantaged and disabled of that part of the community who suffer from disabilities in those areas.

query_text: The case is an appeal from a judgment of the Single Judge of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, which allowed a criminal revision petition filed by the fourth respondent against an order of the Additional Junior Civil Judge, Sattenapalli. The fourth respondent had filed a complaint against the appellant and his parents for offences under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code 1860 and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961. The appellant and his parents were charged for offences under Section 498A of the IPC along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. However, the Trial Court did not frame charges against the appellant under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC, despite an additional charge-sheet being filed by the investigating officer. The issues before the court are whether the Trial Court erred in not framing charges against the appellant under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC, and whether the High Court was correct in allowing the criminal revision petition and directing the Trial Court to frame charges under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC. The case is governed by the Indian Penal Code 1860 and the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973.
ratio: The court held that the Trial Court had erred in not framing charges against the appellant under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC, as there was sufficient material on record to support the charges. The High Court was correct in allowing the criminal revision petition and directing the Trial Court to frame charges under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decision of the High Court. The court held that the Trial Court had erred in not framing charges against the appellant under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC, and the High Court was correct in allowing the criminal revision petition and directing the Trial Court to frame charges under Sections 406 and 420 of the IPC. The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decision of the High Court.

query_text: The State of Bihar granted the exclusive privilege of manufacturing and supplying wholesale country liquor within specified local areas to more than one contractor in each zone. The dispute relates to the licence fee which is payable by each of the contractors within one zone. Whether the licence fee so calculated is for each zone and the grantees of exclusive privilege contractors in each zone have to pay this total licence fee in equal proportions. The Bihar Excise Act, 1915, Section 22, 29, 43(5)
ratio: The High Court has held that each of the licensees in one zone will have to pay the total licence fee in equal proportions.
ruling_text: The High Court's interpretation is correct and the petitioner no.1's interpretation is incorrect. The petitioner no.1, the State of Bihar, is required to collect the licence fee from each of the contractors in one zone in equal proportions.

query_text: The Tamil Nadu Government formed a government company, Tamil Nadu Dairy Development Corporation Limited (the Corporation) in 1972 to take over the entire business activity of the Diary Development Department of the State Government. The government transferred 296 posts along with the incumbents and 331 posts with incumbents to the Corporation with effect from July 1, 1972 and July 1, 1974, respectively. The employees were treated on deputation foreign service to the Corporation. The issue was whether the employees were entitled to the terminal benefits as provided in GO 378 or GO 1921. The Tamil Nadu Government issued GO 378 and GO 1921 to provide terminal benefits to the employees who opted to join the service of the Corporation or the Federation.
ratio: The court held that the employees were not entitled to the terminal benefits as provided in GO 378. However, they were entitled to the benefits as provided in GO 1921, except for the provisions regarding family pension and application of Future Liberalised Pension Rules.
ruling_text: The court upheld the provisions of GO 1921, except for the provisions regarding family pension and application of Future Liberalised Pension Rules. The court directed that the respondents shall be entitled to the benefit of family pension on the basis of prorata pension given to them. The court also held that the employees after their permanent absorption with the Federation shall be entitled to the benefit of the liberalised pension rules, if any, in future. The court upheld the provisions of GO 1921, except for the provisions regarding family pension and application of Future Liberalised Pension Rules. The court directed that the respondents shall be entitled to the benefit of family pension on the basis of prorata pension given to them. The court also held that the employees after their permanent absorption with the Federation shall be entitled to the benefit of the liberalised pension rules, if any, in future.

query_text: The case involves two criminal appeals arising from the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Criminal Appeal No.1031/87. The appellants were convicted under Section 302IPC for causing the death of K. Sivaramakrishnaiah based on the evidence of PWs.1, 2, and 3 and two dying declarations Ex.P.15 and Ex.P.13. The main issue is whether the appellants are guilty of causing the death of K. Sivaramakrishnaiah based on the evidence presented. The case is governed by the Indian Penal Code (IPC), specifically Section 302 which deals with murder.
ratio: The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellants mainly relying on the two dying declarations Ex.P.15 and Ex.P.13. The court held that the evidence of PWs.2 and 3, who were not related to the deceased, could be utilized for the purpose of corroboration.
ruling_text: The appeals are dismissed, and the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302IPC are upheld. The court found that the appellants were responsible for causing the death of K. Sivaramakrishnaiah based on the evidence presented, including the two dying declarations and the testimony of PWs.2 and 3. The court rejected the argument that the injuries caused were not sufficient to cause death.

query_text: The case involves a private complaint filed by the first respondent against two appellants for cheating and conspiracy. The complainant alleges that the appellants induced him to pay Rs.50,000 for purchasing shares of certain companies and promised to make him a Director. However, the appellants did not fulfill their promise, and the complainant did not receive any share certificates. The main issue is whether the appellants committed the offence of cheating and conspiracy under Sections 415, 420, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, Sections 415, 420, and 120B.
ratio: The court found that the complainant became the Director of the companies and continued in that position for two and a half years. The court also found that the complainant paid the amount of Rs.50,000 to a broker of the stock exchange and not directly to the company. The court held that the ingredients to make out an offence under Sections 415, 420, and 120B were not brought out for framing any charge against the appellants.
ruling_text: The court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and restored the order of the Magistrate, discharging the appellants. The court found that the appellants did not commit the offence of cheating and conspiracy under Sections 415, 420, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The court held that the complainant's evidence did not establish the ingredients required to make out an offence under the said sections. Therefore, the court restored the order of the Magistrate, discharging the appellants.

query_text: The case concerns the decision of the Departmental Selection Committee in reducing the qualifying marks for the post of Supervisor Instructor Class III, after the publication of result to facilitate the inclusion of candidates constituting horizontal reservation. The main issue is whether the decision of the Departmental Selection Committee to reduce the qualifying marks for the post of Supervisor Instructor Class III, after the publication of result, is valid. The case is governed by the provisions of the Constitution of India and the relevant rules and regulations governing the recruitment process.
ratio: The court held that the decision of the Departmental Selection Committee to reduce the qualifying marks for the post of Supervisor Instructor Class III, after the publication of result, is not valid as it is arbitrary and violates the principles of natural justice.
ruling_text: The court set aside the decision of the Departmental Selection Committee and directed the authorities to consider the claims of the candidates in accordance with the original qualifying marks. The court upheld the principles of natural justice and fairness in the recruitment process and emphasized the importance of following the rules and regulations governing the same. The decision reaffirms the importance of maintaining the integrity of the recruitment process and ensuring that it is free from arbitrariness and bias.

query_text: The Andhra University Act, 1926, prescribes the minimum qualification for entry into higher course of study. The Government prescribed an Entrance test for admission to medical colleges. Some candidates, who were unsuccessful, filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the test prescribed and the method of selection for admission. The issues were whether the Government had the power to prescribe the test, whether it affected the personal liberty of the candidates, and whether it encroached upon the power of Parliament under Entry of List I of the VII Schedule to the Constitution. The Andhra University Act, 1926, and the Constitution of India, 1950, were the relevant statutes.
ratio: The Court held that the Government had the power to prescribe the test as it was not against any law and prescribed the minimum number of marks at the qualifying examination for eligibility to the Entrance test. The test did not affect the personal liberty of the candidates as it was only an additional requirement for admission. The test did not encroach upon the power of Parliament under Entry of List I of the VII Schedule to the Constitution as it had no relation to a test prescribed by the Government or by a university for selection of number of students from out of a large number applying for admission to particular course of study.
ruling_text: The Court dismissed the writ petitions and upheld the validity of the Entrance test prescribed by the Government. The Court held that the Government had the power to prescribe the Entrance test for admission to medical colleges and it did not affect the personal liberty of the candidates or encroach upon the power of Parliament under Entry of List I of the VII Schedule to the Constitution.

query_text: The property described in the schedule to the lease deed Ex.A-1 was leased by respondent No.to deceased K. Subba Rao father of appellants Nos.to and respondent Nos.and and husband of respondent No.10.The lease deed dated February 26, 1944 was for term of six years.The lessee had to pay pattam of Rs.75/- for taking the usufruct and rent of Rs.100/- for the building.The lessee had to expend Rs.25/- out of the above amount for the repairs of the house and for maintenance of the compound every year.The balance of Rs.150/- was to be paid in monthly.instalments of Rs.12.50.The respondent alleged that the appellants had sublet separate portions of the building.Respondent No.1, therefore, filed petition, under Section 11(4)(1)(iii) of the kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control Act) Act of 1959 against the appellants and respondent Nos.to for ordering them to surrender possession of the buildings alone but the lease embraced the buildings and the paramba (compound) and that the petition to evict the evict the buildings alone on the strength of the lease is not maintainable. Whether the lease Ex.A-1 is composite lease in respect of the land and the building thereon or whether it contains two independent transactions, one in respect of the building in question and the other for the remaining properties and the trees. The kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control Act) Act of 1959 (Act of 1959)
ratio: The lease consists of two separate transactions, one for the building and the other for the trees. The rent of Rs.75/- per year is fixed for taking the usufruct from the trees and Rs.100/- per year as rent for the building. The building is also described in the schedule to the lease deed and is identifiable, apart from the compound in which the trees are located. There is, therefore, separate identity of the land and the buildings.
ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed. The court held that the lease is not composite and indivisible transaction for both the buildings and the paramba. It is two separate transactions, one for the building and the other for the trees. The appeal is dismissed.

query_text: The case involves a dispute over the sale of agricultural land in Andhra Pradesh, India. The respondent sold a portion of his land to the appellant in 1971, and later sold another portion to the appellant in 1972 through two separate agreements of sale. The respondent claimed that the sales were necessary to repay loans taken from the Andhra Bank. The appellant, however, argued that the sales were intended to defeat the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973. The main issue in this case is whether the sales of the agricultural land were intended to defeat the provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973. The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, is the statute at issue in this case. The Act sets a ceiling on the amount of agricultural land that an individual or family can own.
ratio: The court found that the sale in 1971 was not intended to defeat the provisions of the Act, as the respondent was under compelling necessity to sell the land to repay loans taken from the Andhra Bank. However, the court held that the lands covered under the two agreements of sale in 1972 shall be included in the holding of the purchaser as well as the owner, as agreement of sale does not divest the rights in the land.
ruling_text: The court ruled in favor of the appellant and held that the lands covered under the two agreements of sale in 1972 shall be included in the holding of the purchaser as well as the owner. This case highlights the importance of complying with the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, and the consequences of attempting to defeat its provisions. The court's decision reaffirms the principle that agreement of sale does not divest the rights in the land and the land covered under the agreement of sale shall be included in the holding of the purchaser as well as the owner.

query_text: The appellant, Infosys Technologies Limited, registered the trademark 'Infosys' in 1987 in classes 16, 9, and 7. The first respondent, Jupiter Infosys Limited, filed applications for rectification removal of the trademark from the register under Sections 46 and 56 of the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 (the 1958 Act). The IPAB allowed the applications and directed the removal of the trademark from the register. Whether the first respondent is a person aggrieved for the purposes of Sections 46 and 56 of the 1958 Act. Whether the IPAB erred in directing the removal of the trademark from the register under Section 46(1)(b) of the 1958 Act. The Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 and the Trade Marks Act, 1999.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that the first respondent was not a person aggrieved for the purposes of Sections 46 and 56 of the 1958 Act. The Court also held that the IPAB erred in directing the removal of the trademark from the register under Section 46(1)(b) of the 1958 Act without considering the proviso to that section.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court set aside the order of the IPAB and remanded the matter back to the IPAB for fresh consideration. The Supreme Court clarified the legal position regarding the requirement of a person to be aggrieved for the purposes of Sections 46 and 56 of the 1958 Act. The Court also emphasized the need for the IPAB to consider all relevant provisions of the statute while passing orders.

query_text: The appellant, M s. National Transport Company, is a transport undertaking without its transport. The appellant was the sole transporter by road of the cement manufactured by the Associated Cement Company at Sindri to different stockists at various places in Bihar and West Bengal. The assessee was not registered under section 4 of the Bihar Taxation on Passengers and Goods (Carried by Public Service Motor Vehicles) Act, 1961. Whether the appellant is liable to pay tax under the Bihar Taxation on Passengers and Goods (Carried by Public Service Motor Vehicles) Act, 1961 for engaging trucks for transporting cement from the factory to the stockists. The Bihar Taxation on Passengers and Goods (Carried by Public Service Motor Vehicles) Act, 1961 provides for the levy of tax on all passengers and goods carried by public service motor vehicles.
ratio: The court held that the appellant was in-charge of the trucks for the purpose of its business during the entire course of transportation of the cement from the factory to the various stockists and, as such, came within the definition of owner under section 2(d) of the Act.
ruling_text: The appeal was dismissed. The appellant was held liable to pay tax under the Bihar Taxation on Passengers and Goods (Carried by Public Service Motor Vehicles) Act, 1961 for engaging trucks for transporting cement from the factory to the stockists as it was in-charge of the trucks for the purpose of its business during the entire course of transportation of the cement.

query_text: The case is about an auction of arrack shops in the twin cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad for the excise year 1979-80. The auction was held in September 1979 and the shops were grouped into one lot, which was against the administrative instructions issued by the Excise Commissioner. The main issue in the case is whether the auctioning authority had the power to regroup the shops into one lot and whether the auction was conducted in accordance with the rules and administrative instructions. The Andhra Pradesh Excise Act, 1968, and the Andhra Pradesh Excise (Lease of Right to Sell Liquor in Retail) Rules, 1969, are the statutes relevant to the case.
ratio: The court held that the auctioning authority had no power to regroup the shops into one lot as it was against the administrative instructions issued by the Excise Commissioner. The court also held that the auction was not conducted in accordance with the rules and administrative instructions.
ruling_text: The court set aside the auction and directed the auctioning authority to conduct a fresh auction in accordance with the rules and administrative instructions. The case highlights the importance of following rules and administrative instructions in conducting auctions. It also emphasizes the need for transparency and fairness in the auction process to ensure that the rights of all parties are protected.

query_text: The case is about the murder of Rajeswaran by setting him on fire on the night of 21st July, 1994 at Palavilai village. The victim was admitted into the Government hospital, Nagercoil with burn injuries and he died in the hospital on 24.7.1994. The appellants and two others were also charged for attempting to murder PW1the brother of the deceased by stabbing him. The issues in this case are whether the appellants are guilty of the offences punishable under Section and Section read with 34IPC, Section 302, Section 324IPC and Section 302read withSection 34IPC. The statute involved in this case is the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the appellants cannot be found guilty of the offence underSection 302and that there is no scope to invokeSection 34IPC.
ruling_text: The appellants were convicted for the offence underSection 302with the aid ofSection 34IPC and the sentence of life imprisonment was confirmed. Their conviction and sentence underSection 324read withSection 34was also confirmed. The court found the appellants guilty of the offence underSection 302with the aid ofSection 34IPC and sentenced them to life imprisonment. They were also found guilty underSection 324read withSection 34IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for six months. query_text: The appellant was a tenant in a shop owned by the father of the respondent. After the father's death, the respondent and his sisters became the owners of the shop. The respondent filed an application for eviction of the appellant on the ground of bona fide personal requirement for running a wholesale business in Ayurvedic medicines. Whether an application for eviction on bona fide requirement of non-residential premises is maintainable under the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973. The Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973.
ratio: The provision of the Act allowing eviction on bona fide personal requirement of non-residential premises was declared unconstitutional by the Punjab Haryana High Court and this Court. However, the landlord is entitled to seek eviction of the tenant from the non-residential building.
ruling_text: The appeal is allowed, the impugned judgment of the High Court is set aside, and the original provisions of the Act which were operating before coming into force of the amendment are restored. The landlord can seek eviction of the tenant from the non-residential building on the ground that he requires it for his own use. The appellant's contentions were rejected by the court, and the respondent was allowed to evict the appellant from the shop on the ground of bona fide personal requirement for running a wholesale business in Ayurvedic medicines. The court upheld the decision in Harbilas Rai Bansal vs. State of Punjab Anr.(1996) SCC, which held such provision to be unconstitutional, and restored the original provisions of the Act which were operating before coming into force of the amendment. The landlord can seek eviction of the tenant from the non-residential building on the ground that he requires it for his own use.

query_text: The appellant, a firm, claimed preferential right under Section 11 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 to have mining lease in respect of an area advertised for regrant by the State of Mysore. The appellant made an application to the State of Mysore for renewal of the prospecting licence but the State Government did not renew the same. The appellant thereupon made an application for revision to the Central Government for the purpose of obtaining renewal of the prospecting licence but the revision application was not allowed. Whether the appellant had preferential right under Section 11 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 to have mining lease in respect of an area advertised for regrant by the State of Mysore and whether the respondent without properly applying its mind to the facts of the case turned down its application for revision without giving any reasons for the order passed. The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.
ratio: The court held that the order passed by the Central Government was not a speaking order as it gave no reasons for the rejection of the revision application and gave no indication as to why the appellant's claim to preferential rights under Section 11 was ignored. The court further held that a speaking order is necessary in the case of a decision under Rule 58 of the Mineral Concession Rules where the State Government has not given any reasons for rejecting the application of a party as such decision affects important rights of parties and if given in summary manner without hearing being allowed deprives a party of his right to know why the decision had gone against him.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Central Government. The court directed the Central Government to consider the appellant's application for revision afresh and to pass a speaking order giving reasons for its decision. The court emphasized the importance of passing a speaking order in the case of a decision under Rule 58 of the Mineral Concession Rules where the State Government has not given any reasons for rejecting the application of a party. The court held that such an order affects important rights of parties and if given in summary manner without hearing being allowed deprives a party of his right to know why the decision had gone against him. The court further held that in the absence of a speaking order, the court may have to examine the case de novo without anybody being the wiser for the review by the Central Government.

query_text: The testator, Bhim Sain Arora, married Saraswati after his first wife died. He made a will bequeathing his entire property to his wife, Saraswati. ratio: The court held that the will was executed by the testator with free will and mind, and there was no evidence of fraud, coercion, or undue influence. ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the grant of probate of the will in favor of the respondent. The court upheld the validity of the will, finding no evidence of undue influence, fraud, or coercion. The court emphasized the importance of proving undue influence, fraud, or coercion in cases where the propounder of the will has taken a prominent part in its execution. query_text: The petitioner, an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card holder, applied for a postgraduate medical seat through the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) and the Institute of National Importance Combined Entrance Test (INI-CET) for the year 2023. ratio: The court ruled that the petitioner, as an OCI card holder, is entitled to the same rights and privileges as Indian citizens in terms of education, including appearing for entrance examinations and seeking admission to professional courses. ruling_text: The court directed the respondent to consider the petitioner's candidature for the remaining counselling rounds for PG medical seats, including seats reserved for SC/ST/OBC and other categories, as well as specially earmarked seats for Bhutanese candidates, if they are unfilled. The court also clarified that this facility should be open to other candidates who hold OCI cards issued prior to 04.03.2021 and who can participate in the counselling based on their performance in the NEET test and their ranking. query_text: The case involves a dispute over the seniority list of casual labourers treated as temporary who were subsequently absorbed in temporary permanent cadre in the Indian Railways. The Indian Railway Establishment Manual, specifically Para 2511(a), is the statute at issue in this case.
ratio: The court held that the amended Para 2511(a) of the Manual would be applicable prospectively, and that the seniority list prepared by the Department in the year 2000 is not open to challenge after the list of 2001 is held to be correct.
ruling_text: The court ruled in favor of the Union of India, holding that the amended Para 2511(a) of the Manual would be applicable prospectively, and that the seniority list prepared by the Department in the year 2000 is not open to challenge after the list of 2001 is held to be correct. The court's decision in this case clarifies the method of calculating seniority for casual labourers treated as temporary who were subsequently absorbed in temporary permanent cadre in the Indian Railways. The court held that the amended Para 2511(a) of the Manual would be applicable prospectively, and that the seniority list prepared by the Department in the year 2000 is not open to challenge after the list of 2001 is held to be correct. This decision provides clarity and certainty for both the employees and the employer regarding the calculation of seniority in the Indian Railways.

query_text: The case is about a murder of a woman named Dulli, who was the mother of PW-1, Radhey Lal. ruling_text: The court set aside the conviction and sentence of the accused and quashed the judgment and order of the Additional Sessions court and the High Court. query_text: The respondents, members of the United Basel Mission Church (UBMC) of South Kanara and Coorg, instituted a suit in the Court of Munsif, Mangalore, praying for a declaration that the resolution dated May 9, 1961, passed in the extraordinary meeting of the District Church Council of UBMC of South Kanara and Coorg, proposing the merger of UBMC of South Kanara and Coorg with the Church of South India (C.S.I.), was void, illegal and ultra vires the provisions of Religious Societies Act, 1880. ratio: The court held that the suit was maintainable, but the respondents were not entitled to file the suit in a representative character. The court also held that there was no fundamental difference between UBMC and CSI, and the impugned resolution was legal and valid.

query_text: The case involves multiple accused persons who were convicted under the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (TADA Act) for their involvement in a conspiracy to commit murder. query_text: The appellant, State Government, issued notices under Section 4(1) and declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act on 1.6.1982 and 17.8.1983 respectively to acquire certain lands. Subsequently, an award was passed by the Land Acquisition Officer on 25.3.1985. The respondents challenged the award contending that the award was not in conformity with Section 11 of the Act inasmuch as the award has determined the compensation for the land only and the amount of compensation regarding the superstructure and trees that were standing on such lands was left to be decided separately. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894
ratio: The award made by the Land Acquisition Officer was complete with respect of the land. It was therein that for the structures and trees the award will be announced separately, because the assessment for the structures and trees standing thereon had not been received from the respective departments.
ruling_text: The High Court has accepted the contention advanced on behalf of the respondents herein (petitioners before the High Court) and held as follows The Land Acquisition Collector made the award on March 25, 1985 relating to the land and not for the super-structures and trees standing thereon. The award rendered by the Land Acquisition Collector was not the one envisaged under Section 11 of the Act. The same envisages the award for the Unit, namely, the land, buildings and super-structure and standing crops and trees thereon. The acquisition proceedings would lapse in so far as the award relates to that portion of the acquired land on which the super-structures and trees were standing on the date the award has been made. The appellant herein (respondent before the High Court) in its written statement took stand in the following terms The award is complete with respect of the land. It was therein that for the structures and trees the award will be announced separately, because the assessment for the structures and trees standing thereon had not been received from the respective departments. However, the High Court has accepted the contention advanced on behalf of the respondents herein (petitioners before the High Court) and held as follows The Land Acquisition Collector made the award on March 25, 1985 relating to the land and not for the super-structures and trees standing thereon. The award rendered by the Land Acquisition Collector was not the one envisaged under Section 11 of the Act. The same envisages the award for the Unit, namely, the land, buildings and super-structure and standing crops and trees thereon. The acquisition proceedings would lapse in so far as the award relates to that portion of the acquired land on which the super-structures and trees were standing on the date the award has been made. Aggrieved by the above orders of the High Court the present appeals are filed. An identical issue came up before this Court in Mohanji Another vs. State of P. Others wherein it was held that the award made by the Land Acquisition Officer was complete with respect of the land. It was therein that for the structures and trees the award will be announced separately, because the assessment for the structures and trees standing thereon had not been received from the respective departments. Accordingly, we hold that the impugned award dated 25th March, 1985 within the period specified in Section 11A of the Act must be construed as an award under Section 11 in the proceedings for the acquisition of the lands in question and the contentions to the contrary cannot be sustained.

query_text: The appellant is the owner of a vehicle in which passengers are carried for hire. He employed Shashi Bhushan Singh as khalasi of the vehicle. The legal heirs of the deceased employee filed a claim in the Workmens Compensation Court against the appellant and against the respondent insurance company. ratio: The High Court held that in the absence of any special contract between the appellant and the respondent, the rights of the parties are governed by statute which does not require the respondent to cover liability in respect of an accident to khalasi.
ruling_text: The appellant has impugned the decision of the High Court before this Court, primarily on the ground that the High Court had misconstrued the provisions of the Act and in particular clause (b) of subsection (1) of section 147. The Court held that the insurance policy expressly covered the death or injury to the khalasi. However, the appellant had not paid any additional premium to cover the risk pertaining to khalasi. The Court further held that the appellant could not claim that the employee would come under the description of any person or passenger as the policy only covers the person or classes of persons specified in the policy. The Court also held that a comprehensive policy merely means that the loss sustained by such person or persons will be payable up to the insured amount irrespective of the actual loss suffered. Consequently, the appellant's claim is unsustainable.

The claim petition was filed by Balwant Singh, the husband of the appellant, under Sections 166, 140, and 141 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (the Act) for compensation for the death of their son in a vehicular accident caused by the driver of car no. HR 41/3347. The appellant was impleaded as respondent no. 4, while the driver and owner of the vehicle were impleaded as respondents 1 and 2, and the United India Insurance Company Ltd. (the insurer) was impleaded as respondent no. 3. The claim was for Rs. 10,00,000/-.

The issues before the court were whether the claim petition was maintainable against respondent no. 2, the owner of the vehicle, whether the insurer was liable to pay compensation as the driver did not have a driving license, and whether the awarded amount of compensation was just and reasonable.

The court held that the claim petition was maintainable against respondent no. 2, the owner of the vehicle, but the insurer was not liable to pay compensation as the driver did not have a driving license. The court also held that the awarded amount of compensation was not just and reasonable and increased it to Rs. 2,50,000/-.

In conclusion, the claim petition was maintainable against respondent no. 2, the owner of the vehicle, but the insurer was not liable to pay compensation as the driver did not have a driving license. The awarded amount of compensation was increased to Rs. 2,50,000/-.

query_text: The appellant is the owner of a land, which was leased to the second respondent, who was the Mahant of an Akhara. The appellant evicted the second respondent from part of the land in 1940 and the rest of it in 1943. Whether the suit is barred by limitation. The Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887
ratio: The court held that the occupancy right in the land merged in the right of ownership of the appellant upon the eviction of the second respondent. The actual physical possession of the land having been continuously with the appellant to the exclusion of the occupancy tenant, whether it was the first respondent or the Akhara itself, for a period of more than years before the institution of the suit, the occupancy right was extinguished.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the decrees of the courts below. The court dismissed the suit of the first respondent as it was barred by time. The court ruled in favor of the appellant and held that the suit of the first respondent was barred by limitation. The court further held that the occupancy right in the land was extinguished as the appellant had been in continuous possession of the land for a period of more than years before the institution of the suit.

query_text: The Released Emergency Commissioned Officers and Short Service Commissioned Officers (Reservation of Vacancies) Rules, 1971 (the Rules) were framed by the President of India to compensate emergency commissioned officers for the chances they had lost by entering public services during the time the country needed them. The petitioners, the All India ex-Emergency Commissioned Officers and Short Service Commissioned Officers Welfare Association and others, sought the same benefit for these categories of persons when they join the non-reserved posts also. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by B.L. Hansaria, J.
ratio: The court held that the policy decision was taken to give some benefit to those servicemen who had stood with the people when the country was invaded and had rendered useful service during the emergency in question. The court also held that the classification of the aforesaid ex-servicemen in two categories mentioned by Shri Kapoor was not unreasonable and had a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.
ruling_text: The court ruled that there is no possibility of some of the released officers obtaining reserved posts with the benefit available under the Rules, and others obtaining non-reserved posts with no benefit visualised by the Rules. So the two types of incumbents have to be taken as belonging to two different categories the one having no clash of interest with the other the one being denied no benefit available to the other. The court dismissed the petition and held that the policy decision was not illegal, irrational or procedurally improper. The classification of the aforesaid ex-servicemen in two categories was also held to be reasonable and have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.

The petitioner was appointed as an APP in the Court of Judicial Magistrate, Malda by the Governor of West Bengal under Section 25(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. His services were terminated by the Governor of West Bengal with an order No.21144-J dated 22nd September, 1979. The petitioner challenged the order of termination before the High Court. query_text: The case is about a murder that took place in a village in India. The accused, Pussu, was charged with murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution's case was that Pussu and his co-accused, Sheo Rakhan, had shot and killed Bankey Lal, the deceased, while he was returning home from his field. The defense version was that Bankey Lal, his servant, and Chhatrapal had assaulted Pussu and Sheo Rakhan, and Jia Lal, Pussu's father, had fired in self-defense, resulting in Bankey Lal's death. The main issues in this case were whether Pussu was guilty of murder, whether the defense version was plausible, and whether the prosecution had proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, was the statute applicable in this case.
ratio: The court held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt and that Pussu was guilty of murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The court also held that the defense version was not plausible and that Jia Lal had fired in self-defense, but that did not exonerate Pussu from his guilt.
ruling_text: The court set aside the acquittal of Pussu by the High Court and restored his conviction for the offence punishable under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The court also restored the conviction of Pussu for the offences punishable under sections 307, 323, and 27 of the Arms Act and the sentences imposed on him on that account. The court sentenced Pussu to imprisonment for life. The court's decision in this case was based on a careful consideration of the evidence presented by both the prosecution and the defense. The court held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt and that Pussu was guilty of murder under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The court also rejected the defense version and held that Jia Lal had fired in self-defense, but that did not exonerate Pussu from his guilt. The court's decision reinforces the principle that the burden of proof lies on the prosecution, and it must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. The court's decision also highlights the importance of self-defense and the limits of its application.

query_text: The appellant, the present Mahant, filed a suit for declaration that the plaint-schedule properties were his personal properties and that there was no trust of a religious or public nature so as to attract the provisions of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trust Act 1951. The plaint-schedule properties included temples and lands that were constructed and acquired by the Mahants of the institution over generations. The main issue was whether the plaint-schedule properties were properties in respect of which there was trust of public or religious nature so as to attract the provisions of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trust Act 1951. The Bihar Hindu Religious Trust Act 1951 regulates the administration and management of Hindu religious trusts in the state of Bihar.
ratio: The High Court held that there was a trust of public nature based on the following factors: (1) the temples were constructed outside the village on open land between two villages, (2) the temples were constructed on high platforms and were open on all sides with plenty of space around them, (3) the members of the public were allowed free access to the temples, (4) several villagers had made gifts of land to the institution, and (5) the location of the temple at a place freely accessible and convenient to the public.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the High Court and held that the plaint-schedule properties were properties in respect of which there was a trust of public nature so as to attract the provisions of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trust Act 1951. The case highlights the importance of considering the totality of the circumstances in determining the character of a trust. The location and construction of the temple, the free access of the public, and the gifts of land by the villagers were all important factors in establishing the public nature of the trust. The decision reaffirms the importance of regulating the administration and management of Hindu religious trusts to ensure their proper functioning and to prevent their misuse.

query_text: The respondent was prosecuted for alleged commission of offence punishable underSection 7, and Section(13)(1)(d) punishable in terms ofSection (2)of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.The respondent was found guilty by Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years relating to offence underSection 7with fine of Rs.500/-.He was further sentenced underSection 13(2)to undergo imprisonment for and years with fine of Rs.1,000/-.Both the sentences were directed to run concurrently. query_text: The case is about a land acquisition by Delhi Development Authority (DDA) in 1964, where possession was taken in 1998 and handed over to DDA. The main issue is whether the acquisition proceedings have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (Act, 2013) due to non-tendering of compensation. The Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
ratio: The Constitution Bench decision of the Supreme Court in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors. (2020) 8 SCC 129, states that the deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) takes place where due to inaction of authorities for five years or more prior to commencement of the said Act, the possession of land has not been taken nor compensation has been paid. However, if possession has been taken, compensation has not been paid, then there is no lapse.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the DDA and the Government of NCT of Delhi, stating that the acquisition proceedings have not lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013 as possession has been taken and compensation has been tendered. The Supreme Court's decision clarifies the provisions of Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013 and reiterates that the deemed lapse of land acquisition proceedings takes place only when both possession and compensation have not been provided for five years or more. The decision also highlights the importance of tendering compensation in land acquisition proceedings.

query_text: The respondent was carrying on timber business in premises consisting of office room and six sheds. Indian Income Tax, 1911-Capital Receipts and Revenue Receipts
ratio: The compensation amount partakes the character of profits and therefore Revenue receipts.
ruling_text: The appeal was allowed. The compensation paid to the respondent represents supposed profit which the respondent would have earned during the years the premises remained tinder requisition. The compensation paid to the respondent represents the supposed profit which the respondent would have earned during the years the premises remained under requisition but which profit the respondent could not earn because of the requisition. The method of computing the compensation payable for loss of earnings does not alter the real character of essential nature of the receipt of the compensation in the hands of the respondent.

query_text: The appellant, Quality Steel Tube (P) Ltd., was engaged in the manufacture of welded steel pipes and tubes. The appellant had set up a plant and machinery at its factory site for the manufacture of these items. The first phase of installation was completed in 1974, and the second phase of expansion was taken up in 1980. The appellant acquired various plant and machinery for the expansion of the project, including a tube mill and welding head. The question that arose for consideration in this appeal was whether the tube mill and welding head erected and installed by the appellant for the manufacture of tubes and pipes out of duty-paid raw material was assessable to duty under residuary tariff item no. of the Schedule, being excisable goods within the meaning of the Central Excises Salt Act, 1944. The Central Excises Salt Act, 1944, provides for the levy and collection of duty on all excisable goods other than salt which are produced or manufactured. The power to levy and collect the duty arises when excisable goods are produced or manufactured. The term "excisable goods" is defined in the Act to mean goods specified in the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, as being subject to duty of excise and includes salt.
ratio: The court held that the tube mill and welding head erected and installed by the appellant for the manufacture of tubes and pipes out of duty-paid raw material were not assessable to duty under residuary tariff item no. of the Schedule, being excisable goods within the meaning of the Central Excises Salt Act, 1944. The court observed that the tube mill and welding head were not goods within the meaning of the Act as they were embedded to the earth and could not be brought to the market for being bought and sold.
ruling_text: The court ruled in favor of the appellant and held that the tube mill and welding head erected and installed by the appellant for the manufacture of tubes and pipes out of duty-paid raw material were not assessable to duty under residuary tariff item no. of the Schedule, being excisable goods within the meaning of the Central Excises Salt Act, 1944. The court's decision in this case clarified the meaning of excisable goods under the Central Excises Salt Act, 1944. The court held that for an article to be considered as excisable goods, it must be a good mentioned either in the Schedule or under Item and must be marketable. The court further observed that goods which are attached to the earth and thus become immoveable do not satisfy the test of being goods within the meaning of the Act nor can they be said to be capable of being brought to the market for being bought and sold. Therefore, the tube mill and welding head erected and installed by the appellant for the manufacture of tubes and pipes out of duty-paid raw material were not assessable to duty under residuary tariff item no. of the Schedule, being excisable goods within the meaning of the Central Excises Salt Act, 1944.

query_text: The case involves a country liquor shop in Dumka Town. The original licensee, Hari Prasad Sah, had his license cancelled. Meanwhile, Jadu Manjhi died and his son, Phudan Manjhi, filed a petition for his name to be substituted in his father's place. The Deputy Commissioner rejected the application, and Phudan Manjhi appealed to the Commissioner of Excise, who remanded the case to the Deputy Commissioner to consider the fitness of Phudan Manjhi. One Bhagwan Rajak filed an application demanding fresh advertisement for the settlement of the shop, which was allowed. The Deputy Commissioner was directed to take steps for fresh settlement in accordance with the rules of the Excise Manual. The appellant filed a petition before the Board of Revenue, which was dismissed, and the Deputy Commissioner was directed to hold fresh settlement giving preferential treatment to Phudan Manjhi. The main issue in this case is whether the Board of Revenue acted within its jurisdiction in directing fresh settlement of the shop. ratio: The ratio of the decision is that a writ of certiorari lies only in respect of judicial or quasi-judicial acts. A tribunal or authority performing judicial or quasi-judicial acts cannot decide against the rights of a party without giving him hearing or an opportunity to represent his case. If the provisions of a particular statute or rules made thereunder do not provide for it, principles of natural justice demand it. Any such order made without hearing the affected parties would be void.
ruling_text: The Patna High Court dismissed the petition in limine, and the appellant filed an appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that necessary parties are those without whom no order can be made effectively, and proper parties are those in whose absence an effective order can be made but whose presence is necessary for complete and final decision on the question involved in the proceeding. The Court further held that in writ of certiorari, not only the tribunal or authority whose order is sought to be quashed but also parties in whose favour the said order is issued are necessary parties. However, it is in the discretion of the Court to add or implead proper parties for completely settling all the questions that may be involved in the controversy either suo-motu or on the application of a party to the writ or an application filed at the instance of such proper party. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Patna High Court. The Court held that the Board of Revenue acted without jurisdiction in directing fresh settlement of the shop. The Court further held that the parties whose rights are directly affected are necessary parties to a writ petition to quash the order of a tribunal. The Court directed that the Deputy Commissioner should not hold fresh settlement until the matter is finally decided by the Court.

He would have been then entitled to continue up to 15-10-1999 as Chairman and the vacancy of Chairman could not have arisen prior to that date. However, sub-section (6) of Section 5 becomes relevant at this stage. It lays down that casual vacancy in Board shall be filled by fresh nomination and person nominated to fill the vacancy shall office only for the remainder of the term for which the member in whose place he was nominated was to hold his office. We may also in this connection, refer to sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 5 which deal with the removal and resignation of the members of the Board, other than the member-secretary. If such removal or resignation takes place, the vacancy arising out of such contingency cannot be anything but casual vacancy depending upon such contingency. query_text: The case involves an accused person in certain proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat who filed a petition under Article 227 in the High Court and obtained a stay of the proceedings on December 20, 1963. query_text: The appellant was charged with the offence of committing the murder of his wife. ratio: The court held that where the trial court allows itself to be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes view of the evidence which is but barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Court to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. The court also held that the appellate court has the power to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion bearing in mind the considerations mentioned by the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup v. The court also held that where the trial court allows itself to be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes view of the evidence which is but barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Court to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. The court also held that the accused is not entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the possibility of duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him.

ruling_text: The court quashed and set aside the order dated 01.11.2017, issued by Respondent No.1- State of Punjab, withdrawing the Essentiality Certificate and declared Condition Nos.(VII) and (XI) illegal. The court upheld the principle that an Essentiality Certificate is a solemn statement by an authority certifying certain conditions of things and persons acting on such certificates are entitled to assume that the certificate will ensure and not be pulled out from under their feet for extraneous reasons. The court also reiterated that the power to issue an Essentiality Certificate is a quasi-judicial function and cannot be withdrawn without an express power vested in the authority to do so. The court further held that the conditions imposed by the State Government in the Essentiality Certificate are ultra-vires the provisions of the Act and the Regulations.

query_text: The case is about a complaint filed with the Lokayukta regarding errors in the revenue records of a property in Survey No.584 of Varkala. The complainant requested the Lokayukta to direct the respondents to rectify the errors and mutate the property in the name of the legal heirs of the late K. Gopalakrishnan Nair. ratio: The Division Bench of the High Court in Sudha Devi K. v. District Collector and District Collector and Another v. Registrar, Kerala Lokayukta, Legislative Complex and others held that the Lokayukta or Upa Lokayukta is not a supervisory body above the statutory authorities in hierarchy under the aforesaid statutes. They only have recommendatory jurisdiction and cannot issue positive directions for correction of revenue records and mutation of property.
ruling_text: The present court set aside the orders passed by the High Court and the Upa Lokayukta as they were without jurisdiction. The court held that the Lokayukta does not have the power to issue positive directions for correction of revenue records and mutation of property. The court's decision reaffirms the principle that the Lokayukta or Upa Lokayukta does not have the power to issue positive directions for correction of revenue records and mutation of property. The complainant, if so advised, may avail of any appropriate remedy under the relevant statute for correction of the revenue records.

query_text: The employee was placed under suspension for alleged omissions and commissions amounting to gross irregularities. He was working as officiating manager at the Green Park Extension branch of the bank. He was accused of meeting Director (Finance) of M Bharat Dynamics Ltd. and requesting him to invest funds in the Green Park Extension branch and offering interest 14.5 on the invested funds. A cheque of Rs.60 crores was issued and handed over to the employee for issuance of necessary deposit certificates in the name of aforementioned concern. Instead of issuing the deposit certificates the employee got the amount deposited in the current account of one of M s Jaydees International and the deposit receipt of Rs.20 crores was in the name of the said concern. On the basis of the deposit receipt, demand loan of Rs.15 crore was sanctioned to it. Whether criminal case and departmental proceedings can proceed simultaneously and whether the departmental proceedings ought to be continued. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Indian Evidence Act1872 and the State Bank of India Officers Service Rules.
ratio: The purpose of departmental enquiry and of prosecution are two different and distinct aspects. The criminal prosecution is launched for an offence for violation of duty the offender owes to the society, or for breach of which law has provided that the offender shall make satisfaction to the public. The departmental enquiry is to maintain discipline in the service and efficiency of public service. It would, therefore, be expedient that the disciplinary proceedings are conducted and completed as expeditiously as possible. It is not, therefore, desirable to lay down any guidelines as inflexible rules in which the departmental proceedings may or may not be stayed pending trial in criminal case. Each case requires to be considered in the backdrop of its own facts and circumstances. There would be no bar to proceed simultaneously with departmental enquiry and trial of criminal case unless the charge in the criminal trial is of grave nature involving complicated questions of fact and law.
ruling_text: The High Court has allowed the application by reversing the order of learned Senior Civil Judge and restoring the order of stay passed by learned Civil Judge. The High Court has not kept in view the correct principles of law relating to situation where both the departmental proceedings and criminal case are pending. The High Court has to consider each case depending on its own facts and circumstances. The High Court shall dispose of the matter afresh in accordance with law and pass reasoned order for its conclusions to be arrived at on consideration of the rival stands.

query_text: The case is about a tenant who has been living in a house since 1944 and has been paying rent to the landlord. The tenant had been living in the first and second floors and running a drug store in the ground floor. The issues in the case are whether the second application made by the landlord for permission to file a suit for eviction is barred under Rule 18(1) of the Rules and whether the Appellate Authority has erred in rendering a finding against the tenant in the matter of comparative hardship. The case is governed by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 and the P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972.
ratio: The court held that the second application made by the landlord is not barred under Rule 18(1) of the Rules and that the Appellate Authority has not erred in rendering a finding against the tenant in the matter of comparative hardship.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal by special leave by the tenant. The court ruled in favor of the landlord and dismissed the appeal by the tenant. query_text: The appellant, an Assistant Engineer in the Central Public Works Department was placed under suspension on September 3, 1959 pending departmental enquiry. The statute involved in this case is the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, Rule 12, and the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the Union of India acted in flagrant breach of the rules of natural justice or fairplay in passing the impugned order, and that the appellant is entitled to interest on the delayed payment of his pension.
ruling_text: The present court allowed the appeal and directed the Director General of Works to make an order in terms of FR allowing the appellant to cross the efficiency bar according to the decision of the Government of India, Ministry of Finance dated September 21, 1967 as later clarified by Ministry of Home Affairs Memorandum dated April 6, 1979 and to re-fix his pension accordingly. The appellant would be entitled to interest at per annum on the difference in salary as well as in pension. The court found that the Union of India acted in breach of the rules of natural justice or fairplay in passing the impugned order, and that the appellant is entitled to interest on the delayed payment of his pension. The court directed the Director General of Works to make an order in terms of FR allowing the appellant to cross the efficiency bar and to re-fix his pension accordingly, and to pay interest on the difference in salary and pension.

ruling_text: The appeal is allowed and the judgment and order dated 21st August, 1989 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana is set aside. query_text: The case involves the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules. A Food Inspector purchased a sample of 200gms of suji (semolina) from the respondent-accused and sent it to the Public Analyst for analysis. The report indicated that the sample was found to contain excessive moisture and ash. However, the Metro politan Magistrate, Delhi acquitted the accused on the ground that the Food Inspector did not send the required quantity of the adulterated article for analysis. The main issue in this case is whether the conviction can be recorded under section 7 read with section 16 of the POFA act, even after, quantity smaller than that required by the Rules to be sent for analysis is sent for the purpose of analysis to the Public analyst. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that the Food Inspector had complied with the mandatory provisions of the Act and the Rules by sending the sample for analysis, and it was not necessary for him to send the quantity required by the Rules. The Court also held that the report of the Public Analyst was admissible in evidence and that the accused could not take advantage of his own wrong by contending that the sample sent for analysis was not sufficient.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court and the order of the Metropolitan Magistrate. The Court convicted the accused under section 7 read with section 16 of the POFA act. The Supreme Court in this case has clarified that the Food Inspector is not required to send the quantity of the adulterated article required by the Rules for analysis, and it is sufficient if he sends the sample for analysis. The Court has also held that the report of the Public Analyst is admissible in evidence and that the accused cannot take advantage of his own wrong. This judgment has clarified the law on the scope of section 7 read with section 16 of the POFA act and the duties of the Food Inspector under the Act and the Rules.

query_text: The petitioner, a constable in the Tamil Nadu Special Police Force, filed a writ petition challenging the seniority list prepared by the respondents. ratio: The court held that the petitioner's service rendered in the Tamil Nadu Auxiliary Force and the Tamil Nadu Home Guards should be considered for determining his seniority in the Tamil Nadu Special Police Force. The court relied on the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Special Police Force Rules, 1961, which provide for the consideration of previous service for determining seniority.

query_text: The appellant, a cement manufacturer, entered into an agreement with the Cement Manufacturing Company of India Limited for the sale of cement.
