query_text: The appellant purchased a property through a registered sale deed in 1950. The respondent entered into a rent agreement with the appellant in 1951. In 1974, the respondent filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to convey the property to him. The agreement was allegedly executed by the appellant's mother in 1950. The agreement was not registered, stamped or attested. Whether the High Court had the jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact of the lower appellate court solely on the basis that the evidence of the scribe of the agreement was not discussed by the lower appellate court. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
ratio: The High Court erred in interfering with the findings of fact of the lower appellate court solely on the basis that the evidence of the scribe of the agreement was not discussed by the lower appellate court. The suit for specific performance could only be decreed against the executant of the contract provided the executant had the right to dispose of the property about which the suit was filed.
ruling_text: The appeal is allowed and the judgment of the High Court is set aside. The High Court erred in interfering with the findings of fact of the lower appellate court solely on the basis that the evidence of the scribe of the agreement was not discussed by the lower appellate court. The suit for specific performance could only be decreed against the executant of the contract provided the executant had the right to dispose of the property about which the suit was filed. The appellant had acquired title to the property on the basis of the sale deed which was a registered document in her favour. The suit property was leased out to the respondent under a rent agreement. The mother of the appellant was not a party to the sale deed and had no right to agree to convey the property or to ask her daughter to convey the same in favour of the respondent. The agreement was not genuine and was just got up for the purposes of the suit. The suit for specific performance was further barred as it was filed more than three years after the alleged agreement.

query_text: The case involves a usufructuary mortgage in favor of the appellant's predecessor-in-interest, which was sought to be annulled by the Official Receiver as having been executed within two years of the adjudication of the mortgagors as insolvents, under S.35(iii) of the Travancore Regulation VIII of 1090 (1915) as not having been entered into in good faith and for valuable consideration. ratio: The court held that the burden of proving that a particular transaction is not supported by good faith and valuable consideration lies on the Official Receiver who challenges the transaction. This case highlights the importance of the burden of proof in insolvency proceedings and the correct test for good faith in transactions. The court's decision clarifies the application of the principle of res judicata in such cases and reaffirms the settled law that the burden of proving that a transaction is not supported by good faith and valuable consideration lies on the Official Receiver who challenges the transaction.

query_text: The case is about a dispute over the formation of government in the state of Madhya Pradesh. The BJP and the INC are the two main political parties involved in the dispute. The BJP, which is the largest party in the Legislative Assembly, has claimed that the INC has lost the confidence of the House and that a trust vote should be conducted to determine the legitimacy of the government. The INC, on the other hand, has argued that the Governor's decision to call for a trust vote is premature and that it impinges on the discretion of the Speaker to determine whether the resignations of some of its Members should be accepted. The main issues in this case are whether the Governor has the power to call for a trust vote in the Legislative Assembly, and whether such a decision impinges on the discretion of the Speaker to determine the voluntary and genuine character of the resignations of some of the INC Members. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution of India, also known as the anti-defection law, is the relevant statute in this case. It lays down the conditions under which a Member of Parliament or a Member of the State Legislature can be disqualified for defection.
ratio: The court has held that the Governor has the power to call for a trust vote in the Legislative Assembly, and that such a decision does not impinge on the discretion of the Speaker to determine the voluntary and genuine character of the resignations of some of the INC Members. The court has also held that the pendency of proceedings before the Speaker cannot be a valid basis to not have the confidence of the House in the government determined by the convening of a floor test.
ruling_text: The court has directed that the session of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly, which has been deferred to March 2020, shall be reconvened on March 2020. The meeting to be convened in pursuance of this direction shall be confined to a single agenda, namely, whether the government of the incumbent Chief Minister continues to enjoy the confidence of the House. Voting on this agenda shall take place by show of hands, and the proceedings before the Legislative Assembly shall be video graphed and, if provision exists for live telecast of the proceedings, this shall in addition be ensured. The court has affirmed the power of the Governor to call for a trust vote in the Legislative Assembly, and has directed that the session of the Assembly be reconvened on March 2020 to determine the confidence of the House in the government. The court has also emphasized the importance of ensuring that there is no breach of law and order in the course of the proceedings and that the floor test is conducted in a peaceful manner.

query_text: The case is about a dispute over the ownership of certain properties in the state of Kerala, India. query_text: The case is about a will executed by a man named Nrisingha Prosad Das, who had no children of his own but had a mistress named Binapani with whom he had a son named Ramendra Narayan Das. query_text: The case is about Telco, a leading manufacturer of heavy and medium commercial vehicles, and its dealers. The Registrar of the Restrictive Practices applied to the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Commission for an enquiry into restrictive trade practices allegedly committed by Telco. The main issue is whether the agreement between Telco and its dealers, which restricts the sale of vehicles to designated territories, constitutes a restrictive trade practice under the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969. The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969, defines a restrictive trade practice as a trade practice that prevents, distorts, or restricts competition. The Act requires any agreement relating to a restrictive trade practice to be registered.
ratio: The court held that the agreement between Telco and its dealers did not constitute a restrictive trade practice. The court found that the agreement was reasonable and necessary to ensure an equal distribution of vehicles to consumers at a fair price. ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. The court recognized that restricting the sale of vehicles to designated territories could ensure an equal distribution of vehicles to consumers at a fair price. The court also recognized that such restrictions did not necessarily restrict competition between manufacturers or dealers. Therefore, the court concluded that the agreement between Telco and its dealers did not constitute a restrictive trade practice under the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969.

query_text: The appellant mill produced electricity over 100 volts exclusively for its own consumption. It challenged the levy of the electricity duty by the Government of Madhya Pradesh under the C. Whether the appellant is liable to pay duty under the C. P. Berar Electricity Act as 1949, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1956, and whether the levy of duty on electricity consumed by producer himself being in substance an excise duty could be levied only by the Parliament under Entry List I. The C. P. Berar Electricity Act as 1949, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1956.
ratio: The court held that on a combined reading of the definition of consumer ins.2(a) and producer ins.2(d-1) of the C. P. Berar Act, of 1949, a producer, consuming the electrical energy generated by him is also consumer as he consumes electrical energy supplied by himself, falls squarely within the Table unders.3 of the Act prescribing rates of duty payable by a consumer and is therefore liable to pay duty thereunder. The court also held that the present Act for levy of duty upon consumption of electric energy was enacted under Entry 45B of the List II of the Government of India Act, 1935, corresponding to Entry of List II of the Constitution where as the levy of duty of excise on manufacturer production of goods by Parliament is under Entry 84 of List I. The taxable event with respect to a duty of excise is manufacture or production and not consumption the levy upon consumption of electric energy cannot be regarded as duty of excise falling within Entry of List I.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the levy of electricity duty by the Government of Madhya Pradesh under the C. P. Berar Electricity Act as 1949, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1956. The court held that the appellant is liable to pay duty under the C. P. Berar Electricity Act as 1949, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1956 and the levy of duty on electricity consumed by producer himself being in substance an excise duty could be levied by the State government under the Entry 45B of the List II of the Government of India Act, 1935, corresponding to Entry of List II of the Constitution.

query_text: The case is about a motor accident claim where the insurance policy was taken out on May 7, 1998, but the cover note stated that the insurance would commence from May 8, 1998. The issue is whether the insurance company is liable to pay compensation for the accident that occurred before the commencement of the insurance policy as per the cover note. ratio: The court held that since the cheque for the premium amount was received by the insurance company at 4 pm on May 7, 1998, the insurance must be deemed to have commenced from that time, and the owner of the vehicle must be deemed to have been covered by the insurance policy at the time of the accident.
ruling_text: The insurance company is liable to pay compensation for the accident that occurred on May 7, 1998. The court's decision is fair and reasonable, considering the fact that the insurance company received the premium cheque before the accident occurred. The decision upholds the principle of insurance law that the insured must be covered by the insurance policy at the time of the loss.

ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed. The appellant is convicted of an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to undergo life imprisonment. The conviction is based on the dying declaration (Ex.P.5) and the recovery of a sword at the instance of the appellant.

ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the estate duty paid in K. cannot be treated as an expense for which the appellants are entitled to claim as an additional expense in administering or in realising the property falling unders.48of the Act.

query_text:
* The appellant State of Uttar Pradesh brought an appeal against the judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant against the order of the Additional District Judge, Agra in proceedings under the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling of Land Holdings Act, 1960.
* The question posed for consideration was whether a tenure-holder who had entered into an agreement to sell some of his lands prior to the appointed day and had parted with possession thereof was liable to include in his holding the said lands when actual sale of these lands had not taken place. * Whether the lands covered by the agreements to sell could be said to be comprised of the holding of the respondent tenure-holder on the appointed day.

* The Transfer of Property Act, 1882
ratio:
* The lands covered by the agreements to sell were liable to be included in the holding of the respondent tenure-holder on the appointed day.
* The transferees were protected by Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, but that did not affect the ownership of the lands, which remained with the respondent tenure-holder.
* The protection available to the proposed transferees under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act was only against the transferor and did not affect the rights of third parties like the appellant-State.
ruling_text:

* The order of the Additional District Judge, Agra is modified to include the lands covered by the agreements to sell in the holding of the respondent tenure-holder on the appointed day. * The appellant-State was successful in challenging the judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which had dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant against the order of the Additional District Judge, Agra.
* The lands covered by the agreements to sell were liable to be included in the holding of the respondent tenure-holder on the appointed day, as the transferees were protected by Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, but that did not affect the ownership of the lands, which remained with the respondent tenure-holder.

query_text: The appellant was given permit for the sale of foodgrains in the village Kotetara at the weekly bazar held once in week.On the date of the weekly bazar he lifted certain foodgrains from the Baradwara branch of the Food Corporation of India.It was in the evening at about 5.00 p.m. on that day.He had no vehicle except, the bullock-cart to transport the foodgrains to Kotetara.Kotetara is about kilometers away from Baradwara.He has no shop at Kotetara for storing the foodgrains and therefore, he kept the same at Baradwara at his cycle-shop. ratio: The appellant has given Ex.P.2 to the SHO at the Police Station.This is also corroborated from the contents of the First Information Report in which there is reference to the fact that the appellant did visit the Police Station before the search and seizure of the foodgrains by the SHO.The foodgrains were required to be distributed on the shandy day at Kotetara.He lifted the foodgrain at Baradwara in the evening of such day.So there was no question of distribution of the foodgrains on that day itself.He has to wait for the next weekly shandy day.He has not attempted to sell the same at Baradwara.He has stored it at the cycle-shop.It is, therefore, not legitimate to infer that the appellant has kept concealed the foodgrains for sale in the black market.
ruling_text: The appeal is allowed, the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant are set aside. The appellant has been prosecuted for violating the provisions of Clause 6(4) of the Madhya Pradesh (Khadya Padarth) Sarvajanik Nagrik Poorti Vitran Scheme, 1981, and convicted underSection 3(7)of the Essential Commodities Act.He was sentenced one year imprisonment, the validity of which has been impeached in this appeal. The court found that the appellant has given Ex.P.2 to the SHO at the Police Station and the foodgrains were required to be distributed on the shandy day at Kotetara.He lifted the foodgrain at Baradwara in the evening of such day.So there was no question of distribution of the foodgrains on that day itself.He has not attempted to sell the same at Baradwara.He has stored it at the cycle-shop.It is, therefore, not legitimate to infer that the appellant has kept concealed the foodgrains for sale in the black market. The issues before the court were whether the management had committed unfair labour practices and whether the punishment of dismissal was shockingly disproportionate. The relevant statutory provisions of the Act are Section 2(16), Section 26, and Schedule IV.
ratio: The court held that the management had committed unfair labour practices under Clause (g) of Item of Schedule IV of the Act as the punishment of dismissal was shockingly disproportionate to the charges held proved against the workmen. The court also held that the management had committed unfair labour practices under Clause (a) of Item of Schedule IV of the Act as the punishment of dismissal was a legal victimization.
ruling_text: The court upheld the order of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court and dismissed the appeal. The court ruled that the management had committed unfair labour practices by imposing shockingly disproportionate punishment on the workmen. The court ordered the reinstatement of the workmen with continuity of service and back wages. However, the court also imposed additional penalties on the workmen by depriving them of a portion of the back wages till actual reinstatement and giving them written warnings.

query_text: The disputed land originally belonged to Anwar Ali Khan, which was gifted to Mustaque Ali Khan. Mustaque Ali Khan settled this land with Mohini Devi, the mother of the appellant, by registered patta dated June 19, 1946. The estate of Mustaque Ali Khan vested in the State of Bihar under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Mohini Devi created a trust in the name of her deceased husband, of which the appellant was the Secretary. The disputed land continued to remain in his possession in that capacity. In 1956-57 proceedings were started for the acquisition of the disputed land for extension of the Darbhanga Medical College. An amount of Rs.12, 689/2/- was assessed as compensation for the property which had been acquired and an award was made in the joint names of the appellant and the State of Bihar. The appellant objected to the inclusion of the State in the award and sought reference under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act. That reference was pending in the Court of the District Judge, Darbhanga when on April 16, 1960 proceedings under Section 4(b) of the Act were started in respect of the disputed land. The issues in this case are whether the settlement of the disputed land with Mohini Devi in 1946 by Mustaque Ali Khan was invalid and should be annulled under Section 4(b) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, empowers the Collector to make inquiries in respect of any transfer including the settlement or lease of any land comprised in such estate or tenure or the transfer of any kind of interest in any building etc. and if he is satisfied that such transfer was made at any time after the first of January 1946 with the object of defeating any provisions of the Act or causing loss to the State or obtaining higher compensation thereunder, the Collector may, after giving reasonable notice, annul such transfer and dispossess the person claiming under it.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the settlement of the disputed land with Mohini Devi in 1946 by Mustaque Ali Khan was invalid and should be annulled under Section 4(b) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The revenue authorities and the High Court were influenced by the rental of Rs.3/-per katha at which the settlement had been taken, which they considered to be very low rate, having regard to the situation of the land. However, there was no evidence produced to show what the current rate of rental prevailing at the relevant time was of land similar to the disputed land. Therefore, the impugned orders should have been quashed on this ground alone.
ruling_text: The appeal by certificate from judgment of the Patna High Court by which petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution filed by the appellant was dismissed is dismissed. In conclusion, the settlement of the disputed land with Mohini Devi in 1946 by Mustaque Ali Khan was invalid and should be annulled under Section 4(b) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The revenue authorities and the High Court were influenced by the rental of Rs.3/-per katha at which the settlement had been taken, which they considered to be very low rate, having regard to the situation of the land. However, there was no evidence produced to show what the current rate of rental prevailing at the relevant time was of land similar to the disputed land. Therefore, the impugned orders should have been quashed on this ground alone.

query_text: The appellant is the owner of a vehicle in which passengers are carried for hire. He employed Shashi Bhushan Singh as khalasi of the vehicle. On 21.10.1998, the vehicle met with an accident as a result of which Shashi Bhushan Singh died. The legal heirs of the deceased employee filed a claim in the Workmens Compensation Court against the appellant and against the respondent insurance company. Whether the insurance company is liable to pay compensation on account of the death of the employee. The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Act)
ratio: The High Court held that in the absence of any special contract between the appellant and the respondent, the rights of the parties are governed by statute which does not require the respondent to cover liability in respect of an accident to khalasi.
ruling_text: The appellant has impugned the decision of the High Court before this Court, primarily on the ground that the High Court had misconstrued the provisions of the Act and in particular clause (b) of subsection (1) of section 147. The Court held that the insurance policy expressly covered the death or injury to the khalasi. However, the appellant had not paid any additional premium to cover the risk pertaining to khalasi. The Court further held that the appellant could not claim that the employee would come under the description of any person or passenger as the policy only covers the person or classes of persons specified in the policy. The Court also held that a comprehensive policy merely means that the loss sustained by such person or persons will be payable up to the insured amount irrespective of the actual loss suffered. Consequently, the appellant's claim is unsustainable.

query_text: The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of contract against Rajeshwari Devi, respondent No.3. During the pendency of the suit, Smt.Vinaya Devi, Defendant (respondent No.4 herein) transferred portion of suit land in favour of one Mihir Kumar Chakraborty by Sale Deed dated 16.3.1993. Defendant Sanjay Prasad also transferred portion of suit land in favour of one Shyam Kumar Datta by registered Sale Deed dated 13.7.1993. On 3.12.1997 said Shyam Kumar Datta further transferred portion of the suit land in favour of respondent No.1-Manik Roy and Mihir Kumar Chakraborty vide registered sale deed dated 3.12.1997. Whether the respondents, being transferees pendente lite without leave of the court, can seek impleadment in the suit which was pending for a very long time. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (in short the TP Act)
ratio: The principle of lis pendens embodied in Section 52 of the TP Act is a principle of public policy, and no question of good faith or bona fide arises. The mere pendency of a suit does not prevent one of the parties from dealing with the property constituting the subject matter of the suit. The Section only postulates a condition that the alienation will in no manner affect the rights of the other party under any decree which may be passed in the suit unless the property was alienated with the permission of the Court.
ruling_text: The High Court's view is indefensible and is set aside. The respondents, being transferees pendente lite without leave of the court, cannot seek impleadment in the suit which was pending for a very long time. The principle of lis pendens embodied in Section 52 of the TP Act is a principle of public policy, and no question of good faith or bona fide arises. The mere pendency of a suit does not prevent one of the parties from dealing with the property constituting the subject matter of the suit. The Section only postulates a condition that the alienation will in no manner affect the rights of the other party under any decree which may be passed in the suit unless the property was alienated with the permission of the Court.

query_text:
* The case involves the Modern Ice Factory at Gurdaspur, owned by Mathra Singh and other partners.
* The factory was leased to the respondents, who were to pay a monthly rent of Rs. 1,000.
* The respondents failed to pay the rent for several months, and the petitioners terminated the lease.
* The respondents filed a suit for injunction, claiming that they were entitled to a renewal of the lease. * Whether the respondents were entitled to a renewal of the lease.
* Whether the petitioners were justified in terminating the lease. * The Indian Easements Act, 1882
ratio:
* The High Court held that the respondents were entitled to a renewal of the lease, as they had been in possession of the property for more than 12 years.
* The Court also held that the petitioners were not justified in terminating the lease, as they had failed to give the respondents notice of termination as required by the Indian Easements Act, 1882.
ruling_text:
* The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the High Court had correctly applied the law. * The case highlights the importance of giving notice of termination as required by law, and the rights of tenants who have been in possession of a property for more than 12 years.

The respondents filed a suit for injunction, claiming that they were entitled to a renewal of the lease. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court reversed the decree. The second appeal was filed by the respondents. The learned single Judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court allowed the second appeal and decreed the suit. The petitioners have come up in appeal by special leave.

The main question that arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the respondents were entitled to a renewal of the lease. The High Court held that they were entitled to a renewal of the lease, as they had been in possession of the property for more than 12 years. The Indian Easements Act, 1882 provides that a lessee who has been in possession of the property for more than 12 years is entitled to a renewal of the lease, unless the lessor can prove that the lease was terminable on grounds other than the expiry of the term.

The High Court also held that the petitioners were not justified in terminating the lease, as they had failed to give the respondents notice of termination as required by the Indian Easements Act, 1882. The Act provides that a lessor must give the lessee notice of termination, specifying the grounds for termination, at least six months before the expiry of the term.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the High Court had correctly applied the law. The Court noted that the petitioners had failed to give the respondents notice of termination, and that the respondents had been in possession of the property for more than 12 years. The Court therefore held that the respondents were entitled to a renewal of the lease.

In conclusion, this case highlights the importance of giving notice of termination as required by law, and the rights of tenants who have been in possession of a property for more than 12 years. The case also illustrates the application of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 in matters relating to the renewal of leases.

query_text: The respondent joined the Indian Air Force in 1978 and served for over 15 years. He applied for the post of Data Entry Operator, Grade B, in the National Survey Organization. He was allowed to sit for the written examination and interview but was later denied appointment. Whether the respondent, who only had a matriculation certificate, was eligible for appointment to the post of Data Entry Operator, Grade B, which required a graduate degree with Mathematics or Statistics as one of the subjects. The Ex-Servicemen (Re-employment in Central Civil Services and Posts) Rules, 1979, as amended by the Department of Personnel and Training in 1986, allowed matriculate Ex-servicemen who had put in not less than 5 years of service in the Armed Forces to be considered for appointment to any Group post where the essential qualification was graduation and experience in technical or professional nature was not essential.
ratio: The Calcutta High Court held that the respondent, being an Ex-serviceman who had put in more than 5 years of service in the Indian Air Force, was eligible for appointment to the post of Data Entry Operator, Grade B, despite not meeting the educational qualification prescribed in the notification. The Court further held that the respondent had a reasonable expectation of being appointed to the post, having passed the written examination and interview.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petition filed by the appellant, stating that it was not a fit case for exercise of its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India. The respondent was eligible for appointment to the post of Data Entry Operator, Grade B, and the appellant was directed to accommodate him in the post or any other suitable alternative post within three months from the date of communication of the order. However, the appellant failed to comply with the order, and the matter is still pending before the Calcutta High Court.

query_text: The appellants were employed as Volunteers by the Eastern Railway to help the staff to check ticketless travel. They were paid Rs.8/- per day. They had worked as such for long time without break. By an order dated 31.1.86, the D.R.M., Sealldah withdrew the scheme of utilizing services of Volunteers. The appellants challenged that order before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The issue was whether the appellants were entitled to be treated as temporary employees with all the benefits available to such employees. The Railway Administration was directed to treat all of them as casual employees with temporary status.
ratio: The Tribunal held that the appellants were entitled to be treated as casual employees with temporary status and their service conditions would be governed by the relevant rules of the Railways.
ruling_text: The Division Bench of the tribunal was right in observing that the view taken by the Single Member was wrong as it was not consistent with the decision of 31.7.90. The Division Bench judgment dated 31.7.90 was not challenged and it has thus acquired finality. The view taken by the Tribunal in these cases is correct and does not deserve interference.

query_text: The election petition challenges the election of Shri K. R. Narayanan as the Vice-President of India. The petitioner, Kaka Joginder Singh alias Dharti Pakad, alleges that there was a substantial defect in the nomination papers of the returned candidate, which required their rejection. The petitioner also alleges that there was commission of the offence of undue influence at the election by issuance of whip by the Congress(i) Party to vote for the respondent at the election. Whether the nomination papers of the returned candidate were wrongly accepted, and whether there was commission of the offence of undue influence at the election. The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 and the Indian Penal Code.
ratio: The court held that the nomination papers of the returned candidate were not wrongly accepted, as the defects pointed out were not of a substantial character. The court also held that there was no commission of the offence of undue influence at the election, as there was no allegation that the returned candidate himself or any person with his consent had committed any act amounting to undue influence.
ruling_text: The election petition was dismissed. The court upheld the election of Shri K. R. Narayanan as the Vice-President of India, finding that the nomination papers of the returned candidate were not wrongly accepted and that there was no commission of the offence of undue influence at the election.

query_text: The assessee's main source of income was salary from a limited company. In the previous year ending on 30th March 1964, his total income from salary amounted to Rs.42,900/. In making the assessment, the Income tax Officer levied surcharge and additional surcharge in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act 1963. Whether the words income tax in the Finance Act of 1964 in sub-s. (2) (a) and sub-s. (2)(b) of s. would include surcharge and additional surcharge. The Finance Act 1964, the Income-tax Act 1961, Arts. and 271 of the Constitution, and the relevant entries in List of the Seventh Schedule.
ratio: The court held that the term income tax as employed in the Finance Act of 1964 includes surcharge as also the special and the additional surcharge whenever provided. The court also noted that the phraseology employed in the various Finance Acts showed that the word surcharge has been used to either increase the rates of income-tax and super-tax or to increase those taxes.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and held that the words income tax in the Finance Act of 1964 in sub-s. (2) (a) and sub-s. (2)(b) of s. would include surcharge and additional surcharge. The court's decision clarifies that the term income tax as employed in the Finance Act of 1964 includes surcharge as also the special and the additional surcharge whenever provided. This is an important point for determining the liability of taxpayers in relation to the surcharge.

query_text: The appellant, K. Gopaul, was appointed to the Madras Registration Service as direct recruit and commenced his service on posting as District Registrar in January, 1939. Under the latest Rules governing the Madras Registration Service, the Service consists of two Classes. Class has only one post in it, viz., Inspector-General of Registration. In Class 11, there are two categories: category consists of posts of Inspectors of Registration Offices, and category of posts of District Registrars. Under these Rules, the appellant was promoted as Inspector-General of Registration (hereinafter referred to as I.G.R.) in the post in Class on 8th June, 1956, and was confirmed in that post by the Government Order dated 9th November, 1957, with effect from 9th June, 1956. The appellant challenged the Orders of the Government posting him as Accommodation Controller on the grounds that he had been reduced in rank without complying with the provisions of Art.311 of the Constitution, that the post of Accommodation Controller was lower in rank than that of Deputy Secretary, whereas the post of G.R. was rank higher than that of Deputy Secretary, and that the post of G.R. had been placed in the cadre of A.S. in the State of Madras only and in no other State. The Indian Administrative Service (Cadre) Rules, 1954, framed under the All India Service Act of 1951, and the Fundamental Rules of the Madras Government.
ratio: The Court held that there was no reduction in rank for the appellant for it was clear, on the facts, that the Post of G.R. was not higher in rank but lower than that of Deputy Secretary. The Court also held that the order of the Central Government cannot be held to be void on the ground of discrimination as the strength and composition of the cadre of the I.A.S. constituted for State are to be determined by regulations made by the Central Government in consultation with the State Governments.
ruling_text: The Court dismissed the appeal. The Court found that the appellant had not been reduced in rank and that the post of G.R. had been placed in the cadre of A.S. in the State of Madras only and in no other State due to the unequal treatment meted out by the Government of India. The Court held that this was not discriminatory and dismissed the appeal.

query_text: The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement of sale dated 28.11.1984, alleging that the respondent had agreed to sell his land for Rs.7,500/- per bigha and agreed to execute the sale deed by 15th June, 1985. The respondent denied the allegations and filed a suit for recovery of money, claiming that the appellant had borrowed Rs.11,050/- from him and executed a pronote. Whether the agreement dated 28.11.1984 is enforceable and whether specific performance of the said agreement can be ordered. Whether the agreement has been deliberately undervalued to save the stamp duty and registration fee, making it void on the ground of public policy. Whether the pronote executed by the appellant is enforceable. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, The Registration Act, 1908.
ratio: The Lower Appellate Court held that the agreement dated 28.11.1984 is not enforceable and no specific performance of the said agreement can be ordered as the property in respect of which the agreement had been entered into is vague and unidentifiable. The court further found that the said agreement Exhibit D1 having been deliberately undervalued to save the stamp duty and registration fee, is void on the ground of public policy. The court also affirmed the findings of the trial judge and confirmed the dismissal of the suit for recovery of money on the basis of the alleged pronote.
ruling_text: The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed both the appeals. The court dismissed the appeals and upheld the decision of the Lower Appellate Court that the agreement dated 28.11.1984 is not enforceable and no specific performance of the said agreement can be ordered. The court also confirmed the dismissal of the suit for recovery of money on the basis of the alleged pronote. The court further found that the agreement has been deliberately undervalued to save the stamp duty and registration fee, making it void on the ground of public policy.

query_text: The case involves the State of Bihar and several government officials who were convicted for contempt of court for disregarding a previous order of the High Court. The main issue in this case is whether the officers are liable for contempt of court for expressing their independent opinion in internal files, even if it goes against the orders of the court. The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, defines civil and criminal contempt, and the present case falls under criminal contempt.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that notings made by officers in the files cannot be made the basis of contempt action against each such officer who makes the notings. The expression of opinion in internal files are for the use of the department and not for outside exposure or for publicity.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and discharged the contempt orders passed by the High Court. The Supreme Court has clarified the limits of judicial power while dealing with files of the Government and the Public Service Commission. The court emphasized the need for mutual respect among the various wings of the administration, in the process of disposal of justice.

query_text: The appellant, a Public Sector Undertaking, carries on business in manufacture and sale of Iron Steel and Chemical Fertiliser as its finished product and bi-product, surplus and rejected articles, in course of inter-state trade and commerce and export. The dispute is regarding the assessment year 2001-02, where an extra demand of Rs.19,25,41,763.00 was raised due to non-production of certain declaration forms in Form. The main issue is whether the sales made under the Annual Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), which were treated as Bank transfers, are in fact, sales made in course of inter-state trade and commerce and, therefore, are subject to tax. The Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 and the Central Sales Tax (Orissa), Rules, 1957
ratio: The court held that the sales made under the Annual Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), which were treated as Bank transfers, are in fact, sales made in course of inter-state trade and commerce and, therefore, are subject to tax.
ruling_text: The court set aside the impugned order of the Assistant Commissioner and remit the matter to him for fresh consideration of the appeal. The first appellate authority is directed to dispose of the appeal by reasoned order dealing with all the points of challenge highlighted by the appellant within six months from the date of receipt of copy of the order. The court has remanded the case back to the first appellate authority for a fresh consideration of the appeal and to dispose of the same by a reasoned order dealing with all the points of challenge highlighted by the appellant. The court has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.

query_text: The General Manager, Northern Railway published a panel of 38 enquiry-cum-reservation clerks for selection to the posts of reservation supervisors. The panel was published after considering persons, i.e., four times the number -of existing and anticipated vacancies plus 25 thereof for unforeseen vacancies. The anticipated vacancies included 11 vacancies on account of promotions due to the upgrading of 11 posts in the next higher grade. Representations were made against the constitution of the panel, and the Railway Board decided that the panel should consist of persons only to coy upgraded vacancies, vacancy on account of retirement and vacancies representing 25 for contingencies and the field of selection should be restricted to 24496 and not persons. The issue was whether the decision of the Railway Board to amend the panel was valid and whether it violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Arts.14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Indian Railway Establishment Manual rules made by the Railway Board from time to time underr.157 of the Railway Establishment Code.
ratio: The Court held that the Railway Board had the power to issue general directions under r. of the Railway Establishment Code and that the General Manager was competent to amend the panel with the approval of the Railway Board. The Court also held that the decision of the Railway Board to amend the panel was not perverse and that it did not violate the petitioner's fundamental rights under Arts.14 and 16 of the Constitution.
ruling_text: The petition was dismissed. The Court held that the decision of the Railway Board to amend the panel was valid and that it did not violate the petitioner's fundamental rights under Arts.14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Court also held that the petitioner was not denied equality of opportunity in the matter of promotion as all the enquiry-cum-reservation clerks retained in the panel were senior to him and would have been selected and included in the panel, even if 96 persons were originally called for selection.

query_text: The Union of India, the appellant, approached the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution, challenging notices of demand issued by the Municipal Council, respondent No.1, claiming tax to the tune of Rs.28,400 by way of Service charges due for the period 1954 to 1960, under Article 285 of the Constitution read with Section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890. The main issue was whether the Indian Railways Act, 1890 gets saved under Article 285(1) of the Constitution itself or not. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 and the Constitution of India, 1950.
ratio: The Court held that Section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890 gets saved under Article 285(1) of the Constitution itself. The said Article provides that property of the Union shall, save in so far as Parliament may by law otherwise provide, be exempt from all taxes imposed by the State or by any authority within State. A-B Section 135 of the Railways Act permits taxation of Railways by the local authority in the manner given therein the Central Government being the controlling and the regulating authority permitting liability at given point of time, its extent and manner. The Indian Railways Act being a central enactment has no role to play in sub-Article (2) of Article 285, for that is sphere in which the State legislation operates.
ruling_text: The Court allowed the appeal and held that the Union of India was not liable to pay the Service charges claimed by the Municipal Council. The Court's decision clarified the applicability of the Indian Railways Act, 1890 in relation to the payment of taxes and service charges by the Union of India. The decision also highlighted the importance of the Constitution in providing exemptions to the Union of India from paying taxes imposed by the State or any authority within the State.

query_text: The case is about two accused, Shanker and Suresh, who were charged with murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and rioting under Section 148 of the IPC. The incident took place at a marriage ceremony in Bharveli village, where the accused allegedly assaulted the victim, Sanjay Sorle, resulting in his death. The main issues in the case are whether the prosecution has proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and whether the evidence of the prosecution witnesses is reliable and trustworthy. The case is governed by the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
ratio: The trial court convicted the accused based on the evidence of two prosecution witnesses, PW1 Ganesh Prasad and PW5 Savitri Bai. However, the High Court dismissed the criminal appeals filed by the accused and affirmed the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court.
ruling_text: The present court has examined the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and found several contradictions and distortions in their statements. The court has held that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses is not trustworthy. Based on the analysis of the evidence and the legal principles, the present court has acquitted the accused Shanker and Suresh of the charges under Section 302 and Section 148 of the IPC. The court has held that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses is not reliable. The court has also observed that the standard of proof in criminal trials is proof beyond reasonable doubt and that the prosecution has not met this standard. Therefore, the accused are entitled to the benefit of doubt and should be acquitted.

query_text: The case is about a fight between two parties, the prosecution party and the accused party, resulting in injuries to members of both parties. The prosecution party consisted of P.Ws. 2, 8, 9, and 10, while the accused party consisted of appellants 1-8. The fight took place in front of P.W. 8's house, and the prosecution party was heavily armed. The main issues in the case are whether the accused party was the aggressor, whether the incident took place near the tamarind tree or in front of P.W. 8's house, and whether the accused party was armed with dangerous weapons. The case was tried under the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
ratio: The trial court and the High Court both accepted the prosecution's version of the incident and held that the accused party was the aggressor. The courts also held that the incident took place in front of P.W. 8's house and that the accused party was armed with dangerous weapons.
ruling_text: We agree with the trial court and the High Court's decision that the accused party was the aggressor and that the incident took place in front of P.W. 8's house. We also agree that the accused party was armed with dangerous weapons. In conclusion, we uphold the conviction and sentence of the accused party under Sections 326, 149, 148, and 147 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The sentence of three years imposed on A-8 and the sentence of two years imposed on the other appellants are not excessive.

query_text: The case is about a dispute between the Revenue and the assessee, an educational institution, regarding the validity of notices issued under Section 153C of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The notices were issued based on documents seized during a search and seizure operation conducted on a trustee of the assessee. The main issue is whether the notices issued under Section 153C of the Act are valid, and whether the assessee is eligible for exemption under Section 11 of the Act. The Income Tax Act, 1961, and the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, and the Societies Registration Act, 1860 are the relevant statutes.
ratio: The court held that the notices issued under Section 153C of the Act are not valid as the Satisfaction Note was not properly recorded and the notice was time-barred. The court also held that the assessee is not eligible for exemption under Section 11 of the Act as it was indulging in profiteering and collecting capitation fee.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue and upheld the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) quashing the notices under Section 153C of the Act. The court's decision clarifies that the notices issued under Section 153C of the Act can be challenged on jurisdictional grounds, and the assessee's eligibility for exemption under Section 11 of the Act can be denied if it is found to be indulging in profiteering and collecting capitation fee. However, the court did not deal with the matter on merits insofar as the incriminating material found against the assessee or the trustee is concerned.

query_text: The case is about a suit for partition of properties which belonged to one G. Venkata Rao. He died on or about 18.10.1974 leaving behind three sons, V. Shankaranarayana Rao, V. Sathya Murthy and V. Surendranath and daughter Smt.Leelavathi. The issues in the case are whether the plaintiff proves that the suit schedule immovable and movable properties as described in schedule-I to are the self acquired properties of her father and whether the defendants prove that the suit schedule-II Bank Deposits are the personal properties of each of the defendants. The case is governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that although the properties were purchased with the money of G. Venkata Rao, the same having been done for the benefit of his sons and or by way of family arrangement, were not in benami in character.
ruling_text: The present court has set aside the impugned judgment and remitted the matter back to the High Court for consideration of the matter afresh which would meet the interest of justice. The case highlights the importance of considering the totality of the circumstances while determining whether a transaction is benami or not. The High Court had not considered the question thoroughly and had not taken into consideration the effect and purport of the requisite ingredients for arriving at a decision. Therefore, the impugned judgment has been set aside and the matter has been remitted back to the High Court for fresh consideration.

query_text: The case is about a dispute between a company and the Income Tax Department regarding the disallowance of losses incurred by the company on the sale of shares. The company had sold shares of two companies, Bharat Starch Chemicals Ltd. and Greaves Cotton Co. Ltd., to another company belonging to the same group at a price lower than the market rate. The Income Tax Department disallowed the losses on the grounds that the sale price was much below the market quotation and that the motive behind the transactions was to set off the loss against the profits, hence the transactions were not genuine. The main issues in this case are whether the losses incurred by the company on the sale of shares can be considered as business losses or capital losses, and whether the transactions were genuine or not. The Income Tax Act, 1961, and the Constitution of India, 1950, are the statutes involved in this case.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the Tribunal is the final fact-finding body, and the questions whether a particular loss is trading loss or capital loss and whether the loss is genuine or bogus are primarily questions which have to be determined on the appreciation of facts. The findings of the Tribunal on these questions are not liable to be interfered with unless the Tribunal has taken into consideration any irrelevant material or has failed to take into consideration any relevant material or the conclusions arrived at by the Tribunal are perverse in the sense that no reasonable person on the basis of the facts before the Tribunal could have come to the conclusion to which the Tribunal has come.
ruling_text: The present court dismissed the appeal and held that the losses in respect of the sales of the shares in question, were liable to be allowed as business losses. The court concluded that the Tribunal has taken into account all relevant material and has not taken into account any irrelevant material in basing its conclusions, the decision of the Tribunal is not liable to be interfered with, unless, of course, the conclusions arrived at by the Tribunal are perverse. The court also stated that it is not necessary for the Tribunal to state in its judgment specifically or in express words that it has taken into account the cumulative effect of the circumstances or has considered the totality of facts.

query_text: The case is about the liability of producers to pay sales tax on the turnover relating to the price of gunny bags in which cement was supplied to the State Trading Corporation or its agents in pursuance of the directions given by the Government.
