query_text: The appellant is an Excise Inspector under the U. P. Government and was posted at Baghpat Circle of Meerut at the relevant time. The complainant Ghammanlal is licensed vendor of liquor and drugs in the same area and at the material time he and his brothers had licences for ten shops, seven for the sale of liquor and three for the sale of drugs. The prosecution story is, that on the 22nd March 1948 Ghammanlal approached the appellant with an application, praying, that the latter might recommend him to draw gallons of liquor and seers of Ganja from the bonded warehouse and godown, in view of the Holi festival that was approaching. The accused, it is said, recommended only gallons of liquor and chhataks of Ganja and while making the recommendation he asked Ghammanlal to pay the bribe which he had already promised to pay, at the rate of per cent, upon the total amount of contract for the shops. The issues in the case are whether the accused demanded bribes from the complainant first for doing service to him in the matter of securing licences for his shops and secondly for the favour he showed to him by recommending supplies of liquor and other drugs from the warehouse. The statute involved in the case is Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the accused could not possibly have demanded bribe for anything done by him in regard to the Excise licences because far from rendering any service to the complainant in this connection he did positive disservice to him.
ruling_text: The present court ruled in favour of the appellant and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court. The case highlights the importance of proper examination of the evidence and the relevance of the motive for payment or acceptance of bribe in determining the guilt of the accused. The trial court's estimate of the evidence and its findings on the material facts were reasonable and supported by the evidence adduced before it. The High Court's interference with these findings was unjustified and its approach to the case was wrong from the start. The present court's decision to set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court is in line with the principles of criminal justice and the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused.

query_text: The case involves Ansaria L, who was removed from service by the Divisional Railway Manager, Railways. The only contention raised before the Central Administrative Tribunal was that the Divisional Railway Manager, Railways, was not the appointing authority and, therefore, was not competent to impose the punishment of removal from service. The main issue in this case is whether the Divisional Railway Manager, Railways, had the authority to impose the punishment of removal from service on Ansaria L. The case is governed by the Railway Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules.
ratio: The court interpreted the Rules and held that it would be impossible for the President to deal with all the disciplinary matters of the Government employees. Therefore, delegation of appointment power was made to the General Manager, and disciplinary power was delegated to the Divisional Manager. The General Manager is not the delegator, and consequently, the doctrine that delegator cannot further delegate his powers to the delegatee has no application. Therefore, the delegation of power to impose appropriate punishment is permissible.
ruling_text: The court ruled that the order of the Tribunal is clearly illegal and that the Divisional Railway Manager, Railways, had the authority to impose the punishment of removal from service on Ansaria L. The court's interpretation of the Rules and its ruling that the Divisional Railway Manager, Railways, had the authority to impose the punishment of removal from service on Ansaria L is consistent with the doctrine of delegation of powers. The court's decision is a reminder that the doctrine of delegation of powers is an essential principle of administrative law, and that delegation of powers is permissible as long as it is done within the bounds of the law.

query_text: The appellant, a tenant, claimed occupancy rights under Section 44 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961. The respondents, the landlords, had initiated resumption proceedings under Section 14 of the Act, but had not taken possession of the land. The Act was amended in 1974, inserting Section 44 and omitting Section 14. Whether the appellant was entitled to occupancy rights under Section 44 of the Act, despite having made a concession in the resumption proceedings under Section 14. The Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961
ratio: The court held that the appellant was entitled to occupancy rights under Section 44 of the Act, as the land had not been resumed by the landlords and the provisions of Section 14 no longer applied.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and directed the authorities to confer occupancy rights on the appellant. The court upheld the appellant's claim to occupancy rights under Section 44 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, and emphasized the importance of following the statutory provisions.

query_text: The case is about the validity of imposition of entry tax on glass and plastic bangles under the Karnataka Tax on Entry of Goods Act, 1979. The State Government notified various commodities for purpose of levy of entry tax, including glass sheets and all articles made of glass, and plastic sheets, granules and articles made from all kinds of and all forms of plastic including articles made of polypropylene, polystyrene and the like materials. The main issue is whether glass bangles and plastic bangles are covered by the entries in the Notification and subject to entry tax at 2. The Karnataka Tax on Entry of Goods Act, 1979
ratio: The court held that the glass bangles and plastic bangles are covered by the entries in the Notification and are subject to entry tax at 2. The court followed the rule of construction noscuntur sociis and held that the words and occurring in Entry 30 and Entry 54 assume great importance and reflect the intention of the legislature that it intended to levy tax both on glass sheets as also on finished products of glass articles made of glass, which is found in the second part of Entry 30. The same analogy would extend to Entry 54.
ruling_text: The court confirmed the impugned judgment and held that the glass bangles and plastic bangles are covered by the entries in the Notification and are subject to entry tax at 2. The court upheld the validity of imposition of entry tax on glass and plastic bangles under the Karnataka Tax on Entry of Goods Act, 1979. The court followed the rule of construction noscuntur sociis and held that the words and occurring in Entry 30 and Entry 54 assume great importance and reflect the intention of the legislature that it intended to levy tax both on glass sheets as also on finished products of glass articles made of glass, which is found in the second part of Entry 30. The same analogy would extend to Entry 54.

query_text: The case involves a professor of economics in a college in Motihari, Bihar, whose wife was found burning in their kitchen. The husband and his brother were found standing near the burning body but did not take any steps to extinguish the fire. The wife died as a result of the burn injuries. The issues in the case are whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding with the trial against the husband and whether the evidence proposed by the prosecution can prove the guilt of the accused. The case is governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, specifically sections 226, 227, and 228.
ratio: The court held that at the initial stage of the trial, the truth, veracity, and effect of the evidence proposed by the prosecution are not to be meticulously judged. The standard of test and judgment which is to be finally applied before recording a finding regarding the guilt or otherwise of the accused is not to be applied at the stage of deciding the matter under sections 227 and 228 of the Code. The court also held that strong suspicion against the accused, if it remains in the region of suspicion, cannot take the place of proof of his guilt at the conclusion of the trial.
ruling_text: The court set aside the orders of the High Court and Sessions Court and directed that appropriate charges be framed against the respondent and the trial proceed in accordance with the law. The court's decision highlights the importance of applying the correct standard of test and judgment at the initial stage of the trial. The court's decision also emphasizes that strong suspicion against the accused is not enough to prove his guilt and that the prosecution must prove its case beyond any reasonable doubt.

query_text: The respondent was accused of murdering six of his close relatives. The entire prosecution case rested on the oral evidence of Chanchala (PW.6) who claimed to be an eye-witness to the murder of Hrudananda, one of the six persons alleged to have been killed by the respondent. The main issue was whether the acquittal of the respondent was justified or it must be set aside and the conviction and sentence imposed on the respondent restored. The Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The High Court found it difficult to accept the testimony of Chanchala (PW.6) and gave cogent reasons for rejecting her evidence. The evidence suffered from serious infirmities, including the fact that the witness did not mention the name of the respondent as the assailant for day and half after the murders were committed.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court of India agreed with the reasoning of the High Court and expressed its approval of it. The Supreme Court upheld the acquittal of the respondent, finding that the prosecution had failed to establish the charge against him. The case highlights the importance of reliable evidence in criminal trials and the need for courts to carefully evaluate the credibility of witnesses.

query_text: The respondent formed a partnership firm with his two major sons and two minor sons. The minor sons were admitted to the benefits of the partnership to the extent of their shares. The income of the minors was added to the total income of the respondent under s.16(3)(a) of the Income-tax Act. The respondent claimed earned income relief under s.2(6AA) of the Income-tax Act on the share of the profits of the minor sons which was included in his total income. Whether the respondent is entitled to earned income relief on the share income of the minor sons for the 1949-50 assessment year and on the share income of one minor son for the 1950-51 assessment year included in the computation of the total income of the respondent under the provisions of s.16(3)(a)(ii) of the Income-tax Act. The Income-tax Act, 1922 (11 of 1922), ss.2(6AA), 16(3) (a)(ii).
ratio: The general intention of s.(6AA) of the Income-tax Act is to give relief in cases where the income of minor is included in the total income of the father who has to pay income tax on the consolidated amount of profits. The section means that in the case of firm the father being the partner who is actively engaged in the conduct of the business of the firm while the minor is not, earned income relief should be given to the father to the extent of the minors share of the profits also.
ruling_text: The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and in favour of the assessee. The court held that the respondent is entitled to earned income relief on the share income of the minor sons for the 1949-50 assessment year and on the share income of one minor son for the 1950-51 assessment year included in the computation of the total income of the respondent under the provisions of s.16(3)(a)(ii) of the Income-tax Act. The court based its decision on the general intention of s.(6AA) of the Income-tax Act which is to give relief in cases where the income of minor is included in the total income of the father who has to pay income tax on the consolidated amount of profits. The court also considered the fact that the father was actively engaged in the conduct of the business of the firm while the minor was not.

query_text: The appellants, who are tenants, entered into an agreement with the Church of South India Trust Association for the purchase of a building. However, disputes arose regarding the payment of the balance amount, and the Church repudiated the agreement. The Church then sold the building to the first respondent, who filed a suit for the eviction of the appellants. The main issue in this case is whether the appellants were required to deposit the arrears of rent with the Controller or the appellate authority as a condition for contesting the eviction proceedings. The Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
ratio: The Court held that the appellants were required to deposit the arrears of rent with the Controller or the appellate authority as a condition for contesting the eviction proceedings. The Court further held that the appellants had not shown sufficient cause for not depositing the rent within the prescribed time.
ruling_text: The Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decision of the High Court. The Court's decision highlights the importance of complying with the requirements of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, including the requirement to deposit arrears of rent as a condition for contesting eviction proceedings. The Court's decision also emphasizes the need for tenants to show sufficient cause for not complying with these requirements.

query_text: The case involves a claimant who suffered permanent disability due to a road accident. The claimant was five and a half years old at the time of the accident and was a student of UKG. The claimant suffered multiple injuries, including cerebral edema and brain edema, which resulted in loss of speech, convulsions, and injuries to the face. The lower limb of the claimant was completely paralyzed, resulting in disability. The claimant's father was a professor, and the mother was an IAS officer. The claimant had a desire to become an Executive IAS officer due to his background. The issues in the case are the adequacy of the grant of compensation by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) and the High Court for the permanent disability suffered by the claimant. The case is governed by the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
ratio: The court considered the nature of injuries, the profession of the claimant, and the impact of the disability on the claimant's life to determine the just and reasonable amount of compensation. The court applied the multiplier method to calculate the compensation in pecuniary and non-pecuniary heads.
ruling_text: The court enhanced the compensation awarded by the MACT and the High Court to Rs.51,62,000/-. The court applied the multiplier method to calculate the compensation in pecuniary and non-pecuniary heads. The court granted compensation to the claimant for the permanent disability suffered due to the road accident. The court enhanced the compensation awarded by the MACT and the High Court to ensure justice and provide adequate compensation to the claimant. The court applied the multiplier method to calculate the compensation in pecuniary and non-pecuniary heads, considering the nature of injuries, the profession of the claimant, and the impact of the disability on the claimant's life.

query_text: The case is about two schemes formulated by the appellant to tackle rural poverty and unemployment. The first scheme, the Dairy scheme, aimed to provide training for small landholders in dairy farming. The second scheme, the Veterinary scheme, aimed to train Gopal Sahayaks to provide veterinary assistance to farmers. The issue is whether the appellant could have made available a facility for additional training exclusively for the Gopal Sahayaks. The case was decided based on the Constitution of India, specifically Article 14 which prohibits discrimination.
ratio: The court held that no rational distinction could be drawn between the candidates who had completed training under the Dairy scheme and the Veterinary scheme. The court directed the State Government to consider the claim of the trainees under the Dairy scheme along with Gopal Sahayaks for training as veterinary pharmacists.
ruling_text: The court upheld the decision of the High Court and directed the State Government to consider the claim of the trainees under the Dairy scheme along with Gopal Sahayaks for training as veterinary pharmacists. The court ruled that the appellant could not make available a facility for additional training exclusively for the Gopal Sahayaks as it would be discriminatory. The court upheld the decision of the High Court and directed the State Government to consider the claim of the trainees under the Dairy scheme along with Gopal Sahayaks for training as veterinary pharmacists.

query_text: The case is about a dispute between two brothers over the ownership of a property. The plaintiff brother claimed that the property was a joint family property, while the defendant brother claimed that it was his self-acquired property. The plaintiff brother filed a suit for partition and injunction, which was dismissed by the trial court and the first appellate court. The plaintiff brother then filed a second appeal before the High Court, which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court. The defendant brother then filed the present appeal before the Supreme Court. The main issue in the case is whether the property is a joint family property or the defendant brother's self-acquired property. The other issue is whether the High Court was justified in allowing the second appeal and setting aside the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court. The case is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that the property is the defendant brother's self-acquired property and not a joint family property. The court also held that the High Court was not justified in allowing the second appeal and setting aside the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgement of the High Court. The court restored the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court. The Supreme Court upheld the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court and held that the property is the defendant brother's self-acquired property. The court also held that the High Court was not justified in allowing the second appeal and setting aside the judgement of the trial court and the first appellate court.

query_text: The respondents were placed in the non-supervisory category prior to 2.8.1984. They were placed in the supervisory category by the Railway Board's circular on 2.8.1984. The respondents were disentitled to draw overtime allowance as a result. The Railway Board withdrew the circular on 11.4.2001, and the respondents were placed back in the non-supervisory category. The respondents were entitled to overtime allowance for the period from 2.8.1984 to 11.4.2001. Whether the circular dated 11.4.2001 had retrospective effect or retroactive operation. Whether the original application was barred by limitation. The Indian Railways (Train Superintendents) Recruitment Rules, 1983.
ratio: The circular dated 11.4.2001 withdrew the earlier circular dated 2.8.1984, and the respondents were placed back in the non-supervisory category. The practice prevailing in the Division was that apart from Train Superintendents of Rajdhani Express, others were entitled to overtime allowance. The respondents were entitled to overtime allowance for the period from 2.8.1984 to 11.4.2001.
ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed. The respondents were entitled to overtime allowance for the period from 2.8.1984 to 11.4.2001 as they were placed back in the non-supervisory category by the circular dated 11.4.2001. The circular did not state that it was prospective in nature, and the practice prevailing in the Division was that others were entitled to overtime allowance. The original application was not barred by limitation.

query_text: The case involves five accused persons who were charged under various sections of the Indian Penal Code and the Bombay Police Act for the murder of one Raju alias Avtar Singh and the injury of his companion Keshav Vitthal. The accused were also charged under section 3 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987. The main issue in this case is whether the material placed on record and the documents relied on by the prosecution disclose the commission of an offence under section 3(1) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987. The Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 is the main statute in this case.
ratio: The court held that the material placed on record and the documents relied on by the prosecution did not disclose the commission of an offence under section 3(1) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987. The court also held that the Designated Court was justified in transferring the case to the Court of Sessions, Ahmadnagar, which alone had jurisdiction under the Code.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeals and disposed of the petition, holding that the Designated Court was justified in transferring the case to the Court of Sessions, Ahmadnagar, which alone had jurisdiction under the Code. The court's decision highlights the importance of properly invoking criminal statutes and ensuring that the evidence supports the charge. The court also emphasized the need for the Designated Court to transfer the case to the competent court under the Code when there is no prima facie evidence to frame a charge under section 3(1) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987.

query_text: The appellants are owners of lands in Village Bairam Nagar, Pargana Nahtaur, Tahsil Dhampur, District Bijnore. The lands were notified under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for the purpose of providing houses to Scheduled Castes. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification and the exercise of power under Section 17(1) read with Section 17(4) to dispense with the inquiry under Section 5-A. The issues before the court were whether the lands were waste or arable lands, whether there was urgency to take possession, and whether the acquisition would deprive the appellants of their means of livelihood. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966 were considered in the case.
ratio: The court held that the lands were not waste or arable lands, and that the State was entitled to exercise the power under Section 17(4) to dispense with the inquiry under Section 5-A. The court also held that the right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(e) and Article 21 of the Constitution, and that the State has a constitutional duty to provide house sites to the poor.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the validity of the notification and the exercise of power under Section 17(1) read with Section 17(4) to dispense with the inquiry under Section 5-A. The court upheld the power of the State to acquire land for public purpose, and held that the right to shelter is a fundamental right under the Constitution. The court also emphasized the need for the State to provide house sites to the poor and the need for expeditious inquiry under Section 5-A.

query_text: The case is about the murder of a young lad named Lalit Kumar by three appellants, Mohd.Bhoja, Ismail, and Meheboob, by setting him on fire on 14.3.1992. The alleged motive for this heinous act is that the appellants used to advance monies to young boys, including Lalit Kumar, to enable them to gamble, and demand interest on the monies advanced. The issues in this case are whether the prosecution has proved the guilt of the accused-appellants beyond reasonable doubt and whether the appellants are entitled to the benefit of doubt. The case is based on the Indian Penal Code (IPC), specifically Section 302/34IPC, which deals with murder.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the prosecution has failed to produce a vital document, a written report made by Hanumandas (PW 2) to the Police, which raises a yawning gap in the story of the prosecution. The failure to produce this document gives rise to an adverse inference that, had it been produced, it would have been favorable to the accused-appellants. Additionally, the evidence of Hanumandas (PW 2) and the dying declaration (Ex.49) are not credible and raise serious doubts as to their implicit acceptance.
ruling_text: The present court has ruled in favor of the appellants, holding that they are entitled to the benefit of doubt. The prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused-appellants beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence led on record by the prosecution raises serious doubts, and the prosecution's conduct in suppressing vital documents and witnesses further undermines its case. The appellants are entitled to the benefit of doubt, and the court has ruled in their favor.

query_text: The appellant is an ex-serviceman who was disabled during his service. He was appointed on an ad hoc basis and recommended for regular absorption by the Rajya Sainik Board, Haryana. However, his name was not recommended by the Subordinate Service Selection Board (Board) for regular absorption. Whether the appellant is entitled to regular absorption as of right so long as there exists a vacancy and a person who suffers disability between 20% to 50% is available. The Government of Haryana had issued instructions dated 6-3-1972 providing for the reservation of vacancies for ex-servicemen, including disabled ex-servicemen.
ratio: The procedure adopted by the Board for considering the claims of candidates for regular absorption is just and fair. The appellant did not secure the minimum marks prescribed for viva voce and therefore, could not be recommended for regular absorption.
ruling_text: The Court upheld the decision of the High Court and dismissed the writ petition. The Court held that the procedure adopted by the Board for considering the claims of candidates for regular absorption is just and fair. The appellant did not secure the minimum marks prescribed for viva voce and therefore, could not be recommended for regular absorption. However, the Court allowed the appellant to continue in the post till the regular candidate is available.

query_text: The case is about a complaint made to the Registrar of the Supreme Court by one Attar Singh against Shri M, an Advocate on record, for misappropriation of Rs.242-1-9, being the unspent balance of printing charges of an appeal in the Supreme Court. The issues before the Court are whether Shri M had the requisite authority to withdraw the unspent balance from the Punjab High Court, whether he intimated Attar Singh about the withdrawal of the unspent balance, whether he intimated Attar Singh that any fee remained due and made any demand in that behalf, and whether Shri M was justified in retaining the amount towards fees without lodging bill for taxation against his client. The case is governed by the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, as amended.
ratio: The Court held that Shri M had not proved the specific oral authority for the withdrawal of the unspent balance, and that the Vakalatnama executed by Attar Singh in his favour did not authorise him to withdraw the unspent balance. The Court further held that Shri M had not intimated Attar Singh about the withdrawal of the unspent balance or made any demand for fees, and that he was not justified in retaining the amount towards fees without lodging bill for taxation against his client.
ruling_text: The Court found Shri M guilty of professional misconduct and issued summons to him to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him. The case highlights the importance of maintaining high standards of professional conduct for Advocates on record of the Supreme Court. The Court has made it clear that an Advocate on record cannot retain moneys of his client without his consent or without an order of the Court, and that he is expected to act as a trustee for the client in respect of such moneys. The case also serves as a reminder that Advocates on record are subject to special rules of professional conduct and are liable to disciplinary action if they depart from the high standards set for themselves and demanded by the profession.

query_text: The respondent is engaged in the manufacture and sale of cotton yarn. During the assessment year 1995-1996, the assessee claimed an amount of Rs.61, 28,150/-, being expenditure incurred on replacement of machinery, as revenue expenditure. The assessee believed that such expenditure was merely expenditure on replacement of spare parts in the spinning mill system and, therefore, amounted to revenue expenditure. Whether expenditure incurred on replacement of machinery, in the facts and circumstances of this case, amounts to revenue expenditure deductible undersection 37of the Act or current repairs deductible undersection 31of the Act. The Income Tax Act, 1961(hereinafter referred to as the Act).
ratio: The High Court held that the expenditure on replacement of machinery was revenue in nature and thus, allowable as deduction under the Act.
ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed. The expenditure incurred on replacement of machinery is capital in nature and cannot be claimed as deduction undersection 37of the Act. The High Court decision inJanakiram Mills(supra) case is not good law on which reliance may be placed.

query_text: The case involves five appeals by certificate against the judgment of the High Court of Madras, which accepted the writ alals against the judgment of Kailasam, J., in Writ Petitions Nos.1592, 1593, 1594 and 1601 and 1966 and 3948 of 1965. The case is about the Union of India, the Collector of Customs, Madras, and the Deputy Collector of Customs, Visakhapatnam, appellants before us, prohibiting them from taking any action in pursuance of certain show-cause notices issued by the Deputy Collector of Customs, Visakhapatnam. The issues in the case include the meaning of the expression restrictions imposed by sub-section (1) of Section 12 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, and whether other sections of the Act, such as Sections 22, 23, 12(2), 12(3), and 12(5), should be treated as restrictions imposed by Section 12(1). The case involves the interpretation of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, and the Foreign Exchange Regulation Rules, 1952.
ratio: The court held that the restrictions imposed by Section 12(1) cannot be different for the purpose of the Exchange Act from that for the purposes of Section 167(8) of the Sea Customs Act, 1878. The court also held that regulations made under the Act become for the purpose of obedience or disobedience provisions of the Act and that the regulations must be read as though they were contained in the Act itself.
ruling_text: The court reversed the judgment of the Appeal Court and restored that of the learned Single judge. The court held that the restrictions imposed by Section 12(1) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, cannot be different for the purpose of the Exchange Act from that for the purposes of Section 167(8) of the Sea Customs Act, 1878. The court also held that regulations made under the Act become for the purpose of obedience or disobedience provisions of the Act and that the regulations must be read as though they were contained in the Act itself. The court reversed the judgment of the Appeal Court and restored that of the learned Single judge.

query_text: The petitioner, M s Hindu Jea Band, Jaipur, a partnership firm carrying on the business of playing music on occasions such as marriages and other social functions, questioned its liability to pay contributions under the Employees State Insurance Act, 1948 (the Act) in a petition filed under section 75 of the Act before the Employees State Insurance Court, Jaipur. The petitioner contended that the place where it was carrying on business was not a shop and that its business being one of intermittent or seasonal character, the Act could not be extended to its business. The main issues before the court were whether the place where the petitioner was carrying on business was a shop, and whether the Act could be extended to businesses like the one carried on by the petitioner. The Employees State Insurance Act, 1948
ratio: The court held that the place where the petitioner was carrying on business was a shop, as it was making available on payment of the stipulated price the services of the members of the group of musicians employed by it on wages. The court also held that the fact that the services were rendered by the employees engaged by the petitioner intermittently or during marriages did not entitle the petitioner to claim any exemption from the operation of the Act. The court further held that the power conferred upon the State under section 1(5) of the Act did not suffer from the vice of excessive delegation of essential legislative powers, and that the application of the Act to businesses like the one carried on by the petitioner could not be said to be violative of Articles 14 or 19(1)(g) or section 21 of the Constitution.
ruling_text: The petition was dismissed. The court upheld the validity of the notification issued under section 1(5) of the Act and held that the place where the petitioner was carrying on business was a shop. The court also held that the fact that the services were rendered by the employees engaged by the petitioner intermittently or during marriages did not entitle the petitioner to claim any exemption from the operation of the Act. The court further held that the power conferred upon the State under section 1(5) of the Act did not suffer from the vice of excessive delegation of essential legislative powers, and that the application of the Act to businesses like the one carried on by the petitioner could not be said to be violative of Articles 14 or 19(1)(g) or section 21 of the Constitution.

query_text: The case involves M s. Baburally Sardar of Steward Hogg Market, Calcutta, and Abdul Razzak, partner of that firm, who were charged with an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 read with S.7(1) of that act. The charge was in relation to the sale of adulterated condensed milk. The main issue in the case was whether the appellants had committed an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 read with S.7(1) of that act by storing and selling adulterated condensed milk. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Rules framed thereunder were the relevant statutes in the case.
ratio: The court held that the appellants had committed an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 read with S.7(1) of that act by storing and selling adulterated condensed milk. The court further held that the appellants could not rely on the defence available under S.19(2) of the Act as they had failed to prove that they had purchased the articles of food with written warranty in the prescribed form.
ruling_text: The court upheld the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court on the appellants. The case highlights the importance of ensuring that food sold in the market is not adulterated and that sellers are held accountable for any violations of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. It also emphasizes the need for sellers to comply with the requirements of the Act, including obtaining written warranties in the prescribed form, in order to avoid liability.

query_text: The case is about the interpretation of Regulation (2) (4) of Regulations on Grad Medical Education 1997 framed by Medical Council of India (MCI Regulations). The appellant-University (referred as the University) was established under the Maharashtra University of Health Sciences Act, 1998. The private respondents (students for short) are prosecuting MBBS course in different Medical Colleges affiliated to the University. They appeared for the III MBBS Part examination conducted by the University in December, 2005. The subjects were General Medicine, General Surgery, Obstetrics Gynaecology and Paediatrics. The results were published on 18.2.2006. The students were shown as having failed in one or more subjects and as consequence, as having failed in the examination. Feeling aggrieved, they filed writ petitions before the Bombay High Court. The issue is whether the standards or criteria for passing adopted by the University were contrary to the MCI Regulations and whether the University had shown them as failed by applying Clauses 56(2) and of the University Ordinance of 2002 which wrongly interpreted clauses (2) and (4) of Regulation 12 of the MCI Regulations. The Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, and the Regulations on Graduate Medical Education 1997 framed by Medical Council of India (MCI Regulations)
ratio: The court held that clauses 56(2) and of the University Ordinance of 2002 is illegal and void being inconsistent with and violative of MCI Regulation 12. It also held that MCI Regulation No.12(4) will have to be read and understood in the manner clarified by MCI, in its letter dated 17.9.2002.
ruling_text: The court allowed the writ petitions and directed the University to recalculate the marks based on the MCIs clarification of its Regulation 12(4). The court accepted the interpretation put forth by the University in respect of MCI Regulation 12 as correct and held that clauses 56(2) and of amended University Ordinance 1/2002 are in consonance with clauses (2) and (4) of MCI Regulation 12. It also held that internal assessment marks cannot be clubbed with University examination (external) marks to ascertain whether candidate has passed in Theory with orals, and Practicals. The court further held that the clarification given by MCI in its letter dated 17.9.2002 and the clarification in its reply affidavit are contrary to MCI Regulation 12(4).

query_text: The appellant filed a civil suit before the Munsif Court, Madanapalle (Andhra Pradesh) in 1988 for the enforcement of an agreement executed on 26.6.1986 for sale of an immovable property. The agreement was found to be insufficiently stamped, and the learned Munsif impounded it and forwarded it to the Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) for further action. The RDO imposed a penalty of Rs. 38,950/- on the appellant for the deficiency in stamp duty. The appellant challenged the order of the RDO by filing an appeal before the Senior Civil Judge, which was dismissed as not maintainable. The appellant then filed a revision petition before the High Court, which was also dismissed. The main issue in this case is whether the order of the RDO imposing a penalty on the appellant for the deficiency in stamp duty is maintainable. The Indian Stamp Act, 1899, and the Andhra Pradesh Stamp Act, 1999, are the relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The High Court erred in dismissing the revision petition without considering whether the learned Senior Civil Judge had the jurisdiction to hear the appeal or not. The appellant was ready and willing to deposit the differential amount in court, and the document was not presented for registration. Therefore, Section 47A of the Stamp Act would not come into picture. The court should have followed the procedure laid down in Section 40 of the Stamp Act, which provides for the admission of the document in evidence upon payment of a penalty.
ruling_text: The impugned orders are set aside, and the matter is remanded to the trial court to follow the procedure laid down in Section 40 of the Stamp Act. The present court has ruled in favor of the appellant by setting aside the impugned orders and remanding the matter to the trial court. The court has highlighted the importance of following the correct procedure while dealing with insufficiently stamped documents. The appellant was ready and willing to deposit the differential amount in court, and the document was not presented for registration. Therefore, Section 47A of the Stamp Act would not come into picture. The court should have followed the procedure laid down in Section 40 of the Stamp Act, which provides for the admission of the document in evidence upon payment of a penalty.

query_text: The case is about a lease agreement between a lessor and a lessee for a petrol pump. The lease was for a period of ten years with the right of renewal for a further period of five years and with permission to sub-lease the same. The lessee sub-leased the premises to the petitioner for running a petrol pump. After the expiry of the lease period, the lessor continued to accept the rent from month to month. However, no fresh instrument was executed by the parties. The lessor issued a notice to the lessee terminating the lease and for giving vacant possession of the land on the expiry of 15th January, 1973 after removing the structures by the 16th January, 1973. The lessee did not contest the suit filed on the basis of the notice. The petitioner contested the proceedings and contended that it was holding over after the expiry of the lease, that no notice terminating tenancy was received by it, and that the notice was invalid. The main issue in this case is whether there was a valid termination of the lease and as such the sub-lessee, the petitioner herein was bound to deliver vacant possession. The case is governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
ratio: The court held that in the absence of a registered instrument, the lease must be a monthly lease. The court also held that the notice of termination must be read in the context of the facts of each particular case having regard to the situation of the parties to whom it is addressed. If all the paragraphs of the notice in the instant case are read together in harmony, it would be manifest that the lessee was directed to handover the lease-hold property on 16th January, 1973, and hence the notice was a valid notice of termination of the lease under section 106 of the Act.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the special leave petition. The court held that the notice of termination was valid and the sub-lessee was bound to deliver vacant possession of the property. The court also reiterated that the law does not require that the sub-lessee need be made a party in an ejectment suit if there was a valid termination of the lease.

query_text: The case involves five accused persons who were tried for the murder of Venugopala Reddy. The Additional Sessions Judge, Nellore, acquitted all the accused due to insufficient evidence. The State of Andhra Pradesh appealed the acquittal order, and the High Court reversed the acquittal order in respect of two of the accused. The issues in the case are whether the High Court was justified in interfering with an order of acquittal in a case where two views are possible, and whether the dying declaration of the deceased was voluntary and true. The case is governed by the Indian Evidence Act, specifically section 32, which deals with dying declarations.
ratio: The court held that the High Court had wrongly interfered with an order of acquittal in a case where two views are possible. The court also held that the dying declaration was not voluntary or true, as the Magistrate failed to question the injured regarding his mental capacity to make the statement.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence of the two accused. The court's decision highlights the importance of following proper procedures when recording dying declarations and the need for appellate courts to exercise caution when interfering with orders of acquittal. The court's ruling reaffirms the principle that two views of the evidence are reasonably possible, the finding of acquittal ought not to be disturbed.

query_text: The case is about a property dispute between two parties, the plaintiffs and the defendants, who are descendants of a common ancestor. The plaintiffs claim that they have become co-sharers in the suit property in the year 1941 as a result of some conveyances by members of the defendants' family. The property was in the occupation of military authorities by requisition under the Defence of India Act, 1939, and the Rules made thereunder, for four years from 1942 to 1946. The defendants were in exclusive possession thereafter from 1946 to 1955 when the plaintiff filed suit for partition and possession of his share. The main issue in this case is whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, on the plea that the military authorities had taken possession of the property from the defendants and had restored the possession to them in 1946, and whether the possession of the said authorities was really under or on behalf of the defendants without causing any break in the continuity of their possession. The Defence of India Act, 1939, and the Rules made thereunder, provide for the requisition and possession of immovable property by the Government for the purposes of defence.
ratio: The court held that the possession of the Government was neither by permission of the defendants nor in the character of an agent of the defendants. The orders of requisition, relinquishment of possession and payment of compensation under the Defence of India Act read with Act and the Rules showed that the possession was taken by virtue of the powers under the Act and the Rules irrespective of any consideration as to the rights of the true owner or the occupier who could make claim to compensation. Therefore, possession of Government by requisition under rule 75-A cannot enure for the benefit of the person who was in possession before, for the purpose of enabling such person to acquire prescriptive title.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment of the High Court. The court found that the possession of the military authorities was not under or on behalf of the defendants, and therefore, the period of possession of the military authorities could not be tacked for purposes of limitation by the person to whom possession was restored. The court also found that the plaintiffs had prayed for possession in their plaint, and therefore, the suit was not barred by limitation.

query_text: The case is about the appointment of Thomas as the first respondent by the Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal at Madras in O.A.No.2199/92. The appointment was annulled by the proceedings dated December 1, 1995 in R.C.NO.727/93. The main issue in this case is whether the Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal at Madras had the authority to annul the appointment of Thomas when he was not made a party to the impugned order dated June 15, 1993. The case is governed by the Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal Act, 1986.
ratio: The court held that the Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal at Madras had committed a grave error of law in upsetting the appointment of Thomas when he was not made a party to the impugned order dated June 15, 1993.
ruling_text: The court granted leave and allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned order dated June 15, 1993. The court's decision in this case highlights the importance of following due process and giving all parties an opportunity to be heard before making a decision that affects their rights. The Tamil Nadu Administrative Tribunal at Madras failed to do so, and the court rightly set aside the impugned order.

query_text: The appellant was accused of committing dacoity in the house of one Namdeo Motiram on the night of 11-12-1950 and thereby committed an offence punishable underSection 395, P.C.The defence was that the appellant had been falsely implicated.It was denied that any of the alleged stolen properties had been recovered by the police at his instance or from his possession. The issues were whether the appellant was guilty of the offence underSection 395, P.C.and whether he was in possession of the stolen goods. The statute involved wasSection 411, P.C.
ratio: The ratio of the decision was that the prosecution failed to prove that the ornaments said to belong to the complainant were either in the possession of the accused or that he had the knowledge that they were stolen property within the meaning ofSection 410, P.C.
ruling_text: The court ruled that the acquittal order was erroneously set aside. The appellant was acquitted of the charge under Section 395, P.C., and the prosecution failed to prove that the ornaments said to belong to the complainant were either in the possession of the accused or that he had the knowledge that they were stolen articles. Therefore, the acquittal order was erroneously set aside.

query_text: The husband of the petitioner, who is of Ladakhi origin, was found by the Customs authorities in possession of considerable quantity of gold with foreign markings and Indian currency. Large number of gold pieces of foreign origin, Indian currency and US dollars were also recovered from his residence. He failed to produce the relevant papers though he claimed these articles. He admitted the recovery but maintained that he held the articles for third person. The detention order was challenged on the ground of non-application of mind, denial of fair and adequate opportunity of representing against his detention, and not sending the representation made by him to the Advisory Board in good time. The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974
ratio: The court held that the detention order was vitiated as the detaining authority did not apply its mind to the relevant papers before making the impugned order, and the detenu was denied fair and adequate opportunity of making an effective representation against his detention as the grounds of detention and the copies of documents were furnished in Tibetan language while the detenu knew only Ladakhi.
ruling_text: The court allowed the application and quashed the order of detention, directing that the detenu be set at liberty forthwith. The court emphasized the importance of strict compliance with the provisions of the Act in matters of preventive detention, and the requirement of providing the material to the detenu in a language which he understands to make an effective representation against his detention.

query_text: The case involves M/s Growel Chromates, a division of M/s Grauer and Weil (India) Ltd., who are engaged in the manufacture of Sodium Bichromate and Chromic Acid flakes. The Central Excise (Preventive) Officers of Buisar Division found that the appellants had removed their product, on payment of Central Excise duty and under gate passes, for captive consumption to their Chromic Acid Section situated adjoining to their manufacturing premises, for the manufacture of Chromic Acid flakes. However, those flakes were manufactured with the aid of power and were removed under delivery challans of the appellants without payment of duty. The issues in this case are whether the Chromic Acid Section of the appellants' premises constitutes a unit different from the unit where Sodium Bichromate is manufactured, and whether the appellants were entitled to exemption from duty under Notification No.46/81 dated 1-3-1981. The Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, and the Central Excise Rules, 1944, are the statutes relevant to this case.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the Chromic Acid Section of the appellants' premises is not a separate unit from the unit where Sodium Bichromate is manufactured, and the appellants were not entitled to exemption from duty under Notification No.46/81 dated 1-3-1981.
ruling_text: The present court upheld the order of the Collector directing payment of excise duty, set aside the order of confiscation and imposition of fine in lieu thereof, and upheld the order of imposition of penalty but reduced it to Rs 1,00,000. The court found that the appellants were not entitled to exemption from duty under Notification No.46/81 dated 1-3-1981, and upheld the order of the Collector directing payment of excise duty. However, the court set aside the order of confiscation and imposition of fine in lieu thereof, and upheld the order of imposition of penalty but reduced it to Rs 1,00,000.

query_text: The case is about the excise duty on cinder which is obtained as a result of burning coal in the boilers and furnaces in factories. The cinder is not fully burnt coal and is left out in the boilers. It is sold by the various assessees from their factories. The main issue is whether cinder is liable to be subjected to levy of excise duty. The respondents argue that cinder is not excisable as it does not involve any manufacturing activity. The Revenue, on the other hand, argues that cinder is covered under an entry in the First Schedule to the Tariff Act and is therefore subject to excise duty. The Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and the Central Excise Act, 1944 are the relevant statutes.
ratio: The court holds that cinder cannot be subjected to levy of excise duty as it is not an item of goods which has been subjected to the process of manufacture. The court also notes that the Department has consistently taken the stand that cinder is not excisable as it does not involve any manufacturing activity.
ruling_text: The court rules in favor of the respondents and holds that cinder is not liable to be subjected to levy of excise duty. The court's decision is based on the principle that excise duty is an incidence of manufacture and, therefore, it is essential that the product sought to be subjected to excise duty should have gone through the process of manufacture. Cinder cannot be said to have gone through any process of manufacture, therefore, it cannot be subjected to levy of excise duty.

query_text: The case is about a dispute between two families over a ditch filled with water on the way. The wife of Paltoo Paswan fell into the ditch and was not visible. Krishna Devi, PW-2 scolded Sitaram Paswan, A-1 and asked him to fill up the ditch. On this, A-1 assaulted Krishna Devi with fists. Paltoo Paswan, PW-5 along with his son Vijay Kumar, PW-4 rushed at the spot. Seeing them, A-1 came with sword along with Raj Kumar when they reached the spot. Raj Kumar assaulted Paltoo Paswan, PW-5 on the head with sword and also assaulted Vijay Kumar with sword and Sitaram Paswan, A-1, with Danda. The issues in this case are whether the accused-appellants are guilty of the offences under Sections 323, 324, 341, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The statute involved in this case is the Indian Penal Code.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the prosecution has proved its case by cogent evidence and the accused-appellants are guilty of the offences under Sections 323, 324, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
ruling_text: The ruling by the present court is that the accused-appellants are guilty of the offences under Sections 323, 324, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. However, the High Court acquitted the appellant of the charge under Section 341 IPC and reduced the sentence to three months from six months under Section 323, IPC and six months from one year under Section 324 read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code. The conclusion is that the accused-appellants are guilty of the offences under Sections 323, 324, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code. However, the High Court reduced the sentence to three months from six months under Section 323, IPC and six months from one year under Section 324 read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code. The accused-appellant Sitaram Paswan is entitled for the benefit under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act. Therefore, while confirming his conviction, he is directed to be released on probation on his entering into bond for Rs.10,000/- within the period of three weeks from today before the Court of D.J.M.(Sadar), Sitamarhi, for keeping peace and good behaviour.

query_text: The State of Tehri Garhwal desired to appoint Tehsildar in the State Treasury. It was the practice the State to require prospective candidate to furnish surety bond in the sum of Rs.10,000/-for proper performance of his duties. One Tungeshwar Prasad was selected for employment as Tehsildar. On June 10, 1944, the respondent Jayanand Lakhera submitted surety bond for Tungeshwar Prasad. Tungeshwar Prasad in the course of his service was found to have misappropriated sum of Rs.21,300/-. He was prosecuted and convicted. Thereafter, the State of Uttar Pradesh sought to recover the amount misappropriated from the respondent Jayanand Lakhera. Whether the security bond dated 10-6-1944 was accepted by the Defendant. The Indian Contract Act
ratio: The court held that there was no evidence of any express acceptance of the bond by the Durbar. The court further held that in the absence of evidence of acceptance of the bond, Jayanand Lakhera was not liable to be proceeded against for recovery of the amount of Rs.10,000/-.
ruling_text: The appeal was dismissed. The court held that in the absence of evidence of acceptance of the bond, Jayanand Lakhera was not liable to be proceeded against for recovery of the amount of Rs.10,000/-. The appeal was dismissed.

query_text: The respondents, who had come to India with Pakistan Passport, were ordered to remove themselves out of India within a specified date by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court against the orders, and the single judge held that as soon as it is shown that a person had acquired a passport from Pakistan Government, there is an automatic statutory cesser of his citizenship of India. The Citizenship Act, 1955(57 of1955) s. 9(2) and Citizenship Rules, 1956, Sch.III, r.
ratio: The High Court held that s.9 was intra vires but found that r. of Sch.III of the Citizenship Rules was ultra vires. However, the High Court made it clear that its decision in question would not preclude the Central Government from deciding the question whether the present respondents had acquired citizenship of foreign country or not.
ruling_text: The points raised in these appeals are concluded by the decision of this Court in Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India. The Court held that the question about the status of the respondents has to be tried by the Central Government and it is only after the Central Government has reached the conclusion that the respondents have acquired the citizenship of Pakistan that the authorities can issue an order of deportation against such person. The Court emphasized that the question as to whether person has lost his citizenship of this country and has acquired the citizenship of foreign country has to be tried by the Central Government and it is only after the Central Government has decided the point the State Government can deal with the person as foreigner.

query_text: The case is about a person named R. Vishwanatha Pillai who obtained a community certificate on 14.10.1969 from the Tahsildar. Ambalappuzha stating that he was a member of the Vettuvan community. He was appointed as an Assistant in the Legislative Secretariat in the year 1973 against a post reserved for Scheduled Caste. He was subsequently selected as a direct recruit to the post of Deputy Superintendent of Police against a seat reserved for Scheduled Caste on the basis of the caste certificate obtained by him. He was included in the cadre of the Indian Police Service (IPS). The issue in the case is whether the appellant was entitled to the protection provided under Article 311 of the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder as he had obtained appointment on the basis of a false caste certificate. The statute involved in the case is Article 311 of the Constitution of India and the All India Service (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1969.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the appellant was not entitled to the protection provided under Article 311 of the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder as he had obtained appointment on the basis of a false caste certificate. The appointment was deemed to be void ab initio and the appellant was not considered to be a person holding a post within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution.
ruling_text: The present court dismissed the appeal and held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection provided under Article 311 of the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder as he had obtained appointment on the basis of a false caste certificate. The case highlights the importance of providing accurate information while obtaining a caste certificate and the consequences of providing false information. The appellant was not entitled to the protection provided under Article 311 of the Constitution and the rules framed thereunder as he had obtained appointment on the basis of a false caste certificate. The appointment was deemed to be void ab initio and the appellant was not considered to be a person holding a post within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution.

query_text: The case is between Dr. Ram and Dr. Sharma, both are veterinary doctors in the Bihar Animal Husbandry Service Class-I. Dr. Ram was appointed in the service in 1972 and Dr. Sharma in 1966. Dr. Ram was appointed in the Special Service, a newly created service in 1978, while Dr. Sharma was promoted to the selection grade in the regular service in 1981. The issue is about the seniority of the two doctors and who should be appointed as the Director of the service. The main issue is about the seniority of the two doctors and who should be appointed as the Director of the service. The other issue is about the validity of the Special Service and its creation. The Bihar and Orissa Veterinary Service Class-I Rules, 1935, are the statutory rules applicable to the Animal Husbandry Department.
ratio: The High Court held that the Special Service is not a separate service but a species of the regular service and that Dr. Sharma is entitled to promotion in the regular service with effect from 1-1-1977. The High Court also held that the notification dated November 21, 1986, is illegal and quashed it.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upholds the decision of the High Court and dismisses the appeals. The Supreme Court has dismissed the appeals of Dr. Ram and upheld the decision of the High Court. The Special Service is not a separate service but a species of the regular service and Dr. Sharma is entitled to promotion in the regular service with effect from 1-1-1977. The notification dated November 21, 1986, is illegal and has been quashed.

query_text: The case involves multiple appeals against the West Bengal Taxation Tribunal's decision to impose interest on the turnover tax for the period during which recovery of the tax amount was stopped by orders of the High Court. The main issue is whether an assessee is liable to pay interest under section 10A of the Bengal finance (Sales Tax) Act 1941, on the turnover tax for the period during which recovery of the tax amount was stopped by orders of the High Court. The case involves the interpretation of section 10A of the Bengal finance (Sales Tax) Act 1941, which imposes interest on the tax amount payable by the dealer during the period of default.
ratio: The court held that the appellants are liable to pay interest under section 10A of the Bengal finance (Sales Tax) Act 1941, on the turnover tax for the period during which recovery of the tax amount was stopped by orders of the High Court. The court reasoned that the appellants failed to furnish the correct return as required by section 10 of the Act, and therefore, were liable to pay interest from the prescribed date.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeals and upheld the West Bengal Taxation Tribunal's decision to impose interest on the turnover tax for the period during which recovery of the tax amount was stopped by orders of the High Court. The court's decision reaffirms the importance of complying with tax laws and regulations, and the consequences of failing to do so. It also highlights the principle that interim orders granted by courts do not absolve parties from their statutory obligations, including the payment of interest on tax amounts due.

query_text: The case involves disputed land where Maniraji was recorded as Bhumidar and Smt.Bhagirathi was recorded as Mukarrardar on rent of Rs.9/-. The heirs of Smt.Bhagirathi claimed right in respect of the disputed land while Smt.Subhraji claimed on the basis of a sale deed executed by Smt.Manraji in her favour. The main issue is whether the entry of Mukarrardar in favour of the contesting opposite parties denotes their status as sub-proprietors or not. The North Western Province Tenancy Act, 1901, the Agra Tenancy Act, 1926, and the P. Tenancy Act 1939 were referred to in the judgement.
ratio: The High Court remanded the matter for fresh consideration in accordance with the law after setting aside the order of the revisional authority. The revisional court held that Bhagirathi never remained in possession over the disputed land independently and her possession, whatever it may be, was for and on behalf of the recorded tenure holders, Manraji, Saraswati, etc. The revisional court further held that Bhagirathi never remained in independent possession over the land in dispute, her rights did not mature to any tenancy right on the basis of her possession, and Smt.Manraji had the right to execute the sale deed in favour of Smt.Shubhraji.
ruling_text: The High Court upheld the decision of the revisional court and dismissed the writ petition filed by Smt.Shubhraji. The court held that the entry of Mukarrardar in favour of the contesting opposite parties does not denote their status as sub-proprietors. The court further held that Bhagirathi never remained in independent possession over the disputed land, her rights did not mature to any tenancy right on the basis of her possession, and Smt.Manraji had the right to execute the sale deed in favour of Smt.Shubhraji. Therefore, Smt.Shubhraji is entitled to get her name recorded on the basis of the sale deed.

query_text: The appellant and two others were charged for an offence punishable under section 302 read with section 34 IPC as also for an offence punishable under section 201 read with section 34 before the Additional Sessions Judge, Khammam, who by his judgment dated 15.10.1998 convicted all the accused persons for offences punishable under section 302 read with section 34 and section 201 read with section 34 and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life for the offence under section 201 IPC, no separate sentence was awarded by him. Whether the prosecution has proved the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. The Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The High Court accepted the evidence of PW-5 as to the extra-judicial confession allegedly made by the appellant to PW-5 and the evidence of PW-2 in regard to the quarrel that took place on 29.3.1995. It also accepted the prosecution case in regard to the motive as suggested by the prosecution but in the absence of any direct evidence or other material to establish the actual role played by A-2, the High Court found him not guilty of the offence and acquitted him. While in regard to A-3 the High Court came to the conclusion that there was no material adduced by the prosecution as to his role in the murder of the deceased but placing reliance on his statement made under section 313 Cr.P.C. wherein he admitted the fact that he had assisted the appellant in disposing of the body convicted him only for that offence while acquitting him of the charge of murder.
ruling_text: The court found that the evidence of PW-5 is wholly artificial and his conduct after hearing the confession, shows that if really such confession had been made to him, he would have first gone to the Police Station rather than going in search of the brother of the deceased. The court also found that the evidence of PW-2 does not help the prosecution in proving the guilt as against this appellant. The court also rebutted the argument of the learned counsel for the appellant as to PW-5 not going to the Police Station by saying that it is but natural for a witness like PW-5 after hearing the confession to first bring to the notice of the family of the deceased the factum of his death before any further steps could be taken. The court found that the prosecution has not proved the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt and allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant by the trial court.

query_text: The case is about a company, Maruti Udyog Limited, which is a registered dealer under the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973 and the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The company was assessed to tax by the Excise Taxation Officer, Gurgaon for the Assessment Year 1986-87. The company filed an appeal before the Haryana Sales Tax Tribunal (hereinafter referred to as the Tribunal) challenging the assessment orders of the Excise Taxation Officer, Gurgaon. The company also filed an application for stay of recovery of demand and entertainment of appeal without prior payment of tax and interest as required under Sub-section (5) of Section 39 of the Act. The main issue in this case is the interpretation of the words unable to pay the whole of the amount of tax assessed used in proviso to Sub-section (5) of Section 39 of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973 and the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956.
ratio: The court held that the inability mentioned in the proviso refers to the paying capacity and financial position of the company and its scope cannot be widened to the extent as suggested by the respondents. The word unable used in the proviso has been defined to mean not having sufficient strength, power and means. In relation to money, it means insufficiency of funds. It follows, therefore, that the inability to pay the amount is referable to the paying capacity of the person concerned and not his legal or actual liability to pay the amount demanded.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the order of the Tribunal. The court's interpretation of the proviso to Sub-section (5) of Section 39 of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973 is clear and unambiguous. The inability mentioned in the proviso refers to the paying capacity and financial position of the assessee and not his legal or actual liability to pay the amount demanded. The court has also reiterated the principle that interim orders ought not to be granted merely because prima facie case has been shown. More is required.

query_text: The appellant Sushil Kumar filed a civil suit against the wife of respondent No. 1 and obtained a temporary injunction restraining the wife and her husband from interfering with the possession of some property. ratio: The court held that the bar of Section 195(1)(b)(ii), Cr.P.C. is attracted only when the forgery is committed during the period the document is in the custody of the Court and not when it is outside the Court's custody. The court also held that the Magistrate has the power to frame charges under Sections 471 and 474, Cr.P.C. in the absence of a complaint from a Civil Court.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court. The court directed the Magistrate to proceed with the trial in accordance with law. The court clarified the scope of Section 195(1)(b)(ii), Cr.P.C. and held that the Magistrate has the power to frame charges under Sections 471 and 474, Cr.P.C. in the absence of a complaint from a Civil Court. The court also clarified that the bar of Section 195(1)(b)(ii), Cr.P.C. is attracted only when the forgery is committed during the period the document is in the custody of the Court and not when it is outside the Court's custody.

query_text: The case is about a tenant, Dev Kumar, who was subletting a shop to M s. Ram Saran Rattan Chand without the landlord's permission. The landlord, Smt. ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the tenant had not sublet the premises and had not incurred the liability of being evicted under Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the Act. ruling_text: The present court upheld the decision of the appellate authority and dismissed the landlord's application for ejectment. In conclusion, the court found that the landlord had not provided sufficient evidence to prove that the tenant had sublet the premises. query_text: The case is between the State of Haryana and M s. Liberty Enterprises. query_text: The appellant Union of India objected to the attachment of certain provident fund and pension dues held by it (on behalf of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat) in trust for the fourth respondent, an ex-employee of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat. The attachment was sought in satisfaction of a money-decree held by the first respondent. Whether amounts representing provident fund contributions and pensionary benefits can be attached, having due regard to ss.3 and 4 of the Provident Funds Act, s. of the Pensions Act and s. 60(1), provisos (g) and (k) of P.C.? Whether the Union of India is entitled to move the Court and request it to investigate the question that the whole or part of the sum in its hands on account of the judgment-debtor as provident fund, compulsory deposits and pensionary benefits and, therefore, not liable to be attached? ratio: The court held that the amounts representing provident fund contributions and pensionary benefits cannot be attached, having due regard to ss.3 and 4 of the Provident Funds Act, s. of the Pensions Act and s. 60(1), provisos (g) and (k) of P.C. The Union of India is entitled to move the Court and request it to investigate the question that the whole or part of the sum in its hands on account of the judgment-debtor as provident fund, compulsory deposits and pensionary benefits and, therefore, not liable to be attached. The Rajya Sabha Secretariat staff is not so totally separated from the Union of India that the latter cannot urge, in these proceedings, the claims belonging to employees of the said Secretariat in the civil court even if the attachment of the sums involved is contrary to law.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the decision of the High Court and of the executing court. The court directed the court of the Subordinate Judge to go into the merits of the objection raised by the Union of India as to whether the entire amount or any portion thereof held by it on behalf of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat staff, so far as the judgment-debtor in this case is concerned, represents provident fund and compulsory deposits or pensionary benefits, excluded from attachability in execution of civil decrees under the provisions already adverted to. The court upheld the contention of the appellant that the amounts representing provident fund contributions and pensionary benefits cannot be attached, having due regard to ss.3 and 4 of the Provident Funds Act, s. of the Pensions Act and s. 60(1), provisos (g) and (k) of P.C. The court also held that the Union of India is entitled to move the Court and request it to investigate the question that the whole or part of the sum in its hands on account of the judgment-debtor as provident fund, compulsory deposits and pensionary benefits and, therefore, not liable to be attached. The court also clarified that the Rajya Sabha Secretariat staff is not so totally separated from the Union of India that the latter cannot urge, in these proceedings, the claims belonging to employees of the said Secretariat in the civil court even if the attachment of the sums involved is contrary to law.

query_text: The case involves a dispute over a maintenance allowance payable to a woman, Dulari Bahu, from the property of her husband's brothers. query_text: The case is about a complaint made by the appellant, Upper Doab Sugar Mills Ltd., to the Railway Rates Tribunal against the station to station rates on sugarcane imposed by the respondent, the Railway Company. The complaint was that these rates had been and were unreasonable. The main issues in this case are whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the complaint as regards the reasonableness of rates prior to the institution of the complaint and whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to grant any refund. ratio: The court held that the words is charging in clause (b) and is levying in clause (c) of s.(1) of the Act must be construed to mean is demanding price at the present time for services to be rendered. The Railway Rates Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain or try the complaint as regards the reasonableness or otherwise of rates and charges made prior to the institution of the complaint. ruling_text: The court upheld the decision of the Railway Rates Tribunal that it had no jurisdiction to entertain or try the complaint as regards the reasonableness or otherwise of rates and charges made prior to the institution of the complaint and that it had no jurisdiction to grant any refund. The Railway Rates Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain or try the complaint as regards the reasonableness or otherwise of rates and charges made prior to the institution of the complaint, and it could not grant any refund.
