query_text: The case involves a dispute between two parties over an agreement for the supply of goods. The agreement provided for arbitration, and the appellant filed a claim petition before the International General Produce Association (IGPA) body nominated as the Arbitrators. The Arbitrators passed an Award in favor of the appellant, which was upheld by the IGPA Appellate Board and the Queens Bench Division of the High Court at London. The appellant then filed an execution application in August 1998 before the High Court of Delhi for enforcement of the foreign Award dated 13.8.1996. The main issue in this case is whether the execution application filed by the appellant for enforcement of the foreign Award dated 13.8.1996 is maintainable under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (the Act) or not. The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (the Act) is the statute that governs arbitration and conciliation in India.
ratio: The Delhi High Court held that the execution application filed by the appellant for enforcement of the foreign Award dated 13.8.1996 is not maintainable under the Act as the arbitration proceedings were commenced prior to the coming into force of the Act.
ruling_text: The Delhi High Court dismissed the execution petition, consequently releasing the security of 1.74 crores furnished by the respondent. The appellant then filed a Special Leave Petition before the Supreme Court, which was disposed of observing that the order of the learned Single Judge is appealable under Section 50(1)(b) of the Act. The appellant then filed FAO (OS) No.284 of 1999 before the Division Bench of the High Court, which dismissed the appeal. The Delhi High Court erred in holding that the execution application filed by the appellant for enforcement of the foreign Award dated 13.8.1996 is not maintainable under the Act as the arbitration proceedings were commenced prior to the coming into force of the Act. The Supreme Court has already ruled that foreign awards passed after the commencement of the Act are to be enforced under the Act alone, and the date of commencement of the Act is 25.1.1996. Therefore, the execution application filed by the appellant is maintainable under the Act, and the impugned judgment and order of the Delhi High Court are set aside. The case is remitted to the learned Single Judge of the High Court for proceeding with enforcement of the award in the light of the observations made above.

query_text: The case is about the recognition, renewal including grant of permission in respect of medical colleges. The issue is whether the permission granted by the Central Government is without complying with the statutory requirement and thus violative of Sections 10A and 10B of the Act. The Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and the Regulations framed by Medical Council of India.
ratio: The court held that the compliance with the requirements under the Act and the regulations being mandatory, in absence of their compliance, no permission could be granted by the Central Government for the increase in admission capacity in any course in any Medical College.
ruling_text: The court directed the Medical Council of India to carry out further inspection to find out whether there is compliance of the requirement of the Act and the Rules in all the colleges where increase of strength renewal of permission for a college is permitted by the Central Government by its various orders issued in August, 2003. The court has emphasized the importance of adhering to the statutory provisions and rules prescribed for Medical education. The court has also directed the Medical Council of India to carry out further inspection to ensure compliance with the requirements of the Act and the Rules in all the colleges where increase of strength renewal of permission for a college is permitted by the Central Government.

query_text: The case is about an election petition filed by Asd Lal challenging the election of Kanshi Ram, who contested the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Fazilka constituency in June, 1977. The appellant was candidate of the Janata Party and secured 19,929 votes, while the respondent was candidate of the Congress Party and secured 23,409 votes. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that he was not qualified to contest the election under Section 100(1)(a) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, as he did not make and subscribe the oath prescribed by Clause (a) of Article 173 of the Constitution. He also pleaded that the respondent committed corrupt practices under Sub-sections (5), (2) and (4) of Section 123 of the Act. The issues framed by the trial court were whether the respondent made and subscribed a valid oath at the time of filing his nomination papers, whether the respondent himself hired or procured vehicles for the free conveyance of voters, whether the respondent got handbills (or posters) printed and distributed containing false statement regarding the result of some alleged election to Bombay Metropolitan (Municipal Committee) in which it was shown that the Janata Party had been routed by the Congress, and whether the respondent committed corrupt practice under Sub-section (4) of Section 123 of the Act. The Representation of the People Act, 1951, and the Constitution of India.
ratio: The trial court held that the respondent made and subscribed a valid oath at the time of filing his nomination papers, that the respondent did not hire or procure vehicles for the free conveyance of voters, that the respondent did not get handbills (or posters) printed and distributed containing false statement regarding the result of some alleged election to Bombay Metropolitan (Municipal Committee) in which it was shown that the Janata Party had been routed by the Congress, and that the respondent did not commit corrupt practice under Sub-section (4) of Section 123 of the Act.
ruling_text: The High Court of Punjab and Haryana dismissed the petition with costs. The appellant has not been able to prove any of the allegations made in the election petition, and the trial court's findings have been upheld by the High Court. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed.

query_text: The lands of respondents in village Mola Agri were requisitioned by the Central Government in 1963 under section 29 of the Defence of India Act, 1962. The requisitioned lands were subsequently acquired under section 36 of the Act in the year 1965. The Special Land Acquisition officer, Meerut, determined the compensation payable to the respondents in the year 1966. Not being satisfied with the compensation determined by him, the respondents sought reference to arbitration under section 37(2) of the Act for determination of proper compensation. The Central Government appointed different Arbitrators to decide their claims. In one arbitration, an award dated 16.3.1979, was made awarding compensation at the rate of Rs.2.60 per sq.yd with interest at per annum from the date of acquisition till date of deposit. In another arbitration, an award dated 8.9.1986 was made awarding compensation at Rs.2.60 per sq.yd.with solatium at the rate of and interest at per annum on the additional amount from the date of acquisition till date of payment. Whether award of interest by the High Court on the compensation for acquisition of requisitioned property under Defence of India Act, 1962 is impermissible. The Defence of India Act, 1962, the Defence of India Act, 1971, the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, and the Interest Act, 1839, and the Interest Act, 1978.
ratio: The court held that award of interest on the compensation amount for acquisition of requisitioned property under Defence of India Act, 1962 is permissible on equitable grounds when there is inordinate delay in payment of compensation. The court also held that the provisions of the Defence of India Act, 1962, and the Defence of India Act, 1971, do not provide for payment of solatium or interest, but the Interest Act, 1839, and the Interest Act, 1978, recognize and preserve the power of court to grant interest in such circumstances.
ruling_text: The court upheld the award of interest at per annum on the compensation amount. The court upheld the award of interest at per annum on the compensation amount for acquisition of requisitioned property under Defence of India Act, 1962, on equitable grounds when there is inordinate delay in payment of compensation. The court also held that the provisions of the Defence of India Act, 1962, and the Defence of India Act, 1971, do not provide for payment of solatium or interest, but the Interest Act, 1839, and the Interest Act, 1978, recognize and preserve the power of court to grant interest in such circumstances.

query_text: Four respondents made two applications to the Settlement Officer Consolidation for permission under sub-s. (1) of s.16A of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act 1953 for transfer by way of exchange of certain plots in villages. The proceedings for consolidation were in progress in all the 11 villages. The settlement officer refused the permission under sub-section (2) of s.16A of the Act and the same was confirmed by the Deputy Director of Consolidation. Whether s.16A(2) of the Act is mandatory and whether the Settlement Officer is bound to grant permission to respondents as the exchange was not likely to defeat the scheme of consolidation. The U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act 1953
ratio: The Court held that s.16A(2) of the Act is mandatory and the Settlement Officer is bound to grant permission to respondents as the exchange was not likely to defeat the scheme of consolidation.
ruling_text: The Court allowed the appeal and directed the Settlement Officer to pass an order keeping in view the principles of law set out in the judgment. The Court upheld the decision of the High Court and directed the Settlement Officer to grant permission to respondents for transfer by way of exchange of certain plots in villages as the exchange was not likely to defeat the scheme of consolidation.

query_text: The appellant is a cooperative society registered under the Punjab Cooperative Societies Act, 1961. It operates a sugar mill and hires seasonal workmen on a daily wage basis. The respondent was one such workman who was appointed in the 1991-92 crushing season. He raised an industrial dispute under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the State of Punjab referred the dispute to the Labour Court. The main issue before the Labour Court was whether the termination of the respondent's services was justified and, if not, to what relief/exact amount of compensation he was entitled. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the Punjab Cooperative Societies Act, 1961, were the relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The Labour Court held that the termination of the respondent's services was not justified as he had not been called for work in the subsequent crushing seasons, and his juniors had been called instead. The Labour Court directed the appellant to re-employ the respondent from the season in which juniors to him were called and workman was not called, and to pay him back wages and other monetary benefits.
ruling_text: The High Court upheld the Labour Court's decision, and the Supreme Court granted leave to appeal. However, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment and held that the termination of the respondent's services did not come within the purview of the term retrenchment as defined in Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Supreme Court directed the appellant to maintain a register for all workmen engaged during the seasons and to make publications in neighbouring places when the new season starts, engaging the respondent in accordance with seniority and exigency of work if he reports for duty. The Supreme Court's decision clarified the definition of retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act and held that the termination of the respondent's services did not come within its purview. The Supreme Court directed the appellant to maintain a register for all workmen engaged during the seasons and to make publications in neighbouring places when the new season starts, engaging the respondent in accordance with seniority and exigency of work if he reports for duty.

query_text: The appellants and respondents were partners in a firm called Shivraj Fine Art Litho Works. The appellants filed a civil suit for dissolution of the partnership and accounts. The respondents raised an objection that the court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit in view of the provisions of Part X of the Companies Act, 1956. Whether the provisions of Part X of the Companies Act, 1956, which contain special provisions for the winding up of unregistered companies, including partnerships with more than seven members, affect the operation of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, in the matter of winding up of such partnerships. The Indian Partnership Act, 1932, and the Companies Act, 1956.
ratio: The provisions for winding up of the affairs of a firm contained in Chapter VI of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, are left untouched by Section 590 of the Companies Act, 1956. Section 590 makes it clear that Part X of the Act does not affect the operation of other enactments providing for any partnership, association, or company being wound up.
ruling_text: The appeal was dismissed by special leave. The provisions for winding up of the affairs of a firm contained in Chapter VI of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, are not affected by the provisions of Part X of the Companies Act, 1956. A suit for dissolution of a partnership can be maintained under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, even if the partnership has more than seven members and is an unregistered company as defined in the Companies Act, 1956.

query_text: The case is about a man named Selvamani Nadar who was killed by another man named Kapadia. The incident took place on 1st May 1990, at around 8:30 pm, near Kulachal-Nagercoil Mail Road. The accused hit the deceased with a stick on his head, resulting in profuse bleeding. The deceased was taken to the Government Hospital at Kulachal and then to Nagercoil for further treatment, but he succumbed to his injuries and breathed his last at around 1:25 am on 2nd May 1990. The main issue in this case is whether the accused is guilty of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I of the IPC. The Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The court held that the accused is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I of the IPC and not murder under Section 302 of the IPC. The court based its decision on the fact that the accused used a small stick to hit the deceased, and the place where the assault took place was dimly lit. The court also considered the background facts leading to the assault and held that the case is covered by Section 304 Part I of the IPC and not Section 302 of the IPC.
ruling_text: The court altered the conviction of the accused from murder under Section 302 of the IPC to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I of the IPC. The court in this case carefully examined the facts and evidence presented by both the prosecution and the defense. The court ultimately held that the accused is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I of the IPC and not murder under Section 302 of the IPC. The court's decision is based on a careful analysis of the facts and evidence presented in the case, and it is in line with the principles of criminal law.

query_text: The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant alleging that he had committed offences under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code and section 13 of the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963. The appellant was acquitted by the trial court after compounding the offence, but the High Court set aside the acquittal and directed the trial court to proceed with the trial. Whether the offence under section 13 of the Maharashtra Act is compoundable, and whether the High Court can set aside an acquittal based on compounding. The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963.
ratio: The offence under section 13 of the Maharashtra Act is not compoundable, and the High Court has the power to set aside an acquittal based on compounding if the compounding is invalid in law.
ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed, and the order of the High Court is upheld. The appellant's acquittal was based on the compounding of an offence which was not compoundable, and the High Court rightly set aside the acquittal. The power of the High Court to set aside an acquittal based on compounding is upheld.

query_text: The case is about an incident that occurred on 25.12.1987 at 9.30 M. in Varachha road area of the City of Surat in the State of Gujrat. The incident involved eight accused who were armed with weapons like knife, gupti, hockey stick etc. They attacked four persons, namely, Ramanbahi Mohanbhai, Bhogilal Ranchhodbhai, Karsanbhai Vallabhbhai and Dhirubhai Mohanbhai. Ramanbahi Mohanbhai died as a result of the attack. The main issue in the case is whether the prosecution has proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The case is governed by the Indian Penal Code.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the prosecution has proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. This is based on the evidence of the injured eyewitnesses and other eyewitnesses, as well as the dying declaration of the deceased.
ruling_text: The present court has upheld the conviction and sentence of the accused. The court has found that the prosecution has proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and has upheld their conviction and sentence.

query_text: The appellant was born in India but left for Pakistan in 1951 at the age of 13. He stayed there till 1955, when he came to India as a Pakistani citizen with a Pakistani passport. In 1963, he was deported to Pakistan. In 1964, he again came to India with a Pakistani passport. The issue was whether the appellant had voluntarily acquired Pakistani citizenship and whether the Government of India was required to make a detailed enquiry before passing an order that he had voluntarily acquired Pakistani citizenship. The Citizenship Act, 1955 and the Citizenship Rules, 1956
ratio: The Supreme Court held that the Government of India was not called upon to make any detailed enquiry when the provisions of part of Schedule III of the Citizenship Rules, namely, that the authority must regard obtaining of a foreign passport on a particular date as conclusive proof that the Indian citizen had voluntarily acquired the citizenship of another country before that date, were clearly applicable. It was only when plea was raised that a citizen had not voluntarily obtained the passport that he should be afforded an opportunity to prove that fact.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal. The appellant had voluntarily acquired Pakistani citizenship and the Government of India was not required to make a detailed enquiry before passing an order that he had voluntarily acquired Pakistani citizenship.

query_text: The appellant and Kumud Ranjan Roy were neighbors in village Belgrarm, Burdwan district. They had hostility due to previous litigation and local elections. On March 5, 1964, at around 11.30 a.m., Kumud was working in his courtyard with Madhusudan Das. They heard a row outside the front door of Kumud's house. Madhusudan opened the door and was hit by the appellant with a kencha on his left thigh. Kumud and some neighbors rushed to the spot and found the appellant at the entrance of Kumud's house. The appellant and his associates beat three of the neighbors. Madhusudan died due to the injury. Whether the appellant was guilty of causing grievous injury to Madhusudan and whether the other accused persons shared the common intention with the appellant. Section 302 and Section 323 of the Penal Code.
ratio: The Trial Court and the High Court found no reason to doubt the veracity of the prosecution evidence. The appellant and his associates had rushed at Kumud's house to injure Kumud or the inmates of his house and not Madhusudan. The appellant struck at the very first person who opened the door, and that was how the unfortunate man came to receive the injury. The other accused persons had no particular animus against Madhusudan, and there was no satisfactory evidence to attribute injuries caused to Ws.9, 10, and any of the other appellants.
ruling_text: The appeal was dismissed, and the appellant's conviction under Section 302 and the sentence of three years rigorous imprisonment imposed upon him by the Trial Judge was upheld. The appellant was rightly convicted by the Trial Court, and that conviction was equally rightly upheld by the High Court. The defence theory of an attack on the appellant's house was flimsy and had no tangible facts to support it. The fact of blood at the entrance of Kumud's house and the trail of blood within the house, coupled with the evidence of the neighbors, clinched the prosecution version that it was the appellant who came there with his men to attack Kumud's house.

query_text: The Chandramalai Estate management refused to comply with some demands raised by workmen. The matter was referred for conciliation, but efforts failed on November 30, 1955. The union gave strike notice and went on strike with effect from December 9, 1955. The Government referred the dispute to the Industrial Tribunal, and the strike was called off on January 5, 1956. The issues were whether the price realized by the management for the rice sold to the workers after decontrol was excessive, whether the workers were entitled to get cumbly allowance with retrospective effect from the date it was stopped, and whether the workers were entitled to get wages for the period of the strike. TheIndustrial Disputes Act, 1947
ratio: The court held that the strike was unjustified and that the workmen were not entitled to any wages for the period. The court stated that when conciliation attempts failed, it was reasonable for the union to take the normal and reasonable course provided by law to settle the dispute by asking the Government to make a reference to the Industrial Tribunal before deciding to strike.
ruling_text: The court upheld the Tribunal's decision on the first and second issues, but set aside the decision on the third issue, holding that the strike was unjustified and that the workmen were not entitled to any wages for the period. The court emphasized that strike is a legitimate weapon in the hands of workmen, but it should not be resorted to hastily without exhausting reasonable avenues for peaceful achievement of the object. The court also highlighted the importance of following the procedures provided by law for settling industrial disputes.

query_text: The petitioner, Amrutal Someshwar Joshi, was convicted by the trial court under Section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death for killing three persons including a child aged about three years in a brutal and diabolical manner with the intention of committing robbery. The same was confirmed by the High Court. The petitioner filed a review petition seeking review of the judgment dated 10.8.94 in Criminal Appeal No.87/94. The main issue was whether the petitioner's age should be considered as a mitigating circumstance in the matter of awarding death sentence. The Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The court held that the petitioner's age was not a mitigating circumstance that would prevent the imposition of the death penalty. The court noted that the petitioner was not of tender age at the time of the commission of the offence and that the crime was heinous and brutal.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the review petition and confirmed the judgments of the courts below awarding death sentence to the petitioner. The court held that the petitioner's age was not a mitigating circumstance that would prevent the imposition of the death penalty. The court noted that the petitioner was not of tender age at the time of the commission of the offence and that the crime was heinous and brutal. Therefore, the court dismissed the review petition and confirmed the judgments of the courts below awarding death sentence to the petitioner.

query_text: The incident occurred on 12.7.1978 at about 5.30 a.m. The respondents and are brothers and sons of Sheo Balak Misra. On the aforesaid date and time the accused respondents armed with knife and lathi respectively arrived at the Gotha of the Mohan Mishra (hereinafter referred to as the deceased) and accused Hari Shanker started beating the deceased with lathi and also asked his brother Prem Shanker to kill him, whereupon Prem Shanker assaulted the deceased with knife. The issues in this case are whether the respondents were exercising the right of private defence and whether that right was exceeded. The statute involved in this case is the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (in short the IPC).
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the right of private defence is a valuable right that should not be construed narrowly, but if it is exercised, it should not be exceeded.
ruling_text: The respondents were found guilty of offences punishable under Section read with Section 34 of the IPC. The High Court erred in accepting the plea of exercise of right of private defence without any material to substantiate the plea. The respondents exceeded the right of private defence and are therefore convicted of offence punishable under Section Part IIPC. Custodial sentence of years would meet the ends of justice.

query_text: The case involves two complaints filed by an unrecognized union, Casteribe Rajya Parivahan Karmchari Sanghatana, against the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation) alleging unfair labor practices under the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 (MRTU PULP Act). The complaints were filed on behalf of casual laborers who were engaged by the Corporation for cleaning buses and were being paid paltry amounts despite their work being of a permanent nature. The Corporation denied the allegations and argued that the complaints were not maintainable as the union was unrecognized under MRTU PULP Act. The main issues in the case are whether the complaints by the unrecognized union under item no. of Schedule IV of MRTU PULP Act are maintainable, and whether the Corporation indulged in unfair labor practices under items 5, 6, 9, and 10 of Schedule IV of MRTU PULP Act. The MRTU PULP Act is a Maharashtra state law that provides for the recognition of trade unions for facilitating collective bargaining and preventing unfair labor practices. The Act defines unfair labor practices and empowers the Industrial Court to decide complaints relating to such practices.
ratio: The Industrial Court, the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, and the Supreme Court of India all held that the complaints by the unrecognized union were maintainable insofar as unfair labor practices under items 5, 6, 9, and 10 of Schedule IV of MRTU PULP Act were concerned. The courts also held that the Corporation indulged in unfair labor practices under items 5 and 6 of Schedule IV of MRTU PULP Act by continuing the complainants as temporary casual daily wage workers for years together and denying them the benefits of permanency.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court of India upheld the decisions of the Industrial Court and the High Court of Judicature at Bombay and directed the Corporation to give status, wages, and all other benefits of permanency applicable to the post of cleaners to the complainants. The case highlights the importance of recognizing the rights of casual laborers and preventing unfair labor practices. The Supreme Court of India's decision to uphold the decisions of the lower courts and direct the Corporation to give permanency benefits to the complainants is a step towards ensuring justice for workers who have been exploited by their employers. However, the case also highlights the need for unrecognized unions to follow the proper procedures for filing complaints and the need for employers to comply with labor laws and regulations.

query_text: The case involves a tenant, Kashiram Jaiswal, who took possession of certain lands within the municipal limits of the city of Baroda from a trustee of a temple for a period of three years from 1956 to 1958 at an annual rent of Rs.2225. The tenant fell into arrears of rent for the said years, and the trustee filed a suit for its recovery. The issues in the case include whether the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 applies to the lands within the municipal limits of the city of Baroda, and whether the civil court is competent to determine the reasonable rent payable by the tenant. The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, which was made applicable to the Baroda Municipality with effect from August 1, 1956, includes provisions for the reservation of lands within municipal limits for non-agricultural or industrial development.
ratio: The court held that the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 do not apply to lands within the municipal limits of the city of Baroda that have been reserved for non-agricultural or industrial development. The court also held that the civil court is competent to determine the reasonable rent payable by the tenant.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decision of the High Court of Gujarat. The case highlights the importance of understanding the applicability of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 to lands within municipal limits, and the competence of civil courts to determine the reasonable rent payable by tenants in such cases.

query_text: The State of Jammu Kashmir seeks to encourage and promote the industrialisation of the State by exempting local manufacturers of edible oil from the levy of sales tax. The appellants, who are manufacturers of edible oil from outside the State, challenge this exemption as discriminatory and violative of Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. Whether the exemption granted to local manufacturers of edible oil is discriminatory and violative of Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The Jammu Kashmir Sales Tax Act, 1962 and the Constitution of India.
ratio: The court held that the exemption granted to local manufacturers of edible oil is discriminatory and violative of Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The court also invoked its power under Article 142 of the Constitution and moulded the relief to suit the exigencies of the situation by declaring that the exemption granted by Notification No.S.R.O.93 of 1991 to local manufacturers producers of edible oil is violative of the provisions contained in Articles 301and304(a) but the appellants shall not be entitled to claim any amounts by way of refund or otherwise by virtue of or, as a consequence of the declaration contained herein and the declaration of invalidity of the impugned notifications shall take effect on and from April 1,1997.
ruling_text: The court ruled in favour of the appellants and declared that the exemption granted to local manufacturers of edible oil is discriminatory and violative of Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The court upheld the principle of non-discrimination in the levy of sales tax and declared that the exemption granted to local manufacturers of edible oil is violative of Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The court also invoked its power under Article 142 of the Constitution to mould the relief and balance the interests of both the local and out-state manufacturers.

query_text: The case is about NRI students who were admitted to the B.Tech.Cost-Sharing Engineering Course of eight semesters started in the year 1995 by the appellant university. The students were required to make deposit of US 5000 at the time of their admission towards development charges and to pay in addition fee of Rs.20,000/- per semester whereas all the other categories of students were required to pay uniform fee of Rs.20,000/- per semester. From the academic year 1996-97, however, the University increased the fee for NRI students to US 4000 per annum whereas the other students continued to pay fee at the rate of Rs.20,000 per semester. The issues in the case are whether the action of the University in charging fee at different rates from the students on the basis of the batches in which they were admitted arbitrary and unfair and whether the petitioners are estopped from challenging the impugned action. The case is governed by the Cochin University of Science and Technology Act, 1976.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the action of the University in charging fee at different rates from the students on the basis of the batches in which they were admitted arbitrary and unfair and that the petitioners are not estopped from challenging the impugned action.
ruling_text: The ruling by the present court is that the writ petitions are allowed and the University is directed to refund the extra fee charged from the petitioners. The conclusion is that the University is directed to refund the extra fee charged from the petitioners as the action of the University in charging fee at different rates from the students on the basis of the batches in which they were admitted arbitrary and unfair and that the petitioners are not estopped from challenging the impugned action.

query_text: The case involves the classification of the branded word game Scrabble under sub-heading 9503.00 or sub-heading 9504.90 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise and Tariff Act, 1985 (CETA). The assessee, a proprietary firm engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading toys, games, and puzzles, holds a license from M s. W. Spears Sons Ltd., K., to use the brand name Scrabble and manufacture the product in India. The main issue is whether Scrabble is classifiable under sub-heading 9503.00 or sub-heading 9504.90 of the CETA. The Central Excise and Tariff Act, 1985, and the Central Excise Act, 1944, are the relevant statutes.
ratio: The court held that Scrabble is not a puzzle but a board game and falls under sub-heading 9504.90 of the CETA. The court also held that the assessee had deliberately suppressed the fact of manufacturing and clearance of dutiable brand goods Scrabble under sub-heading 9504.90, and the longer period of limitation was invocable.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeals filed by the assessee. The court's decision is based on the analysis of the entries in Chapter 95 of the CETA, dictionary meanings of the word Scrabble, trade meaning of the word Scrabble in India, and the provisions of the Central Excise and Tariff Act, 1985, and the Central Excise Act, 1944. The court held that Scrabble is not a puzzle but a board game and falls under sub-heading 9504.90 of the CETA. The court also held that the assessee had deliberately suppressed the fact of manufacturing and clearance of dutiable brand goods Scrabble under sub-heading 9504.90, and the longer period of limitation was invocable. Therefore, the court dismissed the appeals filed by the assessee.

query_text: The case involves the assessment of the income for the years 1952-53, 1953-54 and 1954-55 of Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan Bahadur, the Ruler of Hyderabad State prior to its integration with the Union of India. The assesses made a settlement of Rs.30,00,000 by transferring that amount to a trust created on that day for the benefit of Princess Niloufer. An agreement was entered into between the Government of India, the assesses, as the settlor of the trust, and the three trustees for the deposit of Rs.30,00,000 with the Government of India. The main issue is whether the sum of Rs.1,00,000 received by the assesses from the Trustees of Princess Niloufer Trust constituted income under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 and if so, whether the assesses was entitled to exemption from tax in respect of the income under the terms of the agreement entered into with the Government of India on 8/10/1949. The Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
ratio: The court held that the sum of Rs.1,00,000 received by the assesses from the Trustees of Princess Niloufer Trust constituted income under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 but the assesses was entitled to exemption from tax in respect of the income under the terms of the agreement entered into with the Government of India on 8/10/1949.
ruling_text: The court ruled in favor of the assesses and held that he was entitled to exemption from tax in respect of the income under the terms of the agreement entered into with the Government of India on 8/10/1949. The court's decision was based on the terms of the agreement entered into between the Government of India, the assesses, as the settlor of the trust, and the three trustees. The court found that the agreement granted exemption in the matter of payment of tax in respect of the said sum of Rs.1,00,000 to the settlor also and that the intention of the parties was that the settlor was to be exempt in any case from payment of tax in respect of the income from that amount and that in the event of the assesses becoming entitled to the beneficial interest under the trust deed, the exemption from payment of tax would be available to him.

query_text: The respondent is a village Panchayat constituted under the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1933. The Act initially empowered the Panchayat to levy tax on houses and lands as one of the taxes enumerated in s. 89(2). In 1939, the section was amended and s. 89(1) made it obligatory on Panchayats to levy tax on houses and lands. The amending Act of 1947 provided that every panchayat shall levy a tax upon the owners or occupiers of houses including farm buildings and conferred power on the Panchayat to tax shops and hotels. The 1952-Amendment conferred power to tax premises where machinery is run by steam etc. In exercise of the powers under s. the respondent, by a resolution of 1952, imposed tax on own houses within its jurisdiction. In 1954, s. was amended and the word buildings was substituted for the words houses and houses including farm buildings. By resolution of 1964, the respondent revised the tax on houses and also stated that for factories the tax would be at concessional rate. The respondent demanded taxes on the appellants factory buildings for the years 1967 to 1970. The appellant challenged the levy unsuccessfully in the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1) since it was only in 1954 that the word building was substituted for the word house, the respondent had no power to impose taxes on the factory buildings by the 1952 resolution and (2) even if the 1952 resolution authorized the levy, since it was replaced by the 1964-resolution, which was not valid as it was not passed in accordance with the Act and the rules, no tax could be levied either under the 1952-resolution or under the 1964-resolution. The Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1933
ratio: The court held that the word house would in its ordinary sense include any building irrespective of its user. Having regard to the nature of the word as used in taxing and municipal legislation, and the nature and purpose of the statute in the present case, it is manifest that the legislature used the word house so that the Panchayat would be in a position to levy taxes on all buildings situated in the village. The court also held that even if the 1964-resolution was invalid, the demands made by the respondent were valid and legal because the 1952-resolution had not been superseded and the levy was not pursuant to the 1964 resolution but was pursuant to the 1952-resolution.
ruling_text: The appeal was dismissed. The court held that the respondent had the power to impose taxes on the appellants factory buildings and that even if the 1964-resolution was invalid, the demands made by the respondent were valid and legal.

query_text: The appellants were landlords who owned an estate including agricultural land, trees, groves, etc. They were heavily indebted to the respondents, who were secured creditors. Proceedings were taken under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act, 1934, and a decree was passed in favor of the respondents in 1938. The nature and extent of property liable to attachment and sale were furnished to the executing authority. By virtue of a notification under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the estate vested in the State, and new rights, namely, bhumidhari rights in the lands in the estate, were created in favor of the appellants who were the successors-in-interest of the landlords. In 1959, the respondents applied under s.24 of the Encumbered Estates Act to recover the amount decreed to them by proceeding against the bhumidhari rights and trees belonging to the appellants. The main issues were whether (1) the bhumidhari rights, and (2) the trees, could be proceeded against. The Encumbered Estates Act, 1934, and the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, were the relevant statutes.
ratio: The court held that though the respondents were mortgagees, their rights as such were extinguished under the Encumbered Estates Act, and the decree in their favor under the Act was only a simple money decree which was not executable except under the provisions of the Act. The court further held that under s. execution can be levied from any property or rights, other than proprietary rights in land, which are reported under s. 19 as liable to be attached and sold. The court also held that on the passing of the U.P. Abolition Act, the proprietary rights of the landlords in the land vested in the State, and the appellants had no proprietary rights left in them. The bhumidhari rights being new rights created for the first time in favor of the appellants under the Abolition Act, were not proprietary rights. The court further held that the requirements of ss.19 and 24 of the Encumbered Estates Act had been complied with, and the respondents were entitled to proceed against such rights.
ruling_text: The court upheld the right of the respondents to proceed against the bhumidhari rights and trees belonging to the appellants. The court held that the bhumidhari rights and trees could be proceeded against in execution under the Encumbered Estates Act, as they were not proprietary rights in land and were reported as liable to attachment and sale under the Act. The court also held that the requirements of the Act had been complied with, and the respondents were entitled to proceed against such rights.

query_text: The Union of India, as the owner of the Central Railway, instituted suit for refund of Rs.2,76,967/- collected as tax from the Railway Administration by the respondent Municipality during the period from 1931 till the institution of the suit in November, 1954. The facts leading up to the suit are that the I.P.Railway, which was Private Company, had land situated within the limits of the respondent Municipality.On this land, stood the railway station, their Water Reservoir at Bhusi, bungalows of Officers, and certain other buildings.There were also vacant lands and some lands on which railway lines were laid out.In this area, which belonged to the I.P.Railway, the Railway.Company itself built roads, supplied water from its Bhusi Reservoir, arranged for the lighting, and provided other services.In fact, up to the year 1916, the Railway used to supply water even to the Municipality from its Bhusi Reservoir on payment.The Municipality was governed, at that time, by the Bombay District Municipal Act No.of 1901 (hereinafter referred to as the Act of 1901) under which tax on lands and buildings situated within the municipal limits used to be charged per cent of the annual rental value, but no tax was levied on the buildings and lands of the I.P.Railway in view ofSection 135of the Indian Railways Act No.of 1890.In the year 1914, the Government of India issued notification underSection 135of the Railways Act declaring that the Administration of the I.P.Railway shall be liable to pay, in aid of the funds of the local authorities set out in the Schedule, the taxes specified against each of those authorities.Against the name of Lonavla Municipality, which is the respondent in this case, the tax mentioned was house-tax.Thus, the exemption granted to the Railway was taken away by this notification in respect of house-tax and house-tax became payable by the I.P.Railway to the Municipality. The main issue in this case is whether the Union of India, as the owner of the Central Railway, is entitled to a refund of the tax collected by the respondent Municipality during the period from 1931 till the institution of the suit in November, 1954. The specific question is whether the Railway was liable to pay the consolidated tax assessed as rate on buildings and lands under Clause (c) of the second proviso toSection 59(1)of the Act of 1901 or the tax on lands and buildings under the notification of 26th July, 1917 issued underSection 135of the Railways Act. The relevant provisions ofSection 59of the Act of 1901 and ofSection 73of the Act of 1925 are set out in the judgement.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the Railway was liable to pay the consolidated tax assessed as rate on buildings and lands under Clause (c) of the second proviso toSection 59(1)of the Act of 1901 and the tax on lands and buildings under the notification of 26th July, 1917 issued underSection 135of the Railways Act. The Court held that the consolidated tax assessed as rate on buildings and lands under Clause (c) of the second proviso toSection 59(1)of the Act of 1901 is a tax on buildings and lands and is not a consolidated tax as suggested by the appellant. The Court also held that the notification of 26th July, 1917 issued underSection 135of the Railways Act made the Railway liable to tax on buildings and lands imposed by the Lonavla Municipality.
ruling_text: The decision of the Bombay High Court is upheld. The Union of India, as the owner of the Central Railway, is not entitled to a refund of the tax collected by the respondent Municipality during the period from 1931 till the institution of the suit in November, 1954. The Railway was liable to pay the consolidated tax assessed as rate

query_text: The case is about eviction of tenants from a residential property in Bombay. The landlord issued a notice terminating the tenancy on the grounds of default in payment of rent and change of user. The tenants did not reply to the notice and the suit for eviction was filed. During the pendency of the proceeding, defendant No.6 was added to the suit as a sub-tenant in respect of the garage. The issues in the case are whether the tenants are liable for eviction on the grounds of default in payment of rent and change of user, and whether defendant No.6 is a lawful sub-tenant. The Bombay Rent Act, 1947 and the Maharashtra Act 18 of 1987 are the statutes applicable in the case.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the tenants are liable for eviction on the grounds of default in payment of rent and change of user, and defendant No.6 is not a lawful sub-tenant as he has not pleaded and proved in the court that the position of sub-tenancy became lawful due to the consent received by him or by defendants Nos.1 to 5 for creation of sub-tenancy.
ruling_text: The present court dismissed both the writ petitions filed by the tenants and defendant No.6 against the common appellate judgment of the High Court. The court held that the tenants were not entitled to the benefit of the amendment in Section 12(3) of the Bombay Rent Act as they were not strictly covered by what is envisaged in the amendment. The court also held that defendant No.6 was not a lawful sub-tenant as he had not pleaded and proved in the court that the position of sub-tenancy became lawful due to the consent received by him or by defendants Nos.1 to 5 for creation of sub-tenancy. The court gave time to the tenants till 21.7.1989 to vacate subject to the undertaking by affidavit that no outsider would be inducted and possession shall be delivered on or before 23rd of July, 1989.

query_text: The appellant was appointed as Assistant Professor, College of Agriculture, Dapoli under Dr. Balasaheb Sawant Konkan Krishi Vidyapeeth Dapoli. He was selected and promoted as Professor of Agronomy in Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth, Rahuri on 17.8.2001. The Committee, considered Statute of the Maharashtra Agricultural Universities Statutes, 1990 and selected the appellant to the post of Head of Department of Agronomy in the University. The High Court set aside the selection on the grounds that the Selection Committee has not at all allowed the aspect of seniority to enter in their mind. The Statute under which selections are made is reproduced herein below-Statute 41- The post of Director (other than Director of Students Welfare), Dean of Faculties and other equivalent posts shall be filled in the nomination or transfer by the Pro-Chancellor. The posts of Associate Deans, Head of Departments, Professors, and other equivalent post shall be filled in by promotion and nomination in the ratio of percent of the vacant post as the Vice Chancellor may, from time to time determine. Provided that, such posts shall be filled in by promotion through the recommendation of the Selection Committee on the basis of merits and seniority in the discipline or group of disciplines, departments or sector and minimum academic qualifications and experiences, as prescribed by the statutes.
ratio: The Court held that the Selection Committee should have applied its mind to the aspect of seniority and given reasons why though the petitioner is senior according to them, selection of respondent No.3 is necessary.
ruling_text: The Court held that the High Court should not have entered into the arena of the experts when it is finally decided by duly constituted Committee of experts in the same field. The Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order passed by the High Court.

query_text: The State of Karnataka appointed stipendiary graduates or local candidates by making special provisions in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. The respondents were recruited under these rules and Rule 3(1) of the said Rules provided that the appointment shall be on contract basis for a period not exceeding one year or until the candidates selected by the recruitment committees report to duty whichever is earlier and that their appointment shall stand terminated on the expiry of the said period. The issue before the court was whether the respondents who were appointed on contract basis and later absorbed into regular service were entitled to have their pay fixed by taking note of the service rendered by them on contract basis and necessary benefit of increment be given by stepping up the salary. The Karnataka Civil Services (Absorption of Persons Appointed on Contract Basis in the category of posts of Primary School Teachers, Secondary School Teachers, Government Junior College Lecturers, First Grade College Lecturers, Lecturers in Polytechnics, Lecturers in Government Engineering Colleges, into State Civil Services) (Special) Rules, 1990
ratio: The court held that the respondents were not entitled to have their pay fixed by taking note of the service rendered by them on contract basis and necessary benefit of increment be given by stepping up the salary. The court further held that the expression local candidate and Rule 41A of the Karnataka Civil Services Rules and Note to Rule was however interpreted in a very strained manner by the Tribunal to uphold the contention raised on behalf of the petitioners.
ruling_text: The court overruled the view taken by the Tribunal in Parameshwarappas case and held that the respondents were not entitled to have their pay fixed by taking note of the service rendered by them on contract basis and necessary benefit of increment be given by stepping up the salary. The court's decision clarifies that the service rendered by contract employees or stipendiary graduates will not be counted for any purpose and their salary is fixed at the emolument which is less than the minimum of the pay scale attached to the post. The court also made it clear that the period of service rendered will not be counted for any purpose. Therefore, the claim of the respondents could not have been brought under Rule 41A at all.

ruling_text: The court dismissed the writ petition filed by the Gram Panchayats challenging the notification and the exclusion of the notified area from their jurisdiction. The court upheld the validity of the notification issued under Section 16 of the Gujarat Industrial Development Act, 1962 and the exclusion of the notified area from the jurisdiction of the Saij Gram Panchayat under Section 9(2) of the Gujarat Panchayat Act, 1961. query_text: The appellants Haricharan Kurmi and Jogia Hajam were charged with dacoity and murder along with four other persons. They were convicted by the Sessions Judge and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. Pending the appeal, the High Court issued a rule for enhancement of the sentence, and finally, the rule was made absolute, and they were ordered to be hanged. The main point raised before the Supreme Court was that the High Court misconceived the ambit and scope of the decision in Ram Prakash v. State of Punjab and treated the confession made by the co-accused as substantive evidence against the appellants. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, ss. 3, 30, and 133.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that though confession mentioned in s. 30 of the Indian Evidence Act is not evidence as defined by s. 3, it is an element that may be taken into consideration by the criminal courts. However, in dealing with the case against an accused person, the court cannot start with the confession of a co-accused person. It must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after forming an opinion regarding the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession to lend assurance to the conclusion of guilt.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the order of the High Court directing that the appellants be hanged. The Court held that there was no sufficient evidence to prove the prosecution case. The Supreme Court reiterated the well-established principles in regard to the admissibility and the effect of confessional statements made by co-accused persons. The Court held that the confession of a co-accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion. The Court also emphasized that in criminal trials, there is no scope for applying the principle of moral conviction or grave suspicion. The presumption of innocence assists the accused person, and he is entitled to the benefit of doubt when the other evidence adduced against him is wholly unsatisfactory.

query_text: The case involves the acquisition of land by the Punjab Town Improvement Trust under the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922. ratio: The court held that the belting awarded by the Arbitrator was correct and that the claimants were not entitled to additional interest beyond the statutory rate of 12% per annum. However, the court also held that the claimants were entitled to solatium and interest for one year from the date of taking possession.
ruling_text: The court upheld the belting awarded by the Arbitrator and set aside the additional interest awarded by the High Court. The court also awarded solatium and interest for one year from the date of taking possession to the claimants. The court's decision in this case clarifies the application of the Land Acquisition Amendment Act, 1984, to acquisitions made under the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922. The court also reaffirmed the principle that additional interest beyond the statutory rate of 12% per annum is not payable. The relevant provisions of the Kerala Agricultural Income-Tax Act, 1950, including sections 3, 5, 17, 18, 19, 31, 32, 34, and 35, are discussed in the judgement.
ratio: The High Court held that the power of revision vested in the Commissioner under section 34 of the Act could not be invoked for the purpose of assessing income that had escaped assessment and that such income could be assessed only by resorting to the procedure under section 35 of the Act within the time limit prescribed therein.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and held that the Commissioner had jurisdiction to make the order under section 34 of the Act. The Supreme Court's decision clarifies the scope of the Commissioner's revisional power under section 34 of the Kerala Agricultural Income-Tax Act, 1950, and the procedure for assessing income that has escaped assessment under section 35 of the Act. query_text: The case is about a dispute over the change of land use from residential to commercial in a residential area in Bangalore, India. The dispute arose when the Respondent No.6, who had purchased a plot of land in the area, applied for permission to convert the land use to commercial for the purpose of running a vegetarian restaurant. The Jayanagar 5th Block Residents Welfare Association filed objections to the application, but later withdrew them. The Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) granted permission for the change of land use, and the Respondent No.6 started running the restaurant without obtaining a license. The main issues in the case are whether the BDA had the jurisdiction to grant permission for the change of land use, and whether the Respondent No.6 was entitled to run a restaurant in the residential area without obtaining a license. The case is governed by the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, and the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976.
ratio: The Supreme Court of India held that the BDA had no jurisdiction to grant permission for the change of land use from residential to commercial, as the land in question was within the residential zone and the Zoning Regulations did not permit the running of a restaurant in the area. The court also held that the Respondent No.6 was not entitled to run a restaurant without obtaining a license, as the BDA had not granted permission for the same.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and held that the BDA had no jurisdiction to grant permission for the change of land use from residential to commercial. The case highlights the importance of adhering to the Zoning Regulations and obtaining necessary permissions before changing the land use. The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms the principle that the jurisdiction of statutory authorities must be exercised within the bounds of the law, and that any violation of the law will not be condoned. The Respondent No.6, who had invested heavily in the construction of the restaurant, was left with the option of using the premises for a permissible use under the Zoning Regulations.

The A.P. Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
ratio: The court held that the building was non-residential and the respondent was entitled to seek eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement.

query_text: The case is about two appeals arising out of suits filed in the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu. The first appeal is about a suit for damages for malicious prosecution, and the second appeal is about a suit for recovery of money on a promissory note. The Limitation Act, 1963, and the Portuguese Civil Code are the relevant statutes.
ratio: The court held that the provisions of the Portuguese Civil Code relating to Limitation are local law within the meaning of Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963, and they continue to be in force in the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu. The court further held that there is no repugnancy between the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the Portuguese Civil Code, and the provisions of the Portuguese Civil Code are saved by Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ruling_text: The court dismissed both appeals. The court held that the provisions of the Portuguese Civil Code relating to Limitation continue to be in force in the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu, and they are not repealed by the Limitation Act, 1963, by necessary implication. The court further held that there is no repugnancy between the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the Portuguese Civil Code, and the provisions of the Portuguese Civil Code are saved by Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963.

query_text: The appellant, Lallan Chaubey, along with his father and brother, was tried for committing the murder of Raj Kumari. The prosecution case was that there was a dispute between the two sides over the sehans (open courtyard) between their houses. On May 31, 1987, Raj Kumari was standing outside towards the east of their house when her younger brother Om Narain started sweeping the land between the two sehans. The appellant forbade him from coming over the land, and when Om Narain persisted, the appellant attempted to assault him. When Raj Kumari intervened, the appellant aimed his gun at the informant and fired, hitting Raj Kumari on the right side of her chest. The issues before the court were whether the appellant had committed the murder of Raj Kumari and whether the trial court had correctly acquitted him. The case was tried under sections 302/307/34 of the Penal Code.
ratio: The High Court examined the evidence adduced by the prosecution in great detail and considered the reasons assigned by the trial court for recording the judgment of acquittal. The High Court held that the trial court had rejected the consistent and otherwise highly credible evidences of the eye witnesses for reasons that were wholly untenable and the judgment of the trial court insofar as the appellant is concerned, had resulted into miscarriage of justice.
ruling_text: The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the trial court and convicted and sentenced the appellant to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court correctly set aside the judgment of acquittal passed by the trial court and convicted the appellant for committing the murder of Raj Kumari. The evidence adduced by the prosecution was consistent and highly credible, and the reasons assigned by the trial court for rejecting it were wholly untenable. The appellant was rightly sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life.

query_text: The appellant, a daily rated worker in the Southern Railway, was terminated from his service after he went on a fast to demand benefits for himself and his co-workers. The termination was made during the pendency of a writ petition filed by the appellant and his co-workers seeking regular employment status. The main issue in this case is whether the termination of the appellant's service constitutes retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and if so, whether the pre-conditions to valid retrenchment have been complied with. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, governs the termination of service of workmen in industries. Section 25F of the Act provides that no workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until the conditions set out in the Act are satisfied.
ratio: The court held that the termination of the appellant's service constitutes retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as it was made for any reason whatsoever and the appellant was a daily rated worker. The court further held that the pre-conditions to valid retrenchment have not been complied with, as the appellant was not given notice, compensation, or an opportunity to be heard.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the termination of the appellant's service. The court directed the Railway administration to regularize the appellant's service and grant him all the benefits and privileges available to regular employees. This case highlights the importance of complying with the pre-conditions to valid retrenchment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The court's decision reaffirms the principle that termination of service must be fair, reasonable, and in accordance with the law. The court's ruling also emphasizes the need to protect the rights of daily rated workers and ensure that they are not discriminated against in comparison to regular employees.

query_text: The case is about the promotion of firemen to the post of leading firemen in the Mysore Fire Force. The promotion was made on the basis of seniority, but respondents challenged it on the ground that the promotion should have been made on the basis of a qualifying examination as prescribed in the Mysore Fire Force (Cadre Recruitment) Rules, 1971. The main issue in the case is whether the promotion to the post of leading firemen should be made on the basis of seniority or a qualifying examination. The case is governed by the Fire Force Act, 1964, and the Mysore Fire Force (Cadre Recruitment) Rules, 1971.
ratio: The court held that the promotion to the post of leading firemen should be made on the basis of seniority and not a qualifying examination. The court further held that the Karnataka Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 1977, which provide for promotion on the basis of seniority, apply to the posts under the present establishment, and the Mysore Fire Force (Cadre Recruitment) Rules, 1971, have been superseded to the extent that they provide for a qualifying examination for promotion.
ruling_text: The court upheld the promotion of the appellants to the post of leading firemen on the basis of seniority. The court's decision in the case reaffirms the principle that promotion to higher posts should be made on the basis of seniority and not a qualifying examination. The court also clarified that the Karnataka Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 1977, apply to the posts under the present establishment, and the Mysore Fire Force (Cadre Recruitment) Rules, 1971, have been superseded to the extent that they provide for a qualifying examination for promotion.

query_text: The case involves a partnership firm, Messrs.N. V. Shanmugam and Co., carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of snuff under a deed of partnership dated April 20, 1955. The partners were P. Ramiah Nadar, Murugavel Nagar and Shanmughavel Nadar. P. Mohan, minor had been admitted to the benefits of the partnership, his share in the net profits being 1/6th. The deed of partnership provided that the partnership could not be dissolved before August 1, 1955. But it was open to the partners to continue the partnership or enter into a fresh partnership on fresh terms and conditions. The main issue in this case is whether the profits earned in the business should be considered as profits earned by an association of persons or whether it should be considered as having been earned by individuals. The Income Tax Act, 1922
ratio: The court held that the profits earned in the business should be considered as profits earned by an association of persons and not by individuals. The receivers appointed by the court were merely the representatives of the real owners of the business i.e. the erstwhile partners of the firm. The primary liability to pay the tax due was that of the real owners. The tax may be levied and recovered from the Receivers under s. 41 of the Act. The fact that there were three receivers did not make them an association of receivers. The three receivers jointly represented the real owners. The real question is whether the Persons whom the receivers represented constituted an association of persons.
ruling_text: The court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. The court ruled that the profits earned in the business should be considered as profits earned by an association of persons and not by individuals. The receivers appointed by the court were merely the representatives of the real owners of the business i.e. the erstwhile partners of the firm. The primary liability to pay the tax due was that of the real owners. The tax may be levied and recovered from the Receivers under s. 41 of the Act. The fact that there were three receivers did not make them an association of receivers. The three receivers jointly represented the real owners. The real question is whether the Persons whom the receivers represented constituted an association of persons.

query_text: The Appellant was a Constable in the year 1995 and was positioned as Head Constable under the ORP Policy in 2001. The main issue is whether the IG has the power to interfere with the recommendation of the SP and whether the IG can substitute his decision to that of the DPC. query_text: The case is about an appeal against the order of the High Court of Judicature at Patna, which dismissed the application for anticipatory bail filed by the appellant in connection with FIR No.79 of 2020 registered under Sections 341, 323, 354B, 504, and of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 3/4 of the Prevention of Witch (Daain) Practices Act, 1999. The Orissa Ministerial Service (Method and Recruitment to Posts of Lower Division Assistants in the Offices of Heads of Department) Rules, 1975
ratio: The court held that the irregular appointees cannot be placed above the regular appointees on the basis of total length of service.

query_text: The respondent was a conductor in the appellant-Corporation. He was charged with consuming alcohol while on duty, not issuing tickets to passengers, and misappropriating funds. The appellant-Corporation conducted an inquiry and found the charges to be true, dismissing the respondent from service. The respondent raised an industrial dispute, which was decided by the Labour Court, Gulbarga. The Labour Court held that the charges of misappropriation were proved, but the inquiry proceedings were illegal and invalid. The Labour Court directed reinstatement and back wages. The appellant-Corporation challenged the award before the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore. Whether the inquiry proceedings were illegal and invalid, and whether the respondent was entitled to reinstatement and back wages. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
ratio: The Supreme Court held that the inquiry proceedings were valid and that the respondent was not entitled to reinstatement and back wages. The Supreme Court noted that the charges of misappropriation were grave in nature and had the effect of disrupting the services of public transport. The Supreme Court also noted that the respondent had failed to test the evidence led by the management and that the testimony of the management's witness was not discarded.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court and of the Labour Court. The Supreme Court held that the respondent was not entitled to reinstatement and back wages. The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the appellant-Corporation to dismiss the respondent from service due to charges of misappropriation and disrupting the services of public transport. The Supreme Court noted that the respondent had failed to test the evidence led by the management and that the testimony of the management's witness was not discarded. The Supreme Court set aside the order of the High Court and of the Labour Court, directing reinstatement and back wages.

query_text: The assessee, Rangachari, assigned a portion of his profits from a partnership firm to his wife and daughters through a deed of settlement. The main issue was whether the profits settled by the assessee on his wife and two daughters could be included in his total income for the purposes of assessment under the Income-tax Act, 1922. The Income-tax Act, 1922, specifically s.16(1)(c) and the third proviso to s.16(1)(c) were relevant to the case.
ratio: The High Court held that the third proviso was not attracted and that the income had accrued to the assessee in the first instance, and had then been applied for payments under the deeds.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the High Court and held that the profits settled by the assessee on his wife and two daughters could be included in his total income for the purposes of assessment. The case highlights the importance of understanding the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1922, and the relevance of the third proviso to s.16(1)(c) in determining the total income of an assessee. The Supreme Court has clarified that profits settled by an assessee on his wife and daughters can be included in his total income for the purposes of assessment.

query_text: The plaintiffs, Bilas Rai Bohra and Sree Ram Bohra, sued the union of india (UOI) for the recovery of Rs.13,448 from the defendant for compensation on account of loss and damage suffered by the plaintiffs owing to non-delivery of bales of cloth which had been consigned on October 20, 1948 by M s Ram Kishun Das Sagarmal of Bombay to the plaints under the description of M s Bansidhar Ganpat Rai. Whether the appeal of the union of india (UOI) before the High Court against the respondent Sree Ram Bohra, respondent No.2, was competent after it had abated against respondent No.1, Bilas Rai Bohra, on account of his heirs and legal representatives being not brought on the record. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
ratio: The High Court held that the appeal had become incompetent and was liable to the dismissed as the joint family had gained by virtue of the decree passed in favour of the joint family through the representation of Bilas Rai Bohra and in case the appeal was permitted to proceed against the joint family in the presence of the other karta Sree Ram Bohra, there might be occasion for the coming into existence of two inconsistent decrees.
ruling_text: The appeal of the union of india (UOI) against the respondent Sree Ram Bohra, respondent No.2, was incompetent after it had abated against respondent No.1, Bilas Rai Bohra, on account of his heirs and legal representatives being not brought on the record. The High Court was right in holding that the appeal against Sree Ram Bohra alone became incompetent as the decree against both the respondents viz., Bilas Rai Bohra and Sree Ram Bohra was joint decree. There was nothing in the decree to indicate for whose benefit it was passed or in what proportions the two decree-holders were to get the decretal amount. The appeal against Sree Ram Bohra was therefore incompetent.

ratio: The court held that the agreement had ceased to operate from 25th February 1978, and therefore, the question of repugnancy of Section 84-B with Sections 9A and 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act did not arise.
ruling_text: The court set aside the decision of the High Court declaring Section 84-B as ultra vires the State Legislature on account of repugnancy with the provisions of Sections 9A and 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The court has also noted that the accused have a criminal history of two cases for giving threats to the witnesses and the family members of the deceased.
