query_text: The case involves the valuation of house-property wholly or mainly used for residential purposes for the purposes of ascertaining the net wealth under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The Central Board of Revenue in pursuance of the rule-making power conferred by Section 46 of the Act promulgated rules known as the Wealth Tax Rules, 1957. These were amended from time to time and Rule BB with which we are now concerned came to be inserted by the Wealth Tax (Amendment) Rules, 1979 with effect from 1-4-1979. The principal question in these cases is whether Rule 1-BB is a provision of substantive law, not expressly rendered applicable to the valuation for the earlier years, and therefore only prospective or whether it is merely procedural attracted to all pending cases. The Wealth Tax Act, 1957 and the Wealth Tax Rules, 1957
ratio: The court held that Rule 1-BB is essentially a rule of evidence as to the choice of one of the well accepted methods of valuation in respect of certain kinds of properties with a view to achieving uniformity in valuation and avoiding disparate valuations resulting from application of different methods of valuation respecting properties of similar nature and character.
ruling_text: The court upheld the decisions of various High Courts and held that Rule 1-BB is merely procedural and attracted to all pending cases. The court's decision clarifies the nature of Rule 1-BB and its applicability to pending cases. It also highlights the importance of uniformity in valuation and the need to avoid disparate valuations.

query_text: The father of the respondent was a partner in a firm and owned property that the firm was occupying as a tenant at will. He transferred the property to two of his sons through a deed of settlement. The firm continued to occupy the property and pay rent to the two donees. The father also requested the firm to transfer five sums of Rs.20,000 each to the credit of his five sons in the firm's books. The sons did not withdraw any amount from their accounts in the firm, and the amounts continued to be invested in the firm for which interest was paid to them. The father continued to be a partner of the firm even after the transfer until the firm was dissolved. Whether the property and the amount of Rs.lakh gifted to the sons could be included in the estate of the deceased under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953. Section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, states that property taken under any gift, whenever made, shall be deemed to pass on the donor's death to the extent that bona fide possession and enjoyment of it was not immediately assumed by the donee and thenceforward retained to the entire exclusion of the donor of any benefit to him by contract or otherwise.
ratio: The court held that the first two conditions of section 10 were satisfied, as the donees had assumed possession and enjoyment of the property and retained such possession and enjoyment to the entire exclusion of the donor. However, the last limb of the condition, which states that the deceased must be entirely excluded from any benefit by contract or otherwise, was not applicable in this case. The court further held that the benefit the donor had as a member of the partnership was not referable to the gift but was unconnected with it.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and held that neither the property nor the amount of Rs.lakh could be included in the estate of the deceased. The court's decision was based on the interpretation of section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, and the facts of the case. The court held that the property and the amount gifted to the sons were enjoyed by the donees to the exclusion of the donor, and the donor did not derive any benefit from the gift. Therefore, the property and the amount could not be included in the estate of the deceased under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.

query_text: The case involves pensioners of the Assam Oil Company Limited, which was nationalized and taken over by the Government of India in 1981. ratio: The court held that the pensioners, who retired before the nationalization of the Assam Oil Company Limited, are entitled to the benefit of the revised pension scheme made admissible to retirees of the Indian Oil Corporation. query_text: The MGM Medical College used to be run by private registered society. The respondents in these two appeals were employees of the College. query_text: The case involves dependents of teaching and non-teaching staff in non-government recognized aided schools and colleges in Uttar Pradesh who died in harness. The issue is whether the respondents are entitled to appointment on class III post of Clerk or whether they can only be appointed on class IV post. The Uttar Pradesh Recruitment of Dependents of Government Servants Dying in Harness Rules, 1974 and the Regulations made in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government under sub-section (4) of Section 9 of the P. Intermediate Education Act, 1921, govern the appointment of dependents of teaching and non-teaching staff in non-government recognized aided schools and colleges in Uttar Pradesh.
ratio: The court held that the respondents are not entitled to appointment on class III post of Clerk and can only be appointed on class IV post. The court further held that the creation of supernumerary post in class III is not required for the appointment of dependents of teaching and non-teaching staff in non-government recognized aided schools and colleges in Uttar Pradesh who died in harness.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeals filed by the State and set aside the orders of the High Court directing the appointment of the respondents on class III post of Clerk. The court held that the respondents are only entitled to appointment on class IV post and that the creation of supernumerary post in class III is not required. The court's decision clarifies the scope of appointment on compassionate grounds for dependents of teaching and non-teaching staff in non-government recognized aided schools and colleges in Uttar Pradesh who died in harness. The court has restricted the appointment to class IV post and has clarified that the creation of supernumerary post in class III is not required. This decision ensures that the right of other persons who are eligible for appointment to seek employment on those posts by direct recruitment is not unduly interfered with.

query_text: The appellant, K.C.P. Limited, a cement factory in Macherla, Andhra Pradesh, offered to supply cement to the Nagarjunasagar Project at a concessional rate of Rs.47.50 per ton. The State Trading Corporation was appointed as the canalising agency for the purchase of cement at a controlled price fixed under the Cement Control Order of 1956. The appellant informed the State Trading Corporation that it had entered into an agreement with the Nagarjunasagar Control Board for the supply of cement for the said project at the concessional rate of Rs.47.50 per ton. The State Trading Corporation allowed the rebate of Rs.7/- per ton, the difference between the ex-works price allowed to the appellant and the concessional rate, and the appellant was paid the ex-works price less rebate. The appellant, as the selling agent of the State Trading Corporation, started supplying cement directly to the said project from 18.4.1958. The appellant recovered the price from the purchaser as agent of the State Trading Corporation. The issues in this case are whether there was a concluded contract between the parties for the supply of cement for the Nagarjunasagar Project at a fixed price of Rs.47.50 per ton, and whether the appellant was entitled to recover the rebate of Rs.7/- per ton from the State Trading Corporation after 1.11.1961. The Cement Control Order of 1956 and the Cement Control Order of 1961 are the statutes relevant to this case.
ratio: The ratio of the case is that there was no concluded contract between the parties for the supply of cement for the Nagarjunasagar Project at a fixed price of Rs.47.50 per ton. The appellant had offered rebate of Rs.7/- on the Control Price of Cement in respect of the cement which was to be supplied by it for the Nagarjunasagar Project and the State Trading Corporation accepted this arrangement. The appellant was entitled to recover the rebate of Rs.7/- per ton from the State Trading Corporation after 1.11.1961 as it had wrongfully debited the amount to their account by making reversal entries.
ruling_text: The Andhra Pradesh High Court has upheld the claim of the State Trading Corporation for recovery of the excess amount for which credit was thus taken by the appellant by making reversal entries in the accounts submitted by it to the State Trading Corporation. The appellant was not entitled to recover the rebate of Rs.7/- per ton from the State Trading Corporation after 1.11.1961 as it had wrongfully debited the amount to their account by making reversal entries. The State Trading Corporation was justified in filing the suit and claiming the amount of rebate which had been wrongfully debited to their account by the appellant.

query_text: The case involves the murder of Padam Singh on the farm of the appellant by Doongar Singh and two others on 4-3-1978. The appellant's car, No. J.F.2118, was used to carry the dead body and throw it into a well on the boundary of village Ramasani. The car was then brought back to the appellant's bungalow, where it was washed the same day. The appellant had his car washed again on 8-3-1978 at a petrol pump owned by Umraokhan. The issue in this case is whether the Sessions Judge was correct in framing a charge against the appellant under Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1860, based solely on the fact that the appellant had his car washed at a petrol pump. The relevant statute in this case is Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1860, which states that "whoever, knowing that an offence has been committed, causes any evidence of the commission of that offence to disappear, with the intention of screening the offender from legal punishment, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both."
ratio: The Supreme Court of India held that the Sessions Judge's order framing a charge against the appellant under Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1973 was illegal as there was no legal evidence or any material on the record of the factual ingredients of an offence under Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1860. The court further held that the charge framed as per Section 228 of the Criminal Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was also illegal.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Sessions Judge and the High Court. The court held that the charge framed against the appellant under Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1860 was illegal and that the appellant was entitled to be discharged under Section 227 of the Criminal Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Supreme Court of India has clarified that in order to frame a charge under Section 201 of the Penal Code, 1860, there must be legal evidence or some material on the record of the factual ingredients of the offence. In this case, the Sessions Judge erred in framing a charge against the appellant based solely on the fact that the appellant had his car washed at a petrol pump. The court has also reiterated the principle that a person is entitled to be discharged under Section 227 of the Criminal Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 if there is no legal evidence or any material on the record of the factual ingredients of an offence.

query_text: The case is about four writ petitions filed at Jodhpur Bench of the Rajasthan, High Court. The issue is whether the Commission had to call candidates by treating the number of posts available in the general category to be (i.e. as originally fixed and on account of non-availability of candidates in SC ST categories). The Rajasthan Judicial Service Rules, 1955 (in short the Rules) and the Rajasthan Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1969 (in short the Higher Judicial Rules)

ruling_text: The High Court directed the Commission to call not less than candidates from the General Category for interview instead of 189. query_text: The respondent was a temporary clerk who was appointed on 10th December 1936 and was confirmed in that post on 1st September 1938. Rule 2046(b) of the Railway Establishment Code

query_text: The case involves a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) that owned a property. The father, Moola Gounder, died intestate leaving behind six legal heirs, including two sons and four daughters. The two sons formed a coparcenary and inherited 1/3 of the property each, while the remaining 1/3 was to be inherited by the mother and the four daughters. However, the mother and two daughters executed a release deed relinquishing their rights in the property in favor of the two sons. The youngest daughter filed a suit claiming partition of the property. The main issue is whether the mother could act as the natural guardian of the minor daughters in respect of the property inherited from Moola Gounder. The Hindu Minority Guardianship Act, 1956, and the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, are relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The High Court held that the property in the hands of the legal heirs of Moola Gounder, after his death, was Joint Hindu Family property and the mother could not have acted as guardian of the minor. It was, therefore, held that the release deed was void ab initio and, as such, was not required to be challenged.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal filed by one of the brothers. The case highlights the importance of understanding the legal framework governing the inheritance of property in a Hindu Undivided Family. The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms the principle that the mother cannot act as the natural guardian of the minor daughters in respect of the property inherited from the father. The release deed executed by the mother and two daughters was held to be void ab initio, and the property remained joint property of all the legal heirs of Moola Gounder.

query_text: The case involves a dispute between two parties over a contract that contains a non-exclusive jurisdiction clause in favor of the English courts. The plaintiff, who is based in India, filed a suit in the Bombay High Court seeking damages for breach of contract. The defendant, who is based in England, filed a similar suit in the English courts seeking payment of the minimum guaranteed amount under the contract. The plaintiff then sought an anti-suit injunction from the Bombay High Court to restrain the defendant from pursuing the English suit. The main issue in this case is whether the Bombay High Court has the power to grant an anti-suit injunction to restrain the defendant from pursuing the English suit, having regard to the non-exclusive jurisdiction clause in the contract. The relevant statute in this case is the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which governs the jurisdiction of the Indian courts.
ratio: The court held that the Bombay High Court does not have the power to grant an anti-suit injunction to restrain the defendant from pursuing the English suit, having regard to the non-exclusive jurisdiction clause in the contract. ruling_text: The court dismissed the plaintiff's application for an anti-suit injunction and allowed the defendant to proceed with the English suit. This case highlights the importance of jurisdiction clauses in contracts and the limitations on the power of courts to grant anti-suit injunctions. The court's decision reinforces the principle that parties to a contract are bound by the jurisdiction clause they have agreed to, and that courts will not interfere with the jurisdiction of a foreign court unless there are strong reasons to do so.

query_text: The appellant company was formed in 1937 in Bhopal State and was exempted by the Ruler of that State from payment of all taxes till October 31, 1948. ratio: The court held that the Taxation Laws (Merged States) (Removal of Difficulties) Amendment Order, 1962 is invalid because no difficulty was proved to have arisen justifying the invocation of the power under s. 6 of Act 67 of 1949. query_text: The case involves three batches of appeals from the Delhi, Madras, and Allahabad High Courts, challenging the taxability of pan masala or gutka under state enactments. ratio: The court held that state legislatures are empowered to levy sales tax on pan masala or gutka, and that the rate of state tax can exceed the limit prescribed by the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeals and upheld the judgments of the Delhi, Madras, and Allahabad High Courts. query_text: The case involves the appellant, who was carrying cows milk in a truck and was intercepted by a raiding party. Samples of cows milk were taken from out of several cans carried by the appellant and were sent for analysis. The samples were found adulterated and the appellant was prosecuted for an offence punishable under s. 16 read with s.7 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The main issue in this case is whether the sale of each sample constituted a distinct and separate offence or there was only one offence committed by the appellant by selling samples of adulterated cows milk from six cans to the Food Inspectors for analysis. The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which prohibits the manufacturing, storing, selling or distributing of any adulterated article of food.
ratio: The court held that the sale of each sample constituted a distinct and separate offence and the appellant was liable to be tried for six different offences in respect of sales of six samples. The court observed that the sale of each sample was a separate sale and each such sale constituted a separate breach of the provisions of s.7 of the Act leading to a separate offence punishable under s.16 of the Act.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and held that the appellant was liable for different offences. The court's decision is based on the interpretation of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and the definition of sale in section 2(xiii) of the Act, which includes within it sale of any article of food for analysis. The court held that the taking of each sample would be necessary and justified for the purpose of analysis, and hence each taking of sample would constitute distinct and independent sale and each such sale would be an offending act attracting the penal provisions of the Act.

query_text: The petitioners, M s. query_text: The first respondent filed a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the High Court of Delhi challenging the acquisition of lands under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The main issue was whether the acquisition of the land would be deemed to have lapsed under subSection (2) ofSection 24of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (the 2013 Act) due to non-payment of compensation, despite physical possession having been taken. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
ratio: The Court held that subSection (2) ofSection 24of the 2013 Act would not apply in this case as physical possession of the land had been taken by the appellant. The Court further held that the acquisition would continue to be valid under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the first respondent would not be entitled to compensation under the 2013 Act.
ruling_text: The Court condoned the delay in filing the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court. The Court held that the acquisition of the land would continue to be valid under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the first respondent would not be entitled to compensation under the 2013 Act. The Court's decision reaffirms the principle that physical possession of land is a crucial factor in determining whether an acquisition has lapsed under the 2013 Act. The Court's decision also clarifies that the 2013 Act would not apply to acquisitions that were initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and had culminated in an award before the 2013 Act came into force. The Court's decision also highlights the importance of ensuring that acquired land is not misused for purposes other than those for which it was acquired.

query_text: The case involved a sum of Rs.85,000/- deposited with the appellant by his sister in January 1946. The appellant's sister migrated to Pakistan between June to August 1949. The Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 and the Limitation Act, 1908 were the statutes involved in the case.
ratio: The court held that the amount was not recoverable under s. 48 of the Act as it stood at the relevant time but was recoverable under s. 48 of the Act as amended. The court also held that the amount was not barred by limitation as the period of limitation had not even begun to run on the date the appellant's sister migrated to Pakistan.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal. The court's decision was based on the interpretation of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 and the Limitation Act, 1908. The court held that the amount was not recoverable under s. 48 of the Act as it stood at the relevant time but was recoverable under s. 48 of the Act as amended. The court also held that the amount was not barred by limitation as the period of limitation had not even begun to run on the date the appellant's sister migrated to Pakistan. The court's decision reaffirmed the principle that procedural amendments to law apply retrospectively in the sense that they apply to all actions after the date they come into force even though the actions may have begun earlier or the claim on which the action may be based may be of an anterior date.

query_text: The case is about four accused, A1 Murli, A2 Harish Chandra, A3 Chandra Pal and A4 Som Nath, who were put to trial for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC. ratio: The High Court accepted the evidence of the prosecution recorded by the trial court but altered the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC into one under Section 304 Part I IPC and reduced the sentence to seven years.
ruling_text: The present court has set aside the order of the High Court converting the offence under Section 302 IPC into one under Section 304 Part I IPC and restored the order of the trial court convicting the respondent under Section 302 IPC. The respondent has been taken into custody to serve out the remaining part of the sentence. query_text: The respondents ancestors were granted a cash allowance called Tainat by the Peshwas. Whether the cash allowance payable was permanent and hereditary, and whether the commutation amount was deductible from the cash allowance for the payment of compensation. The Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienation Abolition Act, 1955, Section 17
ratio: The court held that the Ruler of Jamkhandi had sovereign power and was the fountain head of all sources of authority, and he could change the Tainat cash allowance at his sweet will and pleasure. The court also held that the commutation amount was deductible from the cash allowance while calculating the compensation payable to the respondent.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court. The court upheld the sovereign power of the Ruler of Jamkhandi to change the Tainat cash allowance and held that the commutation amount was deductible from the cash allowance for the payment of compensation. query_text: The case concerns the Industrial Commercial Trust Limited and its subsidiary, the Asian Air Associates, which were established in 1943. The Asian Air Associates entered into a contract with Ramdas and Sons for the purchase of machinery and tools, and later, the first accused, Rusy Mistry, took over both companies and became a partner in the Asian Air Associates. The company entered into a contract with the Director of Munitions Production representing the Government of India for the manufacture, overhauling, repair and modification of Royal Air Force equipment. The company was entitled to actual cost plus 1/2 per cent profit on the actual cost of the work done by it, with depreciation being one of the items to be taken into consideration in determining the actual cost. The issues in this case are whether the accused dishonestly inflated the cost of the machinery purchased from Ramdas and Sons by forging Ex.D, and whether they attempted to cheat the Government by submitting bills based upon depreciation of per cent allowed by the contract entered into between the Asian Air Associates and the Government of India, calculated upon the value of the machinery bought from Ramdas and Sons shown at a higher figure than what was actually paid to them. The Indian Penal Code, Sections 120B, 467, 471, 417, 511, and 34, are applicable in this case.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the accused did not make any claims in the bills on the basis of the depreciation calculated on the inflated costs of machinery purchased from Ramdas and Sons. The bills submitted to the Government of India had no direct bearing on actual capital account of depreciation charges. Therefore, the necessary ingredient of the third charge, i.e., the intention to fabricate the document was only to cheat the Government in the manner stated in the first charge, was not established.
ruling_text: The accused were acquitted of the offences with which they were charged. The accused were acquitted as the prosecution failed to establish that they dishonestly inflated the cost of the machinery purchased from Ramdas and Sons by forging Ex.D and attempted to cheat the Government by submitting bills based upon depreciation of per cent allowed by the contract entered into between the Asian Air Associates and the Government of India, calculated upon the value of the machinery bought from Ramdas and Sons shown at a higher figure than what was actually paid to them.

query_text: The case is about a challenge to the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax Act, 1964, as amended by the Amending Act No.15 of 1973, which sought to levy tax on both lands and buildings in the urban areas of the State of Rajasthan. query_text: The respondent claimed ownership of a portion of a public street in Chaura Bazar near Rai Saheb Jogiwara, Karnal. The main issue was whether the disputed area was a public street or private property. The Haryana Municipalities Act, 1973, defines a street as any road, footway, square, court, public park, alley or passage, accessible to the public, and includes every vacant space notwithstanding that it may be private property and partly or wholly obstructed by any gate, post, chain or other barrier, if houses, shops or other buildings abut thereon, and if it is used by any persons as means of access to or from any public place or thoroughfare.
ratio: The court held that the disputed area was a public street as it was accessible to the public and used as a means of access to or from a public place or thoroughfare. The court also noted that the respondent had constructed a shop on the public street without authorization, and the appellant had the power to have the unauthorized construction removed.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the respondent's suit for damages and held that the appellant had the power to have the unauthorized construction removed. The court's decision reaffirmed the principle that public streets are vested in the Municipal Committee and that unauthorized constructions on public streets can be removed by the Municipal Committee. The decision also highlighted the importance of obtaining proper authorization before constructing any building on a public street.

ratio: The court held that since the appellant had made a request for transfer to Trivandrum, it must be deemed to be a fresh appointment for the purposes of seniority.

query_text: The case involves a loan agreement between a bank and a borrower, with a guarantor providing a personal guarantee. query_text: The case is about a dispute between a security agency, Lingegowd Detective Security Chamber (P) Limited, and a group of workers employed by the agency. The Court has also clarified that the security agency, Lingegowd, is not required to pay the minimum wages as the nature of services rendered by it is not a scheduled employment. The case highlights the importance of the Minimum Wages Act in ensuring that workers are paid fair wages for their work. The decision of the Supreme Court reaffirms the principle that the Act applies to any person who employs one or more employees in a scheduled employment, and that the definition of "employee" in the Act is broad enough to cover workers employed in various capacities.

The Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, the Companies Act, 1956, and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 are the relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The court held that the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the High Court was not justified in issuing the direction. The court further held that the dispute between the parties was eminently a civil dispute and not a dispute under the provisions of the Companies Act.
ruling_text: The court set aside the impugned orders and remitted the matters to the Collector High Court for fresh decision on merits as expeditiously as possible within period of three months, keeping in view the observations made hereinabove. The court's decision highlights the importance of upholding the rule of law and the jurisdiction of civil courts in resolving disputes between parties. The court's observations also serve as a reminder that parties should not be given unfair advantages over each other in the matter of enforcement of statutory rights.

query_text:
The respondent is a consumer of electricity and had a meter installed by the appellant at his factory premises. An inspection was done on 04.07.2000 and the Inspecting staff found that there was tampering with the meter, leading to a demand of Rs.1,07,326/- for actual consumption of energy. The respondent questioned the demand and filed a complaint before the District Forum, stating that there was sparking in the T. Box installed at his factory premises and he had informed the appellant to rectify the defect. However, instead of rectifying the meter, the appellant raised the demand for alleged tampering. * Whether there was tampering with the meter or it was a case of a faulty meter.
* Whether notice was required to be given before raising the demand. The Indian Electricity Act, 1910 and the Indian Electricity Rules, 1956.
ratio:
* The court held that in cases of tampering, there is no scope for reference to the Electrical Inspector in terms of Section 26(6) of the Act.
* The court further held that notice is required to be given only when there is a default in payment of the demand raised and not in cases of tampering.
ruling_text: The Commission dismissed the revision petition filed by the appellant, holding that the direction given by the District Forum was in order and action in terms of Section 26(6) of the Act was required to be taken. The court held that in cases of tampering, there is no scope for reference to the Electrical Inspector in terms of Section 26(6) of the Act and notice is required to be given only when there is a default in payment of the demand raised. The court upheld the direction given by the District Forum and dismissed the revision petition filed by the appellant.

query_text: The case involves two appeals, A.No.3515 of 1997 and A.No.3516 of 1997, challenging the judgment of the Gauhati High Court, Agartala Bench, in Civil Rule No.12 of 1997. The High Court directed the Land Acquisition Collector to consider petitions filed by respondent-landowners under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (the Act) on merits and in accordance with law, holding them to be within the period of limitation stipulated therefor. The main issue in the case is whether the period of limitation for filing a petition under Section 28-A of the Act should be calculated from the earliest or the latest award of the Reference Court. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, specifically Section 28-A, is the statute in question.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the period of limitation for filing a petition under Section 28-A of the Act should be calculated from the date of the latest award of the Reference Court and not the earliest.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the Gauhati High Court, Agartala Bench, and ruled that the period of limitation for filing a petition under Section 28-A of the Act should be calculated from the date of the latest award of the Reference Court. The Supreme Court's decision clarifies the period of limitation for filing a petition under Section 28-A of the Act and ensures that landowners are not denied their right to seek redetermination of compensation due to technicalities.

query_text: The case involves a dispute between a developer and property owners over a development agreement. The property owners claimed that the developer breached the agreement and sought relief under the Consumer Protection Act. The developer disputed the existence of a consumer relationship and argued that the dispute should be resolved through the civil court. The main issues in the case are whether there is a consumer relationship between the parties and whether the dispute is time-barred. The Consumer Protection Act, 1986
ratio: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) held that there is a consumer relationship between the parties and that the dispute is not time-barred. The NCDRC also upheld the directions given by the State Commission with respect to the Completion Certificate, Conveyance Deed, Electricity Connection, etc.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court refused to interfere with the view taken by the NCDRC and disposed of the case by granting liberty to the appellants to resort to the remedy of review before the National Commission. The case highlights the importance of consumer protection laws and the role of consumer forums in resolving consumer disputes. The Supreme Court's decision to uphold the NCDRC's order reaffirms the principle that consumer disputes should be resolved through consumer forums rather than civil courts. However, the Supreme Court also clarified that the legal representatives of the deceased developer are not liable to discharge the obligations which had to be carried out personally by the developer, as such obligations depend purely on the skills and expertise of the developer.

query_text: The case is about an employee of a company who was entitled to LTC (Leave Travel Concession) once in four years to visit any place in India. The company gave him an option to either avail of the facility or encash the LTC facility, subject to the limit of Railway fare of the entitled class up to maximum distance of 1700 k.ms, each way for the employee and entitled family members. The employee challenged the decision in court, arguing that the fixation of the date was arbitrary and discriminatory. The main issues in the case are whether the fixation of the date for the option to encash the LTC facility is arbitrary and discriminatory, and whether it violates the rights of the employees who retired before or after the specified date. The case is governed by the Indian Labor Laws and the specific LTC rules of the company.
ratio: The court held that the fixation of the date for the option to encash the LTC facility is not arbitrary or discriminatory, as it is a policy decision taken by the management and is uniformly applicable to all employees of that class. The court also held that the option to encash the LTC facility does not deprive the employees of their right to avail of the actual travel, and that it is only an exception to the normal policy of actual travel.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the employee's petition and upheld the decision of the company to give the employees the option to encash the LTC facility. The court's decision in this case reaffirms the principle that policy decisions taken by the management are valid and binding on the employees, as long as they are uniformly applicable and do not violate any statutory provisions. It also highlights the importance of considering the impact of policy decisions on all employees, and ensuring that they are fair and reasonable.

query_text: The appellant had entered into agreements with various companies for the distribution of different machineries and equipments within different territories of India. The companies, who are respondents in different appeals, have been manufacturing different types of machines and instruments, which under the terms of the agreements are to be distributed by the appellant as the Marketing Company. The appellant has been appointed as Buyer (Sole Importer) on the terms and conditions mentioned in different agreements. The issue is whether the agreements between the appellant and the respondents contain conditions which amount to restrictive trade practices under clauses (a) and (c) of Section 33(1) of the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969. The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969 (the Act)
ratio: The court held that the agreements between the appellant and the respondents contain conditions which amount to restrictive trade practices under clauses (a) and (c) of Section 33(1) of the Act. The court further held that the objectionable clauses of the registered agreements are prejudicial to the public interest.
ruling_text: The court directed the appellant to discontinue the restrictive trade practices as mentioned in the Notice of Enquiry, and not to repeat the same in future. It was also directed that the objectionable clauses, as mentioned in the Notices be deleted from the respective agreements, within four weeks of the receipt of the order. The court upheld the decision of the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Commission and directed the appellant to discontinue the restrictive trade practices and delete the objectionable clauses from the agreements. The court emphasized the importance of examining every aspect of the matter in the light of the provisions of Sections 37 and 38 of the Act before an order to cease and desist is passed by the Commission.

query_text: The appellant, a cotton yarn manufacturer, objected to the demand of excise duty in respect of the single yarn produced and cleared out of the factory in coils during the period August 1962 to November 1962. The objection was based on the government notification that exempted cotton yarn of certain counts if cleared out of the factory in hanks. Whether the coils of cotton yarn cleared out of the appellant's factory during the period from 17-8-1962 to 14-11-1962 are exempt from excise duty in view of the government notification that exempts cotton yarn of certain counts if cleared out of the factory in hanks. Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, Central Excise Rules 1944, and the Finance Act, 1961.
ratio: The court held that the word hank in the notification means a coil of cotton yarn and not a circular loop or coil of cotton yarn of a specific length. The court also held that the retrospective effect purported to be given to the explanation was beyond the powers of the rule-making authority.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and held that the appellant was entitled to the exemption granted under the notification. The court's interpretation of the word hank in the notification and its ruling on the retrospective effect of the explanation clarified the ambiguity in the notification and protected the appellant's right to the exemption.

query_text: The first respondent joined the service of the State Government in 1938. In 1961, the Government held an enquiry into her date of birth. She was then asked to show cause why certain date should not be taken as her date of birth. The report of the enquiry officer was not disclosed, and the first respondent was not given an opportunity to meet the evidence used against her. The Government refixed the date of birth of the first respondent and ordered that she be compulsorily retired. The issues in this case are whether the High Court in dealing with petition under Art.226 of the Constitution ought not to have proceeded to determine disputed questions of fact, and whether the order refixing the date of birth of the respondent was an administrative order and the High Court had no power to sit in appeal over the decision of the State authorities. The statute involved in this case is the Constitution of India, specifically Art.226.
ratio: The ratio of the decision is that under Art.226 of the Constitution, the High Court is not precluded from entering upon decision on questions of fact raised by the petition. The High Court may in appropriate cases decline to enter upon the enquiry and may refer the party claiming relief to suit. But the question is one of discretion and not of the jurisdiction of the Court. No interference with the exercise of the discretion of the High Court in the present case was called for.
ruling_text: The ruling by the present court is that the order refixing the date of birth of the first respondent was an administrative order and the High Court was right in setting aside the order of the State. The conclusion is that the State Government acted arbitrarily and without giving the first respondent a fair opportunity to meet the case before an adverse decision was taken. The High Court was right in setting aside the order of the State.

query_text: The case is about an employee of Lord Krishna Textile Mill who claims that sum of Rs.5712.61 p. is due to him from the mill, out of which sum of Rs.3722.20 p. had become due before the take over of management of the mill under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act. The issue is whether the low priority given to amounts due to employees relating to the pre-take-over management period in the Second Schedule of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act is unconstitutional. The Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974, Section 21 and the Second Schedule of the Act.
ratio: The court held that the classification of liabilities made in the schedule is in tune with Section 5 of the Act and any law for the acquisition of sick undertaking must ordinarily provide for the discharge of the liabilities and arrange priorities among the liabilities.
ruling_text: The court ruled that the low priority given to amounts due to employees relating to the pre-take-over management period in the Second Schedule of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act is not unconstitutional. The court upheld the constitutionality of the Second Schedule of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act and ruled that the low priority given to amounts due to employees relating to the pre-take-over management period is not unconstitutional.

query_text: The case is about a dispute over the inheritance of a leasehold property in Goa, India. The property was owned by a partnership firm, and the parents of the parties (appellant no.1 and respondent nos.3 herein) succeeded to the lease premises in terms of Deed of Partition dated 29.03.1976. The father Sadanand V. Marathe died on 12.05.1985, and the mother Niarmalabai S. Marathe died on 05.05.1998. After the demise of the parents, respondent no.1 brother of appellant no.1 filed Regular Inventory Proceedings No.11/2013/C dated 08.11.2013, seeking to administer the estate left by the deceased. The appellants herein objected to the exclusion of the lease premises from the list of assets in the inventory proceedings. The main issue in this case is whether a married daughter has the right to inherit a leasehold property in Goa, India. The other issue is whether the provisions of the Goa Rent Act, 1968, which govern the relationship between landlords and tenants, apply to the inheritance of a leasehold property. The Goa Succession, Special Notaries and Inventory Proceeding Act, 2012, the Goa Daman Diu Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1968, and the Portuguese Civil Code are the relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The High Court of Bombay at Goa held that the married daughter would not qualify as a tenant in terms of the Goa Rent Act and that the parties would be governed by the provisions of the Goa Rent Act only. However, the High Court erred in not considering the right of succession of the married daughter under the Inventory Proceeding Act, 2012.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal and held that the married daughter has the right to inherit the leasehold property. The Court further held that the provisions of the Goa Rent Act do not apply to the inheritance of a leasehold property. The Supreme Court of India has clarified the law regarding the inheritance of a leasehold property in Goa, India. The Court has held that a married daughter has the right to inherit the property and that the provisions of the Goa Rent Act do not apply to the inheritance of a leasehold property. This judgment will have far-reaching implications for the inheritance laws in Goa and will provide clarity to many similar cases.

query_text: The case is about a dispute between the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and the Parishioners of St. Marys Church, Kattachira. The Church and its properties were gifted to the Metropolitan of Quilon Diocese by K. Koshy through Ext.-A3-Sale-cum-Gift Deed. The Parishioners contend that they have the right to manage the Church and its properties and that the Metropolitan has no authority to appoint Vicars or Priests. The main issues in the case are whether the 1934 Constitution is applicable to the Parish Churches and whether the Metropolitan has the authority to appoint Vicars or Priests. The 1934 Constitution of the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church governs the affairs of the Parish Churches.
ratio: The Supreme Court in Thukalan Paula Avira37 and M.A.Metropolitan38 has held that the 1934 Constitution is applicable to the Parish Churches and that the Metropolitan has the authority to appoint Vicars or Priests. The Division Bench erred in holding that the Metropolitan had no authority to appoint Vicars or Priests.
ruling_text: The Single Judge was right in holding that the St. Marys Church is constituent of Malankara and the power to appoint Vicars, Priests etc.is vested with the first plaintiff-Malankara Metropolitan or his representatives. The Division Bench erred in holding that the Metropolitan had no authority to appoint Vicars or Priests. The 1934 Constitution is applicable to the Parish Churches and the Metropolitan has the authority to appoint Vicars or Priests. The St. Marys Church is constituent of Malankara and the power to appoint Vicars, Priests etc.is vested with the first plaintiff-Malankara Metropolitan or his representatives.

query_text: The petitioners, a private limited company and two individuals, challenged the constitutionality of the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956, and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960, which regulated the prices of newspapers in relation to their pages and sizes, and the allocation of space for advertising matter. The petitioners argued that the Act and the Order violated their right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution and were not saved by Article 19(2). The Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956, and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960.
ratio: The court held that the Act and the Order were void as they violated Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution and were not saved by Article 19(2). The freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) included the freedom of the press, and the impugned Act and Order placed restraints on the latter aspect of the right, which was directly interfering with the freedom of speech and expression.
ruling_text: The court declared the Act and the Order as void. The court upheld the petitioners' argument and declared the Act and the Order as void, as they violated the petitioners' right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution and were not saved by Article 19(2). The court also stated that the State could not make a law that directly restricted one freedom even for securing the better enjoyment of another freedom.

query_text: The appellants are three companies that owned sugar factories and appointed a selling agent, M s Gokul Nagar Sugar Mills Co. Ltd., to sell their sugar output. The Income-tax Officer allowed the deduction of commission paid to the selling agent in the original assessment for the years 1947-48, but later issued notices under S.34(1) (a) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the selling agent rendered no service and the commission was not allowable. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal upheld the Income-tax Officer's decision. Whether the selling agent rendered any service to earn the commission, whether the action taken under S.34(1) (a) was justified, and whether the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal erred in not referring certain questions to the High Court under S.66(1) of the Act. The Income-tax Act, 1922
ratio: The High Court held that the first three questions were questions of fact and declined to direct the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal to refer them. The High Court also held that the fourth question was a question of law and directed the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal to refer it.
ruling_text: The appeals are dismissed as there is no substance in them. The orders of the Income-tax Officer, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, and the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal have been considered, and it is found that all relevant material on record has been taken into account, and the findings recorded on facts against the appellants are reasonable. The Income-tax Appellate Tribunal has acted judicially and considered all the evidence in favour and against the appellants. The findings recorded by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal are based on the material on record and are reasonable. Therefore, the High Court's decision to decline to direct the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal to refer questions Nos.1 to 3 and to direct it to refer question No.4 is upheld.

query_text: The appellant and the respondent were both members of the East India Jute Hessian Exchange Ltd. and were bound by its rules and regulations. The appellant agreed to purchase and the respondent to sell bales of Pakistan raw jute for delivery during October and/or November 1960. Differences arose between the parties in respect of the execution of the contract. The main issue was whether the terms of the bought and sold notes in respect of payment and other matters tallied, and whether there was a concluded contract. The Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act of 1952, s. 11 and the bye-laws framed under it.
ratio: The term as to payment is an important term of a written contract. The bought and the sold notes have to be in writing and in the prescribed form. If there is any discrepancy between the two, prima facie, there is no concluded contract. The bye-laws of the Association make it obligatory that the contract shall be in writing and that it shall be in the form prescribed. Therefore, evidence may not be led to prove that the parties had agreed to certain terms not set out in the bought and sold notes.
ruling_text: The High Court decided in favour of the respondent, and the appellant by special leave came to this Court. The Court held that the term as to payment is an important term of a written contract, and that the bought and the sold notes have to be in writing and in the prescribed form. If there is any discrepancy between the two, prima facie, there is no concluded contract. The bye-laws of the Association make it obligatory that the contract shall be in writing and that it shall be in the form prescribed. Therefore, evidence may not be led to prove that the parties had agreed to certain terms not set out in the bought and sold notes. The Court held that there was no concluded contract between the parties due to the discrepancy in the terms of the bought and sold notes. The Court also held that the bye-laws of the Association make it obligatory that the contract shall be in writing and that it shall be in the form prescribed, and therefore, evidence may not be led to prove that the parties had agreed to certain terms not set out in the bought and sold notes.

query_text: The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of talcum powder. The assessee claimed the benefit of exemption notification issued by the Central Board of Revenue (CBR) in respect of soap-stone. The CBR issued a corrigendum to the notification clarifying that soap-stone is the same as talc. The Revenue rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that soap-stone is not covered by the notification. The assessee approached the High Court. Whether soap-stone is the same as talc and, therefore, entitled to the benefit of the concerned exemption notification. The Central Excise Act, 1944 and the Central Excise Rules, 2002.
ratio: The High Court relied upon the publication of the CBR to come to the conclusion that soap-stone is the same as talc and, therefore, entitled to the benefit of the concerned exemption notification.
ruling_text: The High Court ordered the refund of the excise duty paid by the assessee. The refund ordered by the High Court shall be made to the assessee under the provisions of the law as it now stands.

query_text: The case involves a former Union Finance Minister, P. Chidambaram, who is accused of money laundering in connection with the approval of foreign investment in a media company. The case is being investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED). The main issue in the case is whether the appellant, P. Chidambaram, should be granted regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) in the money laundering case being investigated by the ED. The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) and the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) are the relevant statutes in this case.
ratio: The court held that the appellant is entitled to be granted bail, taking into account the facts and circumstances of the case, including the duration of custody, the availability of the appellant for further investigation, interrogation and facing trial, and the absence of any possibility of tampering with evidence or influencing witnesses.
ruling_text: The court granted regular bail to the appellant, P. Chidambaram, subject to certain conditions. The court's decision to grant regular bail to the appellant, P. Chidambaram, is based on a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, and is in line with the principles of criminal justice. The court has emphasized the importance of ensuring the availability of the accused for further investigation, interrogation and facing trial, while also protecting their rights to liberty and a fair trial.

query_text: The case is about a consignment of bundles of mild steel plates despatched by a Japanese exporter to be delivered at the port of Bombay. The goods were discharged in the docks on 12th September 1959, into the custody of the Bombay Port Trust, the appellant. The plaintiffs, the consignee and the insurer, claimed for the missing bundle but were put off by the appellant with various excuses. The main issue is whether the suit is barred by limitation under section 87 of the Bombay Port Trust Act, 1879, which provides that no suit or other proceeding shall be commenced against any person for anything done or purporting to have been done in pursuance of this Act without one month's previous notice, and not after six months from the accrual of the cause of such suit or other proceeding. The Bombay Port Trust Act, 1879, imposes a duty on the Port Trust to deliver the goods to the consignee. The omission to do so amounts to an act done or intended to be done within the meaning of section 87.
ratio: The court held that the truncated limitation prescribed under the Act will apply and the starting point of limitation is the accrual of the cause of action, which is when the plaintiff came to know or ought to know with reasonable diligence that the goods had been landed from the vessel into the port. The court also held that letters or assurances that the missing packages are being searched for cannot enlarge limitation, once the goods have landed and the owner has come to know of it.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and held that the suit is barred by limitation. The court's decision is based on a strict interpretation of the statutory provision and the rules of limitation. The court emphasized the importance of giving notice and observing the time limit in bringing a suit against the Port Trust. The court also highlighted the need for the consignee to exercise reasonable diligence in ascertaining the whereabouts of the missing goods. The decision may have practical implications for the business community and the Port Trust in handling and delivering goods at the port.

query_text: The case is about the levy and collection of octroi under the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976. The issue is whether the fine contemplated by Section 116 can be imposed by an officer of the Municipal Corporation or only by a criminal court. The main issue is the interpretation of Section 116 of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976, which provides for the levy and collection of octroi and imposes a fine for evasion of octroi. The Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976, is the relevant statute in this case.
ratio: The court held that the fine contemplated by Section 116 can be imposed only by a criminal court and not by an officer of the Municipal Corporation.
ruling_text: The court agreed with the view taken by the Punjab and Haryana High Court that the punishment of fine provided by Section 116 can be imposed only by the criminal court and cannot be imposed by the officers of the Corporation. The court's decision clarifies the procedure for imposing fines under the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976, and ensures that the powers of the officers of the Municipal Corporation are limited to the assessment, collection, and recovery of octroi. The decision also reaffirms the importance of following the normal rule of legislative drafting, which is that wherever it says that a particular Act shall be punishable with fine, it contemplates its imposition by a criminal court only.

query_text: The case involves a money decree granted in O.S.No.226 of 1946 on the file of the Sub-Court, Coimbatore. The defendants in the suit filed an appeal in the Madras High Court in S.No.713 of 1947. During the pendency of the appeal, the defendants deposited the decretal amount in court, and the plaintiff was permitted to withdraw the amount after furnishing security to the satisfaction of the court. Ramaswami Gounder became the surety and gave his agricultural lands as security for the amount permitted to be withdrawn by the plaintiff. The appeal was allowed by the High Court on 31.10.1952, and the money decree was set aside. Consequently, the defendants moved an application for restitution under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) for recovery of the amount withdrawn by the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not repay the amount, and Ramaswami Gounder died. His widow, Rajammal, was impleaded as his legal representative and moved an application for setting aside the auction sale under Order Rule CPC. The issues in this case are whether the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938 (Act) are applicable to the recovery of the amount by way of restitution, secured by the properties of the surety, and whether the auction sale can be set aside under section 23A of the Act. The Tamil Nadu Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, provides for the scaling down of debts and rates of interest relief in regard to the usufructuary mortgages, concessions in regard to interest payable by agriculturists on loans, conditional discharge of arrears of rent due to landholders, and scaling down of interest on arrears of rent.
ratio: The court held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the recovery of the amount by way of restitution, secured by the properties of the surety. The court also held that the auction sale could not be set aside under section 23A of the Act as the appellants were not entitled to the benefits of the Act.
ruling_text: The High Court dismissed the appeal of Rajammal and confirmed the order of the Executing Court. The court also dismissed the application for scaling down the debt and setting aside the sale under the Act, referred to the Subordinate Court, Coimbatore, for disposal in accordance with law. The court has held that the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, are not applicable to the recovery of the amount by way of restitution, secured by the properties of the surety. The auction sale cannot be set aside under section 23A of the Act as the appellants are not entitled to the benefits of the Act. The court has confirmed the auction sales in favour of the auction-purchasers.

query_text: The case is about a suit for partition filed by Ram Saran Lal and his brother Babu Ram against Narendra Nath, s o Pandit Bhagwati Prasad. The plaintiffs claimed partition of properties left by their father Pandit Raman Lal and properties acquired by the joint family. The defendant contested the suit and asserted that after the death of Pandit Raman Lal, the three brothers separated and partitioned the properties left by him. The defendant claimed that all properties mentioned in schedule I and few mentioned in schedule II were acquired by Bhagwati Prasad in his own name. The main issue in the case is whether there was a joint family in existence and whether there was any property available for partition. The case is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
ratio: The Trial Court decreed the suit and directed partition of all the suit properties. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court dismissed the suit accepting his case in toto. The High Court held that the documents relied upon by the plaintiffs did not prove their case at all. The documents relied upon by the defendant clearly established his case and negated that of the plaintiffs.
ruling_text: We have heard learned Counsel for the parties who took us through the relevant documents in the case. The documentary evidence clearly establishes the case of the defendant and negatives that of the plaintiffs. We fully agree with the conclusion arrived at by the High Court on the basis of the said documents. The documents relied upon by the plaintiffs did not prove their case at all. The appeal is dismissed and the judgment of the High Court is upheld. The plaintiffs have failed to prove their case and the defendant has succeeded in establishing his case of separation and partition of the properties long ago.

query_text: The assessee entered into a contract for the forward sale of mustard at a fixed price. The purchaser attempted to cancel the contract before the due date, but the assessee refused to accept the cancellation. The assessee then sent a telegram to the purchaser stating that if the purchaser did not accept settlement of the contract at a lower price within four hours, the assessee would presume that the purchaser had accepted settlement at that rate. The purchaser never responded to the telegram, and the assessee proceeded on the basis that the purchase had been settled between the parties at the lower price. The assessee claimed the difference between the original contract price and the settlement price as income in its return for the relevant assessment year. The main issue in this case is whether the sum of Rs.94,253 or any part of it accrued or arose or could be deemed to accrue or arise, or was received or could be deemed to be received by the assessee as income, profits and gains during the previous year. The Income-tax Act, 1922
ratio: The Income-tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the pendency of the appeal and the dispute between the assessee and its purchaser did not prevent the income from having accrued. They held that what was relevant was whether the transaction had been settled or not and that the assessee not only did not deny that the transaction had been settled but in fact went to the court on the basis of such settlement.
ruling_text: The High Court of Punjab refused the appellants application under section 66(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, for an order directing the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal to refer the question to the High Court for its decision. The court held that the sum of Rs.94,253 or any part of it accrued or arose or could be deemed to accrue or arise, or was received or could be deemed to be received by the assessee as income, profits and gains during the previous year. The court based its decision on the fact that the transaction had been settled between the parties and that the assessee had gone to court on the basis of such settlement.

query_text: The case is about tenants who are being evicted from a building owned by a Trust. The tenants claim that they have been paying rent to the Trust and that the building is still owned by the Trust. The landlord, on the other hand, claims that the building was sold to him by a previous owner and that the tenants have been acknowledging him as their landlord. The main issues in this case are whether the building still belongs to the Trust, whether the tenants have been denying the landlord's title to the building, and whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to hear the eviction petition. ratio: The court held that the building still belongs to the Trust, that the tenants have been denying the landlord's title to the building, and that the Rent Controller did not have jurisdiction to hear the eviction petition.

query_text: The case involves a person belonging to the Jaintia Scheduled Tribe, who is a permanent resident of the United Khasi-Jaintia Hills Autonomous District, which is specified in Part A of the Table appended to paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution. The person is employed in the Secretariat of the Assam Government, and his place of work is within the Shillong Municipality, which is not part of the area described in paragraph 20 of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution. The issue is whether the income of the assessee from his salary arose in the non-scheduled area and is not covered by the tax exemption provided under s.10(26)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Income-tax Act, 1961 provides that a person is entitled to exemption from income-tax if (1) he is a member of Scheduled Tribe as defined inArt.366(25)ofthe Constitution, (2) he is residing in any area specified in Part or Part of the Table appended to paragraph of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, or the State orUnion- Territories mentioned in the section, and (3) theincome in respect of which exemption is claimed is incomewhich accrues or arises to him from any source in the area,State or Union Territories mentioned in the section.
ratio: The court held that the classification contemplated by s.10(26)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 is not artificial and is based on intelligible differentia. The object of this differentiation between income accruing or received from source in the specified areas and the income accruing or received from source outside such areas is to benefit not only the members of the Scheduled Tribes residing in the specified areas but also to benefit economically such areas.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeals of the Department and held that the High Court was in error in striking down s.10(26)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 as violative ofArticle 14of the Constitution. The court upheld the validity of s.10(26)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which provides tax exemption to members of Scheduled Tribes residing in specified areas, subject to the condition that the income in respect of which exemption is claimed is income which accrues or arises to him from any source in the area, State or Union Territories mentioned in the section.

ruling_text: The appeal is dismissed. query_text: The case is about a dispute over the inheritance of land between the appellant, who is the grandson of one of the brothers of the deceased, and the respondent, who is the daughter of another brother. The dispute arose when the mother of the respondent, who had inherited the land from her husband, died. The appellant claimed that he was the nearest heir to the property, while the respondent claimed that she was the sole legal heir. The main issue in this case is whether the appellant or the respondent is the rightful heir to the property. The court had to determine whether the mother of the respondent had inherited the property from her husband or if she had acquired an independent interest in the holding. The court relied on the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, specifically sections 172 and 174, to determine the mode of succession.
ratio: The court held that the mother of the respondent had inherited the property from her husband, and therefore, the appellant, being the son of her husband's brother, was the preferential heir. The court also held that the language used in sections 172 and 174 of the Abolition Act clearly brings forth the distinction between widow who has inherited an interest from her husband and widow who has acquired an independent interest in the holding.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court. The court held that the appellant was the rightful heir to the property and directed the authorities to mutate his name in the revenue records. The court's decision in this case highlights the importance of determining the origin of the title of the deceased in order to determine the mode of succession. The court relied on the provisions of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, to determine the rightful heir to the property. The court's decision also reaffirms the principle that the words inherited an interest in any holding used in section 172 of the Abolition Act are of the widest possible amplitude and include not only an absolute interest but also a limited interest, precarious interest, and an inchoate interest.

query_text: The case is about a person accused of unauthorized possession of arms and ammunition in a notified area under the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (TADA Act). The accused was found in possession of an AK-56 rifle, a 9mm pistol, and live cartridges. The issues before the court are the proper construction of Section 5 of the TADA Act, the nature of the right of an accused to be released on bail under Section 20(4)(bb) of the TADA Act, and the scope of sub-section (8) of Section 20 of the TADA Act. The TADA Act is a special law enacted to prevent and cope with terrorist and disruptive activities. It provides for the punishment of offences related to terrorist and disruptive activities and contains provisions for the investigation, trial, and punishment of such offences.
ratio: The court held that the prosecution is required to prove that the accused was in conscious possession, unauthorizedly, in a notified area of any arms and ammunition specified in the Arms Rules, 1962 or bombs, dynamite, or other explosive substances. The accused is entitled to prove the non-existence of facts constituting any of these ingredients as part of his defense. The court also clarified that the requirement of notice to the accused before granting extension beyond the prescribed period of days in accordance with the further proviso to clause (bb) of sub-section (4) of Section 20 of the TADA Act only requires production of the accused before the court and not written notice to the accused giving reasons therein.
ruling_text: The court answered the questions referred to it as follows: (1) The prosecution is required to prove that the accused was in conscious possession, unauthorizedly, in a notified area of any arms and ammunition specified in the Arms Rules, 1962 or bombs, dynamite, or other explosive substances. The accused is entitled to prove the non-existence of facts constituting any of these ingredients as part of his defense. (2) The indefeasible right of the accused to be released on bail in accordance with Section 20(4)(bb) of the TADA Act read with Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure in default of completion of the investigation and filing of the challan within the time allowed is a right which ensures to, and is enforceable by, the accused only from the time of default till the filing of the challan and it does not survive or remain enforceable on the challan being filed. (3) The meaning and scope of sub-section (8) of Section 20 of the TADA Act are indicated by the Constitution Bench in Kartar Singh and do not require any further elucidation by this court. The court clarified the meaning and scope of Section 5 of the TADA Act, the nature of the right of an accused to be released on bail under Section 20(4)(bb) of the TADA Act, and the scope of sub-section (8) of Section 20 of the TADA Act. The case is now remanded to the appropriate division bench for decision on the petitioners claim for grant of bail on merits.

query_text: The appellant was assessed in the status of Hindu joint family for the years 1949-50 and 1950-51. The validity of the rectification order passed under Section 35(5) of the Act was challenged in the writ petition on the grounds that the rectification was made after four years from the date of the final order under Section 33-A(2) and that the notice under Section 35(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was issued after the Income-tax Act, 1961 came into force. The Income-tax Act, 1922, and the Income-tax Act, 1961.
ratio: The High Court held that the rectification order made under Section 35 of the Act was not barred by limitation as the period of four years was to be computed from the date of the final order passed under Section 33-A(2) and not from the date of the order passed under Section 35(5) of the Act. The High Court further held that the notice under Section 35(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was not saved by the repealing Section 297 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and consequently, the proceedings under Section 35 of the old Act were void ab initio.
ruling_text: The High Court dismissed the writ petition, and the appellant appealed to this Court by certificate. The appeal was dismissed by this Court as the rectification order passed under Section 35(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was barred by limitation, and the notice under Section 35(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 was not saved by the repealing Section 297 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Therefore, the proceedings under Section 35 of the old Act were void ab initio.

query_text: The case is about a writ petition filed by the Distilleries and Chemical Mazdoor Union, Meerut against the State of P., the ESIC and the Company, namely, Central Distilleries and Breweries Limited (CSBL) merged with Shaw Wallace Distilleries Limited (SWDL) for seeking direction in the nature of mandamus not to realise any contribution from the workmen of respondent No.2-herein. ratio: The High Court was justified in passing the judicious order after considering the equities by directing the employer and the employees to make ESIC contribution for the future i.e.from the date of disposal of the writ petition and should not bear with the liability for the past inasmuch as the employees of the respondent No.2 has not availed any medical facilities from ESIC and at the same time the employer was providing the medical facilities due to interim order of the High Court.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the High Court and dismissed the appeal filed by the ESIC. The Supreme Court held that the view taken by the High Court was on account of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and that passing of the final order by the High Court directing the payment of ESI contribution from the date of the judgment does not amount to postponing the enforcement of notification and the same is also not in violation of the principles laid down by this Court in the various judgments referred to above. The order passed by the High Court, in our opinion, is perfectly justified in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and it has been repeatedly held by this Court that such relief can be granted in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and that there can be an exception as in the present case and, therefore, it cannot be said that the directions issued by the High Court are not correct or that they are contrary to the power under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The High Court, in our opinion, while disposing off the writ petition filed by the Union has taken just, pragmatic, fair and judicious view after considering all the equities and facts and circumstances of the case.

ratio: The ratio of the decision is that the annual letting value of the building or land or both to which the rent restriction legislation is applicable cannot exceed the annual standard or fair rent. query_text: The appellants are firms engaged in the export of Virginia tobacco. The Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, as amended by the Madras General Sales Tax and the Madras Tobacco (Taxation of Sales and Registration) (Andhra Amendment) Act (Andhra XIV of 1955), ss.5, 6.
ratio: The court held that the impugned Act did not infringe any constitutional provision. The court stated that the burden is on the person who assails legislation as discriminatory to establish that it is not based on valid classification, and that the statute is not open to attack on the mere ground that it taxes some persons or objects and not others. The court further stated that the Madras General Sales Tax (Andhra Amendment) Act, 1955, which taxed sales of Virginia Tobacco but exempted sales of Nattu or country tobacco could not be said to be discriminatory and was not obnoxious to Art, as Virginia tobacco has features which distinguish it from country tobacco and can be treated as a class in itself.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the petition and held that the impugned Act did not infringe any constitutional provision. The court held that the Act was not discriminatory and did not violate Art.14 or Art.286 (1)(b) of the Constitution. The court further stated that Virginia tobacco can be treated as a class in itself and the State has the power to impose tax on the sales of Virginia tobacco while exempting sales of country tobacco.
