query_text: The appellant, Shivaraj V. Patil, and his wife, Smt. Alka Bose, took out a mediclaim insurance policy from the respondent, United India Insurance Company, on December 14, 1990. In July 1991, Smt. Alka Bose fell ill and was admitted to the hospital. The appellant lodged a claim for Rs. 8,243/- with the insurance company, but it was not honored. The appellant approached the District Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, but the complaint was rejected. On appeal, the State Commission set aside the order of the District Forum and directed the insurance company to pay the appellant Rs. 8,243/-. The insurance company went in revision before the National Consumer Redressal Commission, which allowed the revision and set aside the order of the State Commission. The issues before the court were whether the insurance company was justified in refusing to renew the mediclaim policy of the appellant and whether the appellant was required to take a fresh mediclaim policy. ratio: The court held that the insurance company was not justified in refusing to renew the mediclaim policy of the appellant on the ground of his past conduct. ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court to the extent it directed the appellant to take a fresh mediclaim policy. The court set aside the order of the High Court to the extent it directed the appellant to take a fresh mediclaim policy.

query_text: The assessee is a sterling company maintaining accounts in pound sterling. The assessee had acquired certain assets prior to April 1, 1961, and the written down value of these assets had been correctly arrived at under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed depreciation under Section 32(1)(iii) and or development rebate and profit under Section 41(2) of the Act for the assessment years 1968-69 and 1969-70. The Income-tax Officer determined the written down value of the fixed assets not in pound sterling, but in equivalent amount of rupees. The assessee challenged this determination before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the written down value of the fixed assets should be determined not in pound sterling, but in equivalent amount of rupees. The issues before the court were whether the Tribunal was right in holding that for the purpose of computation of the admissible amounts of depreciation under Section 32(1)(iii) and or development rebate and profit under Section 41(2) of the Act for the assessment years 1968-69 and 1969-70, the written down value of the fixed assets should be determined not in pound sterling, but in equivalent amount of rupees. The Income-tax Act, 1961, with effect from the assessment year 1962-63, introduced the definition of actual cost.
ratio: The court held that assessment of total income in India will have to be in Indian rupees. The company may keep its accounts in foreign currency. But depreciation will have to be calculated in Indian currency at the point of time of acquisition of the asset. The subsequent fluctuations in the value of pound sterling are immaterial for this purpose.
ruling_text: The court upheld the decision of the Tribunal and held that the written down value of the fixed assets should be determined not in pound sterling, but in equivalent amount of rupees. The court's decision clarifies that while making assessment in India, the rupee value of the capital asset has to be taken into account for calculating its actual cost at the time of acquisition of the asset. The court also reiterated that the date up to which interest under Section 234A will be paid is the date of the regular assessment, i.e., the date of the first order of assessment under Section 143. The quantum of interest, however, may be varied as a result of subsequent orders modifying the assessment pursuant to the direction of any higher authority.

query_text: The appellant transferred a certain amount from its Consolidated Revenue Account to the Investment Reserve Fund which it was entitled to do. By this transfer the appellants surplus on which tax has to be assessed was reduced. The Income-tax Officer directed the appellant to reduce the transfer by certain amount. Whether the Income-tax Officer had the power to direct the appellant to reduce the transfer by certain amount. The Income Tax Act, 1922, s. 10(7) and Schedule rr.2(b) and 3(b)
ratio: The assessment of the profits of an insurance business is by s.10(7) of the Act completely governed by the rules in the Schedule to the Act and there is no general power in the Income-tax Officer to correct any error apart from these rules. Of these rules, rr.2(b) and 3(b) were relevant to the present case. Under r. 2(b) of the Schedule the Income-tax Officer had no power to change the figures in the account of the assessee while r. 3(b) only compelled the Income-tax Officer to allow certain deductions and to include certain amounts in making the assessment. None of these rules warranted the adjustment of accounts made by the Income-tax Officer.
ruling_text: The appeals are allowed and the judgment of the High Court is set aside. The Income-tax Officer had no power to direct the appellant to reduce the transfer by certain amount as the assessment of the profits of an insurance business is by s.10(7) of the Act completely governed by the rules in the Schedule to the Act and there is no general power in the Income-tax Officer to correct any error apart from these rules. Of these rules, rr.2(b) and 3(b) were relevant to the present case and neither of these rules warranted the adjustment of accounts made by the Income-tax Officer.

query_text: The appellants were tried for offences under ss.302, 323 read with s.34, P.C., as also under ss.218 and 302, P.C., on allegations that they had taken one Balwant Singh into custody, tortured him to death and thereafter created false evidence with view to escape from legal punishment in connection with the murder of Balwant Singh. The issue before the court was whether the prosecution discharged the onus of proving convincingly that the appellants were involved in the assault on Balwant Singh that led to his death. The Indian Penal Code, 1860
ratio: The court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the offences charged beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence led by the prosecution was not reliable, and the pleas of alibi raised by the appellants were accepted.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court. query_text: The assessee is a private limited company that acts as managing agents of various companies. During the assessment year 1957-58, the assessee sold shares of three companies resulting in a net profit of Rs. 1,26,027/-. The assessee claimed that the profit was capital gain, but the Income-tax Officer held that it was taxable as the assessee was entitled under its Memorandum of Association to deal in shares. Whether the profit of Rs. 1,26,027/-arose to the assessee in the course of its business as dealer in shares and as such was liable to be assessed as revenue profit? The Income-tax Act 1922
ratio: The High Court upheld the majority view of the Tribunal that the assessee was dealer in shares which were confined to the shares of the managed companies. However, it proceeded to consider the question from an entirely new angle and held that the profit did not arise to the assessee in the course of its business as dealer in shares.
ruling_text: The appeal by special leave from judgment of the Calcutta High Court in an Income-tax Reference is dismissed. The High Court went beyond the matters which were the subject matter of controversy before the departmental authorities and the Appellate Tribunal. It was never the case of the assessee that although it was dealer in shares those shares which were the subject matter of sale were held by way of investment. The assessee made no attempt to make out a case that the shares which had been sold were part of its capital investment. The matter is essentially one of fact and it was not open to the High Court to give its finding on that question. The appeal is dismissed.

query_text: The appellant was employed in the Uttar Pradesh State Handloom Corporation, a public sector undertaking, on temporary basis. The Uttar Pradesh State Handloom Corporation Rules
ratio: The court held that the termination of the appellant's services was not punitive in character and that the principles of natural justice were not required to be followed before terminating his services as he was a temporary employee.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal, stating that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and that the order of termination was not open to challenge. The court ruled in favor of the Corporation, stating that the termination of the appellant's services was not punitive in character and that the principles of natural justice were not required to be followed before terminating his services. The appellant was not entitled to compensation under the law, but the Corporation was directed to pay him a consolidated amount of Rs. 25,000 as he had been put out of employment at an advanced age and it may be difficult for him to get an alternate employment.

query_text: The case is about a tenant who is challenging an eviction order passed by the High Court in favor of the landlord. ratio: The court held that the landlord has a bona fide requirement to demolish and reconstruct the building under Section 14(1)(b) of the Act. The court also noted that the landlord had obtained necessary permissions and had sufficient financial resources to construct a new building.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the eviction order passed by the High Court. The court's decision is in favor of the landlord, and the tenant's appeal has been dismissed. query_text: The appellant was charged under Section 302, Indian Penal Code for shooting dead a person with his licensed gun. The appellant surrendered the gun to the police after the incident. At the trial, the appellant pleaded self-defence. The Sessions Judge accepted the plea and held that the appellant was entitled to the protection of Section 96, Penal Code and had therefore committed no offence. However, the Sessions Judge ordered confiscation of the licensed gun to the Government. Whether the impugned order of confiscation of the gun was legal and justified. Section 517 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and Section 96, Penal Code.
ratio: The Court held that the impugned order of confiscation of the gun was arbitrary and unjust. The Court observed that the Sessions Judge did not give any reason for directing confiscation of the licensed gun and there was no material before him indicating the special circumstances which would warrant departure from the general rule. The Court further observed that there was nothing on the record to show that the Sessions Judge had given an opportunity of being heard to the accused specifically with regard to this matter. The Court also observed that there was absolutely no material before the High Court to show that in the past twenty years during which the appellant had been in lawful possession of this gun under a license, he had ever used or attempted to use this gun for commission of any offence.
ruling_text: The Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order of confiscation of the gun. The Court held that the impugned order of confiscation of the gun was arbitrary and unjust. The Court observed that the Sessions Judge did not give any reason for directing confiscation of the licensed gun and there was no material before him indicating the special circumstances which would warrant departure from the general rule. The Court further observed that there was nothing on the record to show that the Sessions Judge had given an opportunity of being heard to the accused specifically with regard to this matter. The Court also observed that there was absolutely no material before the High Court to show that in the past twenty years during which the appellant had been in lawful possession of this gun under a license, he had ever used or attempted to use this gun for commission of any offence. The Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order of confiscation of the gun.

query_text: The plaintiff and the defendant both claim to be owning two adjoining pieces of land.There is dispute as to the exact dimensions and shapes (triangular or rectangular) of the pieces of land claimed to be owned and possessed respectively by the two parties.The real dispute, it seems, is about the demarcation of the boundaries of the two pieces of land.However, the fact remains, and that is relevant for our purpose, that the piece of land which forms the subject-matter of the suit is in the possession of the plaintiff-respondent.The plaintiff was raising construction over the piece of land in his possession, and that was obstructed by the defendant claiming that the land formed part of his property and was owned by him. The issues in the case are whether the plaintiff has proved his title over the suit property and whether the defendant has succeeded in proving his title over the suit property. The case is decided under Indian law.
ratio: The court held that even if the plaintiff has failed in proving his title, he has succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property which he is entitled to protect unless dispossessed therefrom by due process of law.The court also held that the defendant has failed in proving his title over the suit property.
ruling_text: The court upheld the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, restraining the defendant from interfering with the possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property by the respondent. The court has protected the established possession of the plaintiff and restrained the attempted interference therewith.The defendant has the option to file a suit based on his title against the plaintiff and evict the latter on the former establishing his better right to possess the property.

query_text: The case is about a murder of a man named Hazi Mohd.Yakub by four accused persons. The accused had planned to rob the deceased and if necessary, to kill him. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, Sections 302, 304 Part I, 34, 120-B(1), 212, and 411.
ratio: The court held that the accused are guilty of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, and not culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I. The court also held that the conviction should be under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
ruling_text: The court upheld the conviction of the accused for murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The court found the accused guilty of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and upheld their conviction. query_text: The appellants are owners of property known as Bharat Bhuvan Theatre at Ahmedabad. The respondents are the lessees of the said theatre. query_text: The case is about a tenant who was ordered to be evicted from a shop by a trial court. The tenant appealed the decision and during the pendency of the appeal, the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 was enforced. The tenant deposited the amount required by the Act within one month, but did not include the costs of the suit. The landlord argued that the tenant was not entitled to the benefit of the Act because the costs of the suit had not been deposited. The main issue in this case is whether the non-deposit of costs of the suit can deprive the tenant of the benefit of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 is the statute in question. Specifically, Sections 39 and 40 are relevant to this case.
ratio: The court held that the costs of the suit had to be deposited notwithstanding the fact that the trial court had directed the parties to bear their own costs. The court further held that the words "landlord's full costs of suit" in Section 39 of the Act really meant all those taxable costs which were capable of being ascertained on the date of the deposit.
ruling_text: The court allowed the appeal and held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Section 39 read with Section 40 of the Act and to be absolved from his liability to be evicted from the shop in question. The court's decision in this case highlights the importance of depositing the costs of the suit in order to benefit from the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The court clarified that the costs of the suit are not the same thing as the costs awarded to the plaintiff in a suit, but rather all those taxable costs which are capable of being ascertained on the date of the deposit. The court also emphasized that the word "landlord" in Section 39 of the Act was used purposely to distinguish it from the plaintiff of the suit.

ruling_text: The court set aside the impugned judgment and remanded the case back to the Board to determine the application filed by the first respondent in light of the legal principles explained in the judgment. query_text: The respondent Radha Krishna Moorthy was working as the Additional Regional Transport Officer, Madras (Central) during the period 20-6-1984 to 20-3-1985. The Tamil Nadu Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules.
ratio: The court held that the charges communicated to the respondent are vague and quashed the charges on that ground. The court also held that initiation of enquiry by an officer subordinate to the appointing authority is unobjectionable and that it is not a permissible ground for quashing the charges by the Tribunal.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decision of the Tribunal to quash the charges on the ground that they are vague. The court has ruled that the charges communicated to the respondent are vague and quashed the charges on that ground. query_text: The case involves a borrower who took a loan from Bank of Baroda and failed to repay it. The bank initiated proceedings under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act) and took possession of the borrower's residential property. The borrower challenged the auction of the property and filed a Securitisation Application (SA) under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). The DRT passed an interim order directing the bank to release the property and handover the possession along with the original title deeds on payment of Rs.48.65 lakhs. The bank challenged the order before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) and the DRAT dismissed the appeal. The bank then challenged the order before the High Court, which set aside the orders of the DRT and DRAT and directed the bank to release the property on payment of Rs.65.65 lakhs. The main issue in the case is whether the High Court was justified in directing the bank to release the secured property and handover the possession along with the original title deeds to the borrower on payment of total sum of Rs.65.65 lakhs only. The case is governed by the SARFAESI Act, 2002.
ratio: The High Court erred in directing the release of the secured property and handover of the possession along with the original title deeds to the borrower on payment of total sum of Rs.65.65 lakhs only, as the borrower had not deposited the entire amount due and payable along with the costs incurred by the secured creditor as per Section 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court. The Court held that the borrower cannot be discharged from the entire liability outstanding against him on payment of Rs.65.65 lakhs only. The Court further held that the bank cannot be restrained from selling the mortgaged property secured property and realizing the amount by selling it in public auction, unless the borrower deposits the entire amount due and payable together with all costs, charges and expenses incurred by the secured creditor. The Supreme Court has clarified that the borrower cannot be discharged from the entire liability outstanding against him on payment of a part of the amount due and payable. The bank has the right to sell the mortgaged property and realize the amount by selling it in public auction, unless the borrower deposits the entire amount due and payable together with all costs, charges and expenses incurred by the secured creditor.

query_text: The appellant is engaged in the manufacture and sale of products like cast-iron pipes, manhole covers, bends etc. For the assessment year 1989-90, the Commercial Tax Officer, Narayanguda Circle, Hyderabad levied sales tax upon the turnover relating to said products treating them as general goods. The Third Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act pertains to declared goods in respect of which single-point tax only is leviable under Section 6.
ratio: The court held that the cast iron castings manufactured by the appellants do not fall within the expression cast iron in Entry 2(i) of the Third Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act or within Section 14(iv)(i) of the Central Sales Tax Act.
ruling_text: The court dismissed the writ petition following its earlier decision in Deccan Engineers v. State of A.P. The court's decision was based on the interpretation of the expression cast iron in the statute and held that it does not include cast-iron pipes, manhole covers and bends etc. The appellant's products are, therefore, liable to tax at the general rate and not at the rate of 4.

query_text: The case is about a company that generates power and deals with purchase and distribution of power. The company generated power from its power unit located at Dahanu. The Income Tax Act, 1961
ratio: The court held that the deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 should be allowed to the extent of gross total income and not restricted to business income only.
ruling_text: The court upheld the decision of the Appellate Authority and the Tribunal on the issue of deduction under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961. query_text: The appellant, plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale, filed the suit against the sole defendant. During the pendency of the suit, the defendant died, but the appellant did not bring this to the court's notice. The trial court passed an ex parte decree for specific performance of the contract. The respondents, heirs and legal representatives of the defendant, filed an application for causing abatement of the suit after the judgment was pronounced. The main issue in this case is the interpretation of Order XXII Rule 44 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The question is whether the ex parte decree passed in favour of the plaintiff appellant becomes nullity if the civil court passes the decree in ignorance of the defendant's death and thereafter, even if there is any exemption obtained under Order XXII Rule Sub-Rule of the CPC to bring the heirs and legal representatives of the sole defendant on record. Order XXII Rule 44 of the CPC deals with the procedure where one of several defendants dies and the right to sue does not survive against the surviving defendant or defendants alone, or sole defendant or sole surviving defendant dies and the right to sue survives.
ratio: The High Court held that once the defendant had died and the civil court passed decree in ignorance of the same, and thereafter without there being any exemption obtained by the plaintiff appellant under Order XXII Rule to bring the heirs and legal representatives of the defendant on record before the judgment was pronounced, the ex parte decree so passed in favour of the plaintiff appellant became nullity.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and held that the ex parte decree passed in favour of the plaintiff appellant became nullity as the civil court passed the decree in ignorance of the defendant's death and thereafter, even if there was any exemption obtained under Order XXII Rule Sub-Rule of the CPC to bring the heirs and legal representatives of the sole defendant on record before the judgment was pronounced. The Supreme Court's decision in this case reaffirms the principle that the court must apply its mind and think it fit, in the facts and circumstances of the case, to grant exemption to the plaintiff from bringing on record the legal representatives of the defendant. The court must pass an order exempting the plaintiff from the necessity of bringing on record the legal representatives before judgment in the case is pronounced. If no such order is passed, the ex parte decree so passed in favour of the plaintiff appellant would become nullity.

query_text: The petitioners were detained under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971, for unauthorized milling of paddy and smuggling the resultant rice to Meghalaya for earning undue profit. The petitioners sent representations to the State Government raising various grounds against the validity of the detention orders. The issues before the court were whether the grounds of detention were vague, whether there was inordinate delay in disposing of the representations of the petitioners, and whether the detaining authorities had applied their minds to the facts of the cases. The Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971, empowers the State Government to detain any person if it is satisfied that such person is acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community.
ratio: The court held that the first ground of detention was vague, and the detention orders were vitiated. The court further held that the requirement of Article 22(5) of the Constitution would not be satisfied unless the detenu is given the earliest opportunity to make representation against the detention order, and no opportunity to make the representation can be effective unless the detenu is furnished with adequate particulars of the grounds of detention.
ruling_text: The court ruled that the petitioners were entitled to be released from custody as the detention orders were vitiated due to the vague grounds of detention. The court's decision highlights the importance of providing adequate particulars of the grounds of detention to enable the detenu to make an effective representation. The court also emphasized that the requirement of Article 22(5) of the Constitution must be strictly adhered to, and any violation of this provision would vitiate the detention orders.

query_text: The assessee, M s Kone Elevators (India) Ltd., is a unit of M s Kone Corporation, Finland, who are pioneers in the manufacture of Hi-tech New Generation Elevators. The assessee is registered dealer under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (hereinafter referred to as the 1957 Act) and is engaged in the manufacture, supply, installation, and commissioning of elevators and lifts. The assessee filed monthly returns in form A-2 for the months of April and May, 1995, and was assessed by the Commercial Tax Officer, P. Road Circle, Secunderabad, under the 1957 Act. The assessee claimed deductions of labor charges for composition of tax under section 5G of the said Act, stating that the nature of the work undertaken by it constituted works-contract. However, the assessing authority did not allow the deduction sought for and passed the provisional assessment orders, treating the disputed turnover as falling under Entry of the First Schedule to the said Act. The main issue involved in this civil appeal filed by the department is whether contracts entered into and executed by the assessee were contracts for sale or works-contract. The 1957 Act and the Indian Standards Institutions specifications and code of practice for installation of lifts and elevators.
ratio: The High Court held that the installation of the lift involved skill and technical know-how, which was to be treated as works-contract. However, the Andhra Pradesh Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Hyderabad, held that the disputed turnover related to the manufacture, supply, fabrication, and erection involved in the works-contract and that the said transaction did not amount to contract of sale.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the department and upheld the decision of the Tribunal. The Supreme Court held that the transaction in question was contract of sale and not works-contract. The assessee satisfied the twin requirements to attract the charge of tax under the 1957 Act, namely, that it carried on business of selling the lifts and elevators and it had sold the lifts and elevators during the relevant period in the course of its business. The major component of the end-product was the material consumed in producing the lift to be delivered, and the skill and labor employed for converting the main components into the end-product was only incidentally used. Therefore, the delivery of the end-product by the assessee to the customer constituted sale and not works-contract.

query_text: The plaintiff, a cigarette manufacturing company, entered into various contracts with the defendant, the Union of India, for the supply of cigarettes. The contracts were subject to the terms and conditions in Schedules, including Clause 7 of Schedule relating to Price. The plaintiff believed that no sales tax was leviable on the cigarettes supplied to the defendant as they were dispatched outside the State. However, the Commercial Tax Officer taxed all the sales and levied a total tax of Rs.1,14,960.36 Ps. for the four assessment years 1954-55 to 1957-58. The plaintiff took the matter on appeals but they were all rejected. The plaintiff demanded reimbursement by the Central Government to the extent of the amount of sales-tax actually paid. On rejection of this demand, the plaintiff instituted a suit for the recovery of Rupees 1,14,960.36. The issues in the case were whether the plaintiff company is entitled to claim the amount of sales tax from the defendant when it has not mentioned the same in the tenders, and whether the plaintiff is entitled to the reimbursement of sales tax from the defendant. The case involved the interpretation of Article 286(1) of the Constitution of India, which provides that no sales tax is payable on supplies procured on Central Government account and dispatched outside the State of origin.
ratio: The trial court held that the plaintiff was entitled to assume that no sales-tax was leviable on the goods despatched outside the State. The High Court, on appeal, held that Clause merely contained an opinion on point of law and that the plaintiff could have found out with reasonable diligence whether or not sales-tax was leviable on the sales in question.
ruling_text: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court. The Court held that the Note to Clause in Schedule was a representation on question of fact or at any rate on mixed question of fact and law, and that the plaintiff was entitled to assume that no sales-tax was leviable on the goods despatched outside the State. The Court also held that the plaintiff was entitled to the reimbursement of sales tax from the defendant. The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff was entitled to the reimbursement of sales tax from the defendant. The Court interpreted Article 286(1) of the Constitution of India to mean that no sales tax is payable on supplies procured on Central Government account and dispatched outside the State of origin. The Court also held that the plaintiff was entitled to assume that no sales-tax was leviable on the goods despatched outside the State, and that the defendant was under a fundamental obligation to pay the sales-tax if leviable. The judgment clarifies the legal position on the liability of the Central Government to pay sales tax on supplies procured for the defence services.
